wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Two physicians ruined by losing their recipe books
s: Galen knew two physicians who lost their written recipes: one wasted away from grief and died, the other gave up medical practice.
q: for the one, wasted away by grief at the loss of such writings, died, while the other withdrew from medical practice.
n: Galen's stated reason for teaching a method of compounding rather than a list. Compare his De indolentia on losses in the fire.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Galen's own injury in the palaestra at age 34
s: Galen tore away his own acromion (acromioclavicular separation) while wrestling in his thirty-fifth year. He adds that he could not cure any other grown man the same way, because none could bear the bandaging.
q: for it befell me to suffer thus in the wrestling-school when I was in my thirty-fifth year
n: Greek: ἔτος ἄγοντι ε΄ καὶ λ΄ (in his 35th year, i.e. aged 34; outside knowledge: c. AD 163, in Rome).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Empirical writers generalize from one or two observations
s: Galen charges the appendix author with writing down a 'syndrome of empirical signs' from one or two cases as if it were universal. A trained physician sees such lists as varied but useless.
q: derived from things seen once or twice, they carry a pronouncement of universal character

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Lost first edition: no friend in Rome had copies
s: All of Galen's books in that storehouse perished, and none of his friends in Rome admitted to having copies of the first two books, so companions pressed him to write the treatise again.
q: none of my friends in [363] Rome acknowledged having copies of the first two. Since, then, my companions pressed me to write the same treatise again
n: Explains why the extant De compositione medicamentorum per genera is a second redaction.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Schoolboy stabbed with a stylus died of spasm on day seven
s: The best Empiricist of Galen's day, who had read all the anatomists, treated a schoolchild stabbed in the inner upper arm with a stylus; the child seemed well but died in convulsions on the seventh day.
q: when a child at school had once made a stab with a stylus into the inner region of the upper arm, above its middle parts, applied one of the plaster drugs
n: Galen then explained the error (K13.605-606): a narrow puncture over a nerve needs a fine, heating drug and an open mouth.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Rich man's slave cured cheaply: 'keep this for beggars'
s: The rich man failed to treat his slave's malignant ulcer, sent him to Galen, then asked for the recipe; hearing all the ingredients were cheap, he said to keep it for beggars and teach him a costly one.
q: 'this,' he said, 'keep for beggars; but teach me one of the more costly ones.'
n: The draft has a garbled phrase ('not even (μὴ γοῦν μήτε) when the one who applied it...') just before; the Greek may be corrupt there.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Rich patron had free men and slaves find nerve-wounded test patients
s: After getting Galen's costly recipes, the rich man ordered his free men and slaves to find people with nerve wounds to try them; the drugs worked and he honoured Galen with gifts.
q: ordered both his freemen and his slaves to seek out for him persons with wounded nerves.
n: Greek ἐλευθέροις means free men (the draft's 'freemen'), not freedmen. Testing on recruited patients is a striking social detail.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Bold physician's cantharides trials: two dropsical patients died
s: A daring physician followed the cantharides recipe. His patient formed an abscess in the calf that he incised, water poured out, and the man died some days later. Told to give heads, feet and wings instead, he did so for another patient, who died the same way.
q: A certain bold physician, having read this passage, removed the aforesaid parts of the cantharides and gave them to a dropsical patient
n: Galen adds that some have used a diuretic drug made from cantharides without harm.

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Poisoner discovers blood-drawing herb via a pig's liver; executed blindfold
s: Under torture the poisoner said he saw bloody ichor flow from a pig's liver set on a plant, tested it on a passer-by, and used it for murder; the governor had him led to execution blindfolded so he could not point out the abundant plant.
q: ordered him to be led away to be put to death with his eyes bound, so that he might not show it to anyone on the way.
n: 'Governor of the people' renders ὁ τοῦ ἔθνους ἡγούμενος, i.e. the provincial governor.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Test a new euphorbium plaster on your own shin or forearm
s: If unsure of the euphorbium's strength, spread a little of the plaster on linen and apply it to your own shin or forearm for some hours, then weaken it with cerate or strengthen it with euphorbium.
q: spread a little of what has been prepared on a linen cloth and apply it to your own shin or forearm for some hours
n: A rare explicit self-test of drug strength.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Deep sutures for a transverse thigh wound in a gladiator 'horseman'
s: For a gladiator of the 'horsemen' class with a deep transverse wound above the kneecap, Galen dropped the usual treatment and sutured the muscles deep, after freeing the tendons; his teachers sewed only skin or the muscle surface.
q: I ventured, departing from the treatment named 'according to breadth' (kata platos), to bring together with sutures the separated parts of the muscles toward one another.
n: Hippeis (mounted gladiators) is a known gladiator class.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Forty days of tight bandaging closed a three-finger gap
s: Galen bore forcing bandages for forty days, feeling the clavicle throb as it bent. It came back so close to the humerus that people now doubt it was ever torn away, though the gap had been three fingers wide. The arm wasted and then recovered.
q: I endured this for up to forty days, during which the clavicle was brought so close to the head of the humerus that those who see it now disbelieve that it was ever torn away
n: Galen explains that young, porous bones bend like green wood. The upper arm and forearm atrophied and recovered after the bandages came off.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: First version of this treatise burned in the Temple of Peace fire
s: Galen says his earlier version of the work, two books already published, was stored in a warehouse on the Sacred Way and destroyed when the precinct of Peace and the great Palatine libraries burned.
q: left behind in the storehouse on the Sacred Way together with the others, when the whole precinct of Peace was burned, and the great libraries on the Palatine as well.
n: Outside knowledge: this is the fire of AD 192, also described in Galen's De indolentia. 'Storehouse' renders ἀποθήκῃ.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Five successive high priests renewed Galen's gladiator post
s: No gladiator died under Galen, whereas many had died in earlier years; the next high priest reappointed him after seven months (one took office at the autumn equinox, the next in high spring), and so did the third, fourth and fifth.
q: the second high priest after the one who had then entrusted the treatment to me likewise himself entrusted to me the care of the gladiators, after an interval of seven months.
n: The seasons give the timing of the priestly terms. Outside knowledge: this is a main source for Galen's Pergamene gladiator years.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Physicians in the German war dissected barbarian corpses to no purpose
s: Galen says the physicians in the German war, though allowed to dissect barbarians' bodies, learned no more than cooks know, because they lacked practice on apes.
q: just as the physicians in the German war, although they had license to dissect the bodies of barbarians, did not learn anything more than what cooks know.
n: Outside knowledge: the Marcomannic wars of Marcus Aurelius. A rare report of dissection of human enemy corpses.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Demosthenes of Massalia publishes his anthrax remedy during an outbreak
s: The Massaliote (named Demosthenes in the next unit) made his remedy public for the city because anthrakes were rife and killing many. It is kept in a Cyprian bronze vessel and pressed on with a probe until the anthrax turns black.
q: The remedy of the Massaliote. He set this forth publicly for the city in view of its power, because anthrakes were prevalent and were carrying off many.
n: An epidemic and a public health act in Massalia; no date is given. The ingredients are chrysocolla, roasted nitron, Asian stone, arsenic, sandarach, misy, chalcitis, alum and diphryges.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Hippocrates' towns smaller than one Roman street-block
s: The cities where Hippocrates spent most of his time had no more inhabitants than one street-block of Rome, which explains why Galen saw more rare dislocations.
q: The cities, however, which Hippocrates mentioned as having spent the greater part of his time in did not have more inhabitants than a single street-block of those in Rome.
n: ἄμφοδον: a city block or district.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Cretan henbane and mandrake juice shipped to Rome yearly
s: Henbane juice put up in summer is brought to Rome from Crete every year, and the finest mandrake juice also comes from Crete in earthenware cups.
q: Know that this too is brought from Crete, of the finest quality, in earthenware cups.
n: Galen elsewhere describes the Cretan herb trade for the imperial court (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Drug adulteration by root-cutters, merchants and pedlars
s: Galen has the finest drugs sent to him yearly from each nation because petty-ware sellers corrupt them; worse are the merchants who carry them, and worst the root-cutters bringing roots, juices, fruits and flowers down from the mountains.
q: For you know how the finest drugs are conveyed to me from each of the nations every year, because the wretched sellers of petty wares (ῥωποπῶλαι) corrupt them in every possible way.
n: A key passage on the ancient drug supply chain.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Fraud: 'old oil' faked with pig's fat and common oil
s: Small-ware dealers fake old oil by melting old pig's fat, stripped of its fibres, into common oil, which makes it thick and foul-smelling. The fake is uneven, thicker at the bottom, so sellers stir it before handing it over.
q: they melt old pig's fat, once they have thoroughly stripped it of its fibres, and mix it with common oil.
n: Galen also notes that genuine 'old' oil can be 3 or 30 years old, with very different strength.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen weighed the Roman oil litra: 12 measure-ounces = 10 weight-ounces
s: In Rome Galen weighed the oil litra, which is measured with graduated horns, on a balance and found that 12 measure-ounces of oil weigh 10 weight-ounces. He urges physicians to say whether they mean measure or weight.
q: I, at any rate, in Rome once weighed the so-called litra of oil, which they measure by means of the graduated horns
n: Direct metrological experiment by Galen. He adds that he gave the weights of liquids in another treatise (perhaps the lost or spurious De ponderibus; outside knowledge).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Sykota: fig-fattened livers
s: To show that the viscera delight in sweet things, Galen points to the so-called sykota: livers that grow very large and delicious when the animal is fed dried figs.
q: the so-called sykota (fig-fed livers) are seen, through the eating of dried figs, to become very large and most delicious
n: This is the ancient forerunner of foie gras (iecur ficatum).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen refuses to test an untried drug on rabies patients
s: Galen never tried Heras's plaster on rabid-dog bites, because he had a reliable crab remedy; abandoning sure cures in so dangerous a disease for an experiment seemed terrible and unjust.
q: to abandon the reliable remedies in so dangerous an affection and to betray the safety of the bitten person for the sake of an officious experiment seemed to me terrible and unjust.
n: An explicit ethical limit on human experimentation. The crab remedy is described in other Galenic works (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen came to value Hippocrates's 'help, or do no harm'
s: Galen at first thought the maxim to help or not harm unworthy of Hippocrates, but changed his mind after seeing physicians admired for a drug later laughed at when it failed on other patients.
q: a thing which I at first disdained, so as to think it not even worthy of Hippocrates when he exhorts us to do everything in the art in such a way as to help, or not to harm.
n: Epidemics I.11; a rare personal comment on the maxim.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Dissect apes often; book learning makes 'helmsmen from a book'
s: Galen insists anatomy must be learned by repeated dissection of apes; reading anatomical treatises is like the proverbial 'helmsmen from a book', and Empiricist chance-anatomy is nonsense.
q: And still more nonsensical than this is learning through the anatomical treatises, which resembles those called, according to the proverb, 'helmsmen from a book'.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Damocrates: young physicians hide behind elaborate cataplasms
s: For wounds with spreading inflammation, Damocrates warns against variegated cataplasms. Young physicians use them so as to give slanderers no grounds for accusation, but a confident practitioner should share the patient's fears instead of waiting on fortune.
q: For it is the custom of the young to do this, so that, having escaped the peaks of the inflammations, they may not furnish the slanderers with a cause of accusation.
n: The Greek 'συκοφάνταις' means 'false accusers' and is rendered 'slanderers'.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Galen cites book and case number; commentators tamper
s: Galen gives the book and position of each patient so readers can check him. He accuses many commentators of altering citations and hiding their sources.
q: or suspect that we too are tampering in our citations (παραγράφοντας), which indeed many of the commentators have done.
n: Galen's citation practice: book, number counted from the start or from the constitution, places and headings.

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Poison recipes should be kept silent
s: Galen condemns writers who 'with monstrous liberality' set down preparations of poisons, saying sensible men keep them silent.
q: there have already been some who were ungrudging even in the teaching of these things, displaying a kind of monstrous liberality and writing down the preparations of each of the poisons

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Attalus, king of the Pergamenes, devoted to drugs
s: Galen says the white plaster with pepper was composed many years ago by Attalus, 'king of us Pergamenes', a man devoted to drugs of every kind; Galen doubts a better one of its kind exists.
q: already many years ago by Attalus, who was king of us Pergamenes, a man who devoted himself to drugs of every kind
n: Outside knowledge: Attalus III Philometor (d. 133 BC), known for his work on poisons and drugs. Note Galen's 'us Pergamenes'.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Unnamed rich man worth 500 myriads demands costly drugs
s: Galen tells of an unnamed rich man, worth no more than five hundred myriads, a lover of drugs and of medicine, who scorned cheap remedies. He is the same man Galen mentions without a name in book 1 of On Prognosis from the Pulse.
q: where a man possessing not more than five hundred myriads, a lover of drugs and a lover of medicine, did not think fit to use any of the cheap ones
n: 500 myriads, probably of sesterces or drachmas, is a large fortune; the unit is not stated.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Epigonus freed from prison after curing a powerful man
s: Galen reports that more accurate writers say Epigonus, shut up in prison, was released after curing one of the very powerful men. The Isis plaster is named after him.
q: having been shut up in prison and having cured one of the very powerful men, he was released on that account.
n: A rare anecdote about Epigonus. Galen does not identify the powerful man.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Tiberius Caesar's remedy for herpes
s: Among troches is one 'of Tiberius Caesar' for herpes: diphryges, meconium, split alum and acacia, 3 oz each, taken up with vinegar or water.
q: For herpetes, the one of Tiberius Caesar. ℞ Diphryges, meconium, split alum, acacia, 3 ounces each; taking up with vinegar or water, use.
n: A remedy attributed to the emperor Tiberius.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Polemon the rhetor: Rome an epitome of the world
s: Galen cites the praise given to Polemon the rhetor for calling Rome an epitome of the inhabited world.
q: Polemon the rhetor is praised for having called it an epitome of the inhabited world.
n: Outside knowledge: Antonius Polemon of Laodicea, 2nd-century sophist; the saying is otherwise known mainly from Athenaeus.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: The trainer who misdiagnosed Galen's shoulder
s: The wrestling trainer (paidotribes) took the low shoulder for a dislocation into the armpit and kept extending and levering. Galen felt the armpit with the fingers of his good hand, found nothing out of place, and ordered them to stop.
q: the trainer, seeing that the epomis was low and that the humerus had slipped into the armpit, both extended it and set about levering it
n: Galen diagnosed his own injury by self-palpation.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: A distinguished bystander stops the extension
s: The others thought Galen was going soft from the pain and kept pulling, which could have torn the muscle. By chance a distinguished man saw this was not weakness, sent them away and asked Galen what to do.
q: had not by chance another man, a distinguished one, who saw well that I would never have restrained them from the extension out of softness, dismissed those men
n: The man is unnamed.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Lycus: a child has a bigger brain than an elephant, proportionally
s: Galen cites Lycus' own claim from elsewhere that man has the largest brain relative to body size. A small child has a larger brain than the largest elephant by proportion, so Lycus should have judged heat proportionally too.
q: he says in this way that a small child has a larger brain than the largest elephant, attending not to the bulk of the body alone but adding to it the consideration according to proportion
n: An anatomical fragment of Lycus (ἑτέρωθι, 'elsewhere'), relevant to his reputation as an anatomist (outside knowledge).

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Euclid's Elements cited for greatest common measure
s: The finger method rests on Euclid's theorem on the greatest common measure of two numbers, cited as in the seventh (book) of the Elements.
q: And this theorem has been demonstrated also by Euclid in the (book) of the Elements, and it is the seventh chapter of it.
n: Greek τῶν στοιχείων ἕβδομον: 'the seventh of the Elements', i.e. Book VII (VII.2 gives the GCD algorithm); the draft's 'seventh chapter' is a misreading (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Damocrates's recipes in iambic trimeter preserve proportions
s: Galen quotes Damocrates's white plaster in his own verses because recipes written in metre are easy to remember and keep their proportions exact.
q: Since the compositions of drugs written down in metre are easy to remember and preserve their proportions exactly, it seemed to me better to make mention of these too.
n: Damocrates (Servilius Damocrates, 1st c. AD) verse recipes survive largely through Galen.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen's father's old oil; Galen's own stock for a hundred years
s: Galen inherited very old oil and fat kept by his father and began laying down his own stock while very young. He now has enough for a hundred years, and a drug made with forty-year-old oil and fat has always helped the worst chronic ulcers.
q: because by some chance I had very old oil and fat, my father having kept them for a long time, I myself in turn laid down both in abundance, when I was quite young
n: A rare biographical detail about Galen's father, Nicon (name from outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen improvises drugs on journeys, refined by trial
s: Galen often improvises drugs on journeys. Some proved as good as the most famous, after a first composition by technical conjecture and a second or third correction based on experience.
q: just as you often see me too doing, [862] both on journeys abroad and otherwise. At any rate, some of the ones improvised in such circumstances, when tested by experience, appeared in no way inferior to the most renowned.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen inferred the Egyptian plaster's uses before reading Asclepiades and Criton
s: Galen worked out the uses of Andromachus' grey Egyptian plaster from its ingredients and confirmed them by trial. Only later did he come across the drug books of Asclepiades and Criton, which state its powers.
q: when I also came upon the pharmacological books of Asclepiades and Criton, I learned that they had written, not indefinitely as Andromachus too had done, but with distinctions
n: Shows when Galen first read these sources.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Lost works on Hippocratic anatomy and on Thucydides' plague
s: Galen says he showed elsewhere how Hippocrates' writing differs from Thucydides', in his works on Hippocrates' anatomy and on the plague in Thucydides.
q: in particular in those on the anatomy of Hippocrates, and not least also in those on the plague in Thucydides.
n: Outside knowledge: both works are lost; this is one of the few attestations of a Galenic work on Thucydides' plague.

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Galen's overnight refutation book handed to the sophist's pupils
s: The sophist was applauded and fled; next day Galen gave his 'chorus' a book refuting him, quoted as beginning 'Yesterday you ran away from the argument'.
q: when on the following day a certain book was given by us to his chorus-members, in which there was a refutation of what had thus suddenly been ventured
n: An otherwise unattested polemical pamphlet; the quoted text continues into K11.332-333.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Slimming: one meal, no bath, hard bed, walk naked
s: The fat should eat once a day, skip bathing, sleep on a hard bed and walk about naked as far as possible. Galen would rather say 'eat little', since some who eat once a day eat more than those who eat twice.
q: But also to eat once a day, and to go unbathed, and to sleep on a hard bed, and to walk about naked, as far as may be at all possible.
n: The opposite regimen fattens: two baths, food two or three times a day, a soft bed (K15.196-197).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Old euphorbium worked; an imitator's fresh euphorbium burned
s: Galen had a servant apply 5–6-year-old euphorbium in old oil to a tendon puncture, and it healed. An onlooker used fresh euphorbium the same way on another man, causing heat, biting and pain; Galen switched to the vinegar drug.
q: I gave one of my people old euphorbium and ordered him to triturate it with old oil to the thickness of a liquid cerate and to apply it to the puncture of the tendon in the hand.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Cold water in causus: Galen claims no deaths, too many to count
s: Galen calls cold water the most powerful remedy for kausos. He says none of the patients he gave it to at the proper moment died, and they were too many to remember. In K15.753 he adds that he did not give it to hopeless cases.
q: upon all to whom I gave it—and they are so very many that I do not even remember their number—there followed both benefit and preservation.

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Woman with breast cancer treated by black-bile purgation
s: Galen cured a woman's cancerous condition of the breast by strong evacuation with a black-bile purgative and purges her every spring; if omitted, deep pain returns.
q: I likewise evacuate a certain woman every year at the onset of spring, who had a cancerous condition in the breast, which I cured by evacuating her strongly with a drug that purges black bile.
n: Continuation (pain returns if purgation is omitted) in K11.344-345.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Keranitos troche: bronze mortar, or extra copper scale instead
s: The keranitos troche is ground during the Dog-star heat in a bronze mortar with a bronze pestle. Without a bronze mortar, add a mina (100 dr) of copper scale instead, so the mortar evidently supplies copper.
q: Grind, during the heat under the Dog-star, in a bronze mortar and with a pestle. But if you do not have a bronze mortar, put in 1 mina of scale, which is 100 dr.
n: Shows awareness that a copper vessel adds metal to the drug. The same unit names the 'Bithynian' troche 'prepared in Sicily'.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Warm-oil affusion day and night in the Dog-days
s: The region felt cold, so Galen had warm oil poured over it day and night while he lay naked on a hide. A basin caught the run-off, which was reheated in a cauldron over a fire. When they stopped, his neck muscles tightened, threatening spasm.
q: I was compelled [402] throughout the whole day and night to pour warm oil over it, a hide having been spread beneath my whole body, for I lay naked upon it
n: Season: the burning heat under the Dog-star (τῶν ὑπὸ κύνα καυμάτων).

wt: On Plethora
t: Do not diagnose plethora right after anger, bath or wine
s: Before judging plethora from vein size and redness, wait until the effects of anger, bathing, exercise, wine or other heating have settled; then weigh heaviness, tension, pulses, sleep and appetite.
q: it is not fitting to bring to diagnosis a man who is angry, or has bathed, or is bathing, or has exercised, or has just taken wine

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Detecting breath in apnoea: finger, hair, wool
s: In apparent apnoea the breath is only very small and slow. It can be detected by holding a finger before the nose, or by hanging a hair or fine carded wool there and watching it move.
q: And if one also hangs a hair before it, or a fine piece of wool, thoroughly carded out, one will see these too being stirred.
n: Bedside test for faint breathing.

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Galen's public demonstration: one cholagogue purge cures jaundice
s: Given a feverless jaundiced man full of bile, Galen prepares him for some days and, at the right moment, restores his natural state with a single bile-drawing laxative and nothing else.
q: by giving one of the bile-drawing laxatives (ὑπήλατον), I bring the man back to his natural state by means of such a purgation, without undertaking anything further at all with regard to the body.
n: K11.329 adds that he has shown this many times and converted many.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: 'Sacred' plasters said to come from Egyptian temples
s: The most famous tawny plaster, 'through dittany', is classed with the 'sacred' plasters like the Isis, because they are said to have been brought from the temples in Egypt.
q: it too being one of those named 'sacred', like the Isis, since they say that they were brought from the temples in Egypt.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: High priest of Pergamum entrusts the gladiators to the young Galen
s: Because of his drugs, the high priest of his city entrusted the treatment of the gladiators to Galen alone, although he was only beginning his twenty-ninth year.
q: it seemed good, I know not how, to the high priest in our city to entrust the treatment of the gladiators to me alone, although I was young in age
n: Draft 'myself cutting through the remainder of the tendon' renders ἐντέμνων, literally 'cutting into'; the sense of the surgical step is slightly uncertain.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Dittany 'hiera' plaster from the temple of Hephaestus at Memphis
s: The plaster made with dittany is also called hiera, said to have been found in the temple of Hephaestus at Memphis. Heras' version uses Cretan dittany, and burnt as a fumigant it drives off venomous creatures.
q: saying that this prescription also was found in the temple of Hephaestus at Memphis.
n: Hephaestus here corresponds to Ptah of Memphis (outside knowledge).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: No public bath-houses in Hippocrates' time
s: From Hippocrates' remarks about house equipment, smokeless shelter and plentiful water, Galen infers that bath-houses had not yet been built. Water was still heated in cauldrons at home and poured into tubs.
q: It seems that in the times of Hippocrates these bath-houses had not yet been constructed
n: This is evidence for ancient views on the history of the bath.

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Poisonings among the Thracian Bithynians in Galen's childhood
s: When Galen was a child, among the Thracian Bithynians a man found a herb that made those who took it pass blood and die.
q: what happened among the Thracian Bithynians when we were still children. A certain man found a herb of such a kind that whoever took some of it excreted blood and so perished.
n: Galen was born 129 CE at Pergamum; 'Thracian Bithynians' (Herodotus' Thracian origin of the Bithynians) places this in Bithynia, neighbouring Mysia (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Everyone, even country folk, now bathes daily; rich patients disobey
s: Galen complains that endurance has perished: even country people bathe every day; the poor mostly obey orders, but the rich and powerful are hard to persuade or disobey, so it would be best not to treat them.
q: But since in present-day life endurance has perished among all men, so that by now even those in the fields have become accustomed to bathe every day

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Pedlars sell liquid pine resin as terebinth
s: Dealers in sundries sell liquid pine resin in place of terebinth to buyers who cannot tell them apart; it is sharper in smell, taste and power.
q: similar in consistency to the liquid pine resin, which the dealers in sundries sell in place of terebinth to those who do not know how to distinguish them.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Cyrenaic juice weakened since growers irrigate for yield
s: Fresh euphorbium heats more than Cyrenaic juice, especially present-day Cyrenaic, since growers water the plants to make them grow and yield more juice.
q: especially more than that of the present day, ever since they have been making the plants grow by watering with water and preparing them for an abundant production of juice
n: Outside knowledge: Cyrenaic juice is silphium; this is rare evidence of its cultivation in Galen's time, after Pliny reported it extinct. The draft links 'after one year' to the euphorbium, which the Greek supports.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Physicians who lost their drug stocks died of grief
s: Galen says the method helps when drugs run out on journeys, especially by sea. Even at home, some physicians who lost their stock of drugs wasted away from grief and died.
q: seeing that even while remaining in their own place some have lost the stock of drugs by which they used to treat those in need, so that they wasted away from grief and died.
n: Possibly an allusion to losses in the fire of 192 at Rome, which Galen describes in On the Avoidance of Grief (outside knowledge; the text names no event).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Pale-yellow Pamphylian storax reserved for the emperor
s: The best storax is pale yellow, finest from Pamphylia, and scarce, so it is kept for antidotes and always used when preparing anything for the emperor or a patron willing to pay. Others get the best greyish kind.
q: so that when preparing anything with storax for the emperor at any rate you will always use this one.
n: Evidence that drug grades were matched to the patient's rank and purse. The 'emperor' is presumably Galen's imperial patron.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Layman who feeds a starved patient seems to raise the dead
s: If a physician fails to see that a patient is weak from starvation, another physician or a layman who feeds him looks as if he had raised a dead man. Galen says such errors bring the craft into contempt.
q: for the physician or layman who came in seems to them as if he had even raised up a dead man.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Zythos (barley beer) brewed nowadays
s: On the 'barley water' for thirst, Galen wishes the author had said how the barley is prepared: simply soaked, or as people nowadays do when they make zythos from it.
q: whether simply by steeping it, or as those nowadays do who make zythos from it, or in some other manner
n: This is evidence for barley beer (zythos) in Galen's day, typically Egyptian.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Only quotidian, tertian and quartan periods exist
s: All fever paroxysms recur daily, every third day or every fourth day; Galen mocks sophists who claim fifth-, sixth-, seventh-day or longer periods.
q: all the paroxysms in fevers occur either every day, or every third day, or every fourth day

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Reason finds the composition, experience judges it
s: Galen states that reason discovers the composition of a drug while experience judges its excellence, so drugs composed by art are trusted even by non-rationalists.
q: For reason discovers the composition, but experience judges the excellence of what has been discovered

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Physicians drop proven ancient drugs to look original
s: Most physicians abandon drugs proven since antiquity so as to seem to have something better than their predecessors; the cadmia and ladanum drugs are the best for cicatrization.
q: Now most physicians abandon the drugs which from ancient times have given sufficient proof of themselves to all the best physicians and for this reason have become renowned

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Older anatomists missed the triple Achilles tendon
s: Galen says the tendon descending from the calf to the heel is made of three aponeuroses, a fact missed by anatomists older than him and now demonstrated by companions reading his anatomical books.
q: the tendon descending from the calf appears both robust and thick, as being composed of three aponeuroses. This too had escaped the notice of the anatomists older than I

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Criton found the 12-fold cerate dilution by stepwise trial
s: Galen reconstructs Criton's method: he did not hit on twelvefold cerate at first but went from eightfold to tenfold to twelvefold until the drug stopped biting. This is Galen's model of conjecture corrected by experience.
q: For if, when eightfold had been mixed in, it still appeared biting, he mixed it in tenfold; and just so, if it was still biting at tenfold, he went on to the twelvefold.
n: Galen's inference about Criton's process, not something Criton reports.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Reason and experience compared to weather forecasting
s: Galen says drugs found by reason are hopes confirmed by experience, and hopes differ in strength. We expect rain at the winter solstice far more than at the rising of the Dog-star.
q: For we do not hope alike that there will be rain at the winter solstice and at the rising of the Dog-star.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: One in a thousand masters the art; Empiricists deny reasoning
s: Galen says perhaps one physician in a thousand masters the art, and the rest, like laymen, just follow written recipes. Even notable Empiricists say no compound drug was found by reasoning.
q: For among a thousand, some one person seems to possess the perfection of the art, while the rest, [892] just like laymen, are content if they are able to use correctly the drugs that have been clearly written up.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen warns future researchers against hasty grading
s: Galen says grading emollients into four orders needs much experience on many bodies. Any successor as industrious and truth-loving as he should not judge rashly from two or three uses, and should test on the best specimens.
q: and so, if after me anyone should arise who is, like me, industrious and zealous for truth, let him not make pronouncements rashly on the basis of two or three uses.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Deliberate falsification of numerals by envious copyists
s: Menecrates spelled out numbers because numerals get corrupted by accident and on purpose: the envious turn omicron into theta, or iota into another letter, by adding or scraping strokes. Later copyists put the numerals back, defeating him.
q: who make the letter omicron a theta by drawing another, transverse, line through the middle of the round stroke
n: The Greek reads 'ἐκ τοῦ γράμμα καὶ ῥῶ', presumably a corruption of γάμμα, as the draft notes. Galen concludes that Damocrates' verse texts are more reliable (K13.995-996).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Dialectic: the sign converts only one way
s: 'If he breathes large and rare, he is delirious' is not the same as 'if he is delirious, he breathes large and rare'. The two statements do not convert, they only invert; large, rare breath is a property of delirium, not inseparable from it.
q: For these do not convert (ἀντιστρέφειν) with one another, but only invert (ἀναστρέφειν).
n: The Greek has the finite verbs ἀντιστρέφει/ἀναστρέφει. Galen defends the dialectic his opponents despise, with an Olympic-training analogy.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Hippocrates writes as craftsman, Thucydides as layman
s: Thucydides records everything laymen notice about the sick. Hippocrates leaves out the obvious and records the technical details that even good physicians miss.
q: For Thucydides wrote the things that happened to the sick as a layman for laymen, but Hippocrates as a craftsman for craftsmen.
n: Galen corrects 'the ancients' who thought Hippocrates writes down everything, as Thucydides does (K7.850).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Physicians dry patients out 'like salt-fish' before feeding
s: Galen attacks physicians who starve patients for two or three days at the start of a disease and then switch abruptly to gruels. He compares this to pickling fish.
q: as if curing them like salt-fish, for two or three days or even more
n: In K15.594-595 Galen glosses ταριχεύεσθαι as excessive drying from untimely fasting.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Part 'after the bath' published posthumously from Hippocrates' notes
s: Galen suggests that the section after the bath may be notes Hippocrates wrote for himself, found in his house and published after his death. As a treatise it is unworthy of him, like On Diseases and On Affections.
q: if someone, having found it in the house, published it after the man's death as things written by him in outline
n: This is the so-called Appendix to Regimen in Acute Diseases.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Interpolators insert at the ends of treatises
s: Galen explains that interpolations cluster at the ends of books because readers remember the beginnings. He gives as examples the Aphorisms, On Wounds in the Head and Epidemics II, as well as this book.
q: For because the first parts of treatises are in the memory of many, those who interpolate insert their interpolations into the last parts

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Single cases should be recorded as in Epidemics, with name and days
s: Galen says the author rashly generalized from a particular observation. He should have recorded it as Hippocrates did in the Epidemics, with the patient's name and the day of each event.
q: stating first at the beginning the name of the patient and after this also the days on which each thing happened

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Blood-drawing drugs exist but are poisons Galen will not name
s: Some drugs draw blood from the start through stomach and intestine vessels; physicians class them as deleterious poisons, and Galen refuses to write their names.
q: As for the names of such drugs, even if I knew them with certainty, I would not disclose them in writing.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Aristotle, Theophrastus, Chrysippus, Mnesitheus on the arts
s: Galen says these men kept Plato's view (Philebus) that the arts rest on knowing differences, and that everyone writing 'On Art' gave the same argument.
q: and Aristotle and Theophrastus preserved his opinion, as did Chrysippus and Mnesitheus, and there is no one who did not go through the same argument in his writing On Art.
n: Mnesitheus of Athens, 4th-c. BC physician (outside knowledge), here grouped with philosophers. 'περὶ τέχνης γράμματι' may mean a genre of writings on art rather than one title. At 217 Aristotle and Theophrastus are again cited: things the same in genus can be contraries in species.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Dioscorides of Anazarbus and the materia medica writers
s: Galen says even Dioscorides of Anazarbus and all writers on materia medica knew the flavour distinctions. He lists their nine terms: salty, briny, bitter, sweet, harsh, astringent, styptic, pungent, sour.
q: For things so evident were known even to Dioscorides of Anazarbus, and to all the others who wrote treatises on materia medica.
n: 'καί ... ἐγίγνωσκεν', 'even Dioscorides', is mildly condescending. The work is 'τὰ περὶ ὕλης ὑπομνήματα'.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Patroclus, freedman of Caesar: anointing for gout
s: An anointing salve for gout and arthritis was compounded for Patroclus, a freedman of Caesar, to be used daily: morning before the bath, after the bath and towards evening.
q: Another anointing-salve, the one compounded for Patroclus, freedman of Caesar; it frees the patient from the whole condition.
n: Patroclus, a known imperial freedman (outside knowledge; Suetonius and Martial mention a Patrobius/Patroclus).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Celer the primipilarius: royal myrakopon prepared for him
s: A royal perfumed akopon with Troglodytic myrrh, Falernian wine and some fifteen perfumed oils, boiled 'in the manner of perfumers', was prepared for Celer the primipilarius (senior centurion).
q: The drug is exceedingly good; it was prepared for Celer the primipilarius.
n: A military patient.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Orion the hair-dresser's akopon with lion's fat
s: Andromachus records an akopon of Orion the hair-dresser: wax, propolis, iris, terebinth, opopanax, oils, deer marrow, oesypum, calf's fat, lion's fat and opobalsam.
q: Another akopon, that of Orion the hair-dresser, a good one.
n: A drug credited to a tradesman. The next recipe uses crocodile fat.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Dioscorides judged second to none among materia medica writers
s: Galen faults earlier materia medica writers for not ranking drugs by degree, but singles out Dioscorides as second to none among those who worked on the subject.
q: as indeed did Dioscorides, whom one would say is second to none of those who have devoted their efforts to these matters.
n: Praise of Dioscorides combined with a criticism: he gave powers without stating each drug's order (degree).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Valeria Secunda: Andromachus' patient with malignant ulcers
s: Andromachus headed a recipe 'For malignant ulcers, in the case of Valeria Secunda': Tyrrhenian wax 8 dr, bull's suet, terebinth and burnt lead 4 dr each, used on lint. Galen judges it a soothing drug, not a decisive one.
q: "For malignant ulcers, in the case of Valeria Secunda." One must obviously supply in addition "I used."
n: A named Roman woman patient. Galen faults Andromachus for not saying which ulcers it suits.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Scribonius Largus' well-tried plaster
s: Asclepiades includes a well-tried plaster 'of Scribonius Largus': wax 100 dr (or 50), litharge 50 dr, myrtle oil 1 kotyle, and 2 dr each of burnt misy, burnt chalcitis, burnt split alum, white lead and terebinth.
q: Another, of Scribonius Largus, a well-tried drug.
n: Scribonius Largus, physician to Claudius, author of the Latin Compositiones (outside knowledge). 'Largus' also appears alone at K13.827-828 and K13.937-938.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Erasistratus improvised herb juice when lacking a stomatic
s: Galen's example of improvising: Erasistratus, on a journey without a stomatic drug, made one from herb juice on the spot.
q: as Erasistratus once found a supply of the juice of herbs when he did not have a stomatic drug with him in that place on his journey
n: A small anecdote about Erasistratus not otherwise widely attested (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Bacchius' malagma used by Caesar
s: Andromachus records a malagma of Bacchius 'which Caesar used': pig's fat, wax, elecampane, aromatic reed, panax root, salt, bdellium, ammoniac, rush flower, iris, frankincense, pepper, galbanum.
q: Another malagma, of Bacchius, which Caesar used.
n: Which Caesar is not said.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Thessalus and 'the things from the small tablet'
s: Some think five Epidemics books were written by Thessalus and two by the great Hippocrates. Hence the title 'from the small tablet', because Thessalus gathered everything his father had written so that nothing would be lost.
q: to have been entitled "the things from the small tablet", evidently because Thessalus was eager to gather into one place everything that his father happened to have written
n: An otherwise rare title. Galen says these critics have grasped the character of the books most accurately.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Aristotelians call self-evident premises 'axioms'
s: Analysing Hippocrates' argument as a syllogism, Galen notes that the followers of Aristotle call premises credible in themselves 'axioms'.
q: which premises it is in fact the custom of the followers of Aristotle to call axioms

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Paulus the rhetor: phlegmatic, vomited yellow bile daily
s: Galen's example of a man 'bitter-bilious in the upper parts' is Paulus the rhetor. He had a phlegmatic habit of body, yet yellow bile rose every day and he vomited it after his bath, and his stools held little bile.
q: For in Paulus the rhetor, who had a phlegmatic habit of the whole body, yellow bile floated up every day, and he vomited it first, after the bath, in no small quantity.
n: This passage does not identify him further. He is distinct from the Eudemus case that follows.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Eudemus the philosopher: bilious, bile passed downward
s: The contrasting case is Eudemus the philosopher. He was bilious in temperament, his bile passed downward, he rarely vomited it, and his stools were full of bile.
q: But in Eudemus the philosopher, who was bilious in temperament, it passed downward through the seat
n: Most likely the Peripatetic Eudemus whom Galen treated in Rome (On Prognosis).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Menodotus the Empiricist: bleed only in plethoric syndrome
s: Galen reports that Menodotus the Empiricist held venesection appropriate only in the 'plethoric syndrome'. Galen bleeds also for sudden violent pain, bruises and dislocations, and sometimes treats plethora without bleeding.
q: among whom is also Menodotus the Empiricist, who asserts that phlebotomy has been observed to apply only in the so-called plethoric concurrence
n: Menodotus of Nicomedia, Empiricist, 2nd century AD. This is a fragment of his views.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Long verbatim quotations of Plato's Philebus
s: Galen quotes Plato's Philebus at length (sound as one and unlimited; grammar and music; colours and figures; pleasures) to show that the arts consist in knowing differences.
q: The first passage of Plato concerning the constitution of the arts is stated as follows.
n: Phlb. 17b-e, 12e-13a, 12d (outside knowledge). Useful as an indirect witness to Plato's text. At 213 Galen adds the Sophist and the Statesman for the differences of the arts.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Type-theorists' absurd reckoning: 'twelve twelfth-day fevers'
s: Faced with a paroxysm anticipating two hours daily, these physicians count a 22-hour period on fingers or a diagram and call it twelve twelfth-day fevers, drawing laughter.
q: some on their fingers, others even on a diagram drawn in some book, they say that such a type is twelve twelfth-day fevers.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Asclepiades Pharmakion: ten books of remedies plus theriacs and women's
s: Heras wrote one book of remedies; Asclepiades surnamed Pharmakion wrote ten, besides those on theriacs and women's remedies; Andromachus gathered nearly as many in three books: external, internal and eye remedies.
q: Asclepiades, surnamed Pharmakion, wrote ten, apart from those on the theriacs and on women's remedies
n: Asclepiades Pharmakion (1st c. AD) is lost except through Galen.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Asclepiades's book titles: Marcella (external) and Mason (internal)
s: Asclepiades entitled his five books of external remedies Marcella I to V and his five books of internal remedies Mason I to V.
q: He himself entitles these books the first Marcella, and the second, third, fourth and fifth, just as he entitles the other five, those of the internal remedies, the first Mason
n: Compare K13.642-643, where the Greek assigns 'Marcellas' to the internal remedies (see doubt item).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Mantias the Herophilean, first compiler of drug recipes
s: The first author Galen knows who wrote up many praiseworthy compound drugs was Mantias the Herophilean; his pupil Heraclides of Tarentum imitated him in drugs and in dietetics.
q: first of those I know, by Mantias the Herophilean, whose pupil Heraclides of Tarentum appears to imitate him not only in the use of drugs but also in the dietetic part of the art.
n: Both works are lost; this is a key statement on the origins of Greek recipe collections.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Canon of pharmacologists: Musa, Heras, Andromachus, Asclepiades, Criton, Archigenes
s: Mantias and Heraclides wrote first; recipes were sifted by experience; most successful afterwards were Petronius Musa, Heras, Andromachus, Asclepiades and Criton, and Archigenes and Philippus also wrote many.
q: Among these, those who seem most to have achieved success in the experience of drugs are Petronius Musa and Heras and Andromachus, and Asclepiades and Criton.
n: Note the name form 'Petronius Musa'; compare 'Petronas' in K13.641-642.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Dioscorides of Anazarbus quoted on ranking resins
s: Galen quotes Dioscorides, On Materials book 1, ranking terebinth first among resins, then mastic, pine, fir, peuke and strobilos, and reconciles it with his own ranking by heat.
q: Of all the resins the terebinth takes first place, and after it the mastic (schinine), then the pine (pityine) and the fir (elatine), after which are counted the peuke-pine (peukine) and the strobilos (pine-cone) resin.
n: Dioscorides is extant (De materia medica 1.71); a check on Galen's quotation practice.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen searched all drug writers for a contemporary's recipe
s: Galen could not find a contemporary physician's metallic nerve drug in Asclepiades Pharmakion, Petronas, Andromachus, Heras, Mantias, Heraclides, Archigenes, Philippus, Soranus, Menecrates, Crito or Damocrates.
q: having read everything written on drugs by Soranus and Menecrates and Crito and Damocrates and the others who hold a reputation for knowledge of drugs, in none of them did I find this drug
n: Shows what pharmacological library Galen had; Soranus's drug writings are otherwise lost.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Heraclides of Tarentum's book to Astydamas, trusted for testing
s: Galen calls Heraclides of Tarentum trustworthy because he wrote only what he had tested. He quotes his book addressed to Astydamas: copper scale 1 part, scraped verdigris 4 parts, with eightfold myrtle cerate, for old ulcers.
q: what was written by Heraclides of Tarentum in his book addressed to Astydamas. For he is a trustworthy man if anyone is, writing only those things that have been judged by him through experience.
n: Heraclides was a leading Empiricist of the 1st century BC (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Archigenes, On Drugs book 2, on old ulcers
s: Galen quotes Archigenes' second book On Drugs word for word. Remedies include very old oil on lint, verdigris in rose cerate, starch with calf's fat and Tyrrhenian wax, and many others.
q: What Archigenes wrote about such ulcers in the second book of his work On Drugs is set down, in his own wording and in his very words, as follows.
n: Archigenes of Apamea, physician under Trajan; his works survive only in fragments (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Mantias' book 'The Drug-seller at the Surgery'
s: Galen cites a book titled 'The Drug-seller at the Surgery' by Mantias, and its verdigris plaster (burnt copper, pine resin, wax, verdigris, oil, Cimolian earth, frankincense, copper scale, worked smooth with vinegar for three days). It is used for wounds and cancerous ulcers and also packed into eaten-away teeth (K13.751-752).
q: as indeed has the one written in the book entitled Mantias' "The Drug-seller at the Surgery" (pharmakopōlēs ho kat' iatreion).
n: Mantias, a Herophilean teacher of Heraclides of Tarentum (outside knowledge). The 4 minae of burnt copper looks out of scale beside the drachm amounts.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Heras wrote one book (Narthex); five books of Criton survive besides Cosmetics
s: Galen says Heras wrote a single book on drug composition, the Narthex, while five such books of Criton survive in addition to his Cosmetics.
q: Heras composed one book on the composition of drugs, entitled Narthex. But five such books of Criton survive, apart from the Cosmetics.
n: Key evidence for the size and titles of these lost works. Criton's Cosmetics book 2 is cited at K13.1039-1040.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Hippocrates: 'moderate numbness relieves pain'
s: Galen explains that henbane and poppy were added to the herb plaster for their numbing coldness, citing Hippocrates that moderate numbness relieves pain.
q: And moderate numbness relieves pain, says Hippocrates.
n: Hippocratic Aphorisms 5.25 (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Menecrates' book 'Autokrator hologrammatos'
s: Menecrates, inventor of the 'dia chylon' plaster, wrote a book titled 'Autokrator hologrammatos': dedicated to the emperor, with every number spelled out in full words, not numerals.
q: The book in which the drug is written up is entitled 'Autokrator hologrammatos' (The Emperor, in Whole Letters): 'Autokrator' because it has been dedicated to him
n: Menecrates, physician to Tiberius or Claudius (outside knowledge). Key evidence on how recipe texts were transmitted.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Spurious 'On the Whole Constitution of the Glands'
s: Hippocrates promised a treatise on the glands, but none survives. A later Hippocratean wrote a little book under that title, far below Hippocrates in style and thought, unknown to earlier physicians and to the compilers of the catalogues (pinakes).
q: one of the more recent Hippocrateans wrote a small little book, giving it the title Hippocrates' On the Whole Constitution of the Glands
n: Outside knowledge: the extant Hippocratic De glandulis may be this book. The pinakes reference suggests Alexandrian library catalogues.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Menander's play The Self-Punisher cited for grammar
s: To show that the middle τιμωρούμενος means 'punishing', Galen cites the title of Menander's play Heauton timoroumenos, along with a line of Euripides' Orestes.
q: thus at any rate the play of Menander is entitled Heauton timoroumenos (The Self-Punisher)
n: Outside knowledge: Menander's play is lost (Terence adapted it). The Euripides line is quoted in K18a.384 ('Doing unholy deeds, yet taking vengeance for my father').

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Simonides fragment for στενυγρός ('narrow')
s: To show that στενυγρός simply means 'narrow', Galen quotes Simonides on a man meeting a leopard alone on a narrow path in shadowy mountains. Part of the verse is corrupt.
q: This is also quite clear from what Simonides said, the words running roughly thus: 'Not yet did any man thus in the shadowy mountains,
n: The draft marks λέγονται δὶς ἐν as corrupt (perhaps 'a lion'). A poetic fragment preserved here; check against the Simonides editions (PMG).

wt: On Plethora
t: Stoic cohesive faculty: pneuma holds, matter is held
s: The Stoics, chief proponents of the cohesive faculty, make pneumatic substance what holds together and material substance what is held: air and fire hold, earth and water are held.
q: they say that air and fire hold together, while earth and water are held together.

wt: On Plethora
t: Erasistratus, Hygiene book 1: genesis of plethora
s: Erasistratus says when distributed food is not concocted, worked off or excreted, vessels fill and distend until contents push into the adjacent vessels of pneuma.
q: And when the vessels no longer admit any further packing-in, and other nourishment is brought up from the belly, what is already present takes an impulse towards the adjacent vessels of the pneuma.
n: Galen states (K7.536-537) this is the only work where Erasistratus gives signs of plethos; fragment of a lost work.

wt: On Plethora
t: Herophilean 'three-time semeiosis'
s: The Herophileans, like the Empiricists, introduced a three-time semeiosis: past (idle life, retained excretions), present (fullness, ulcerous sensation, heaviness) and future (benefit after evacuation).
q: he even wrote a part of the so-called three-time semeiosis, which the followers of Herophilus introduced in the same way as the Empiricists
n: Erasistratus omitted the future part, says Galen.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Heraclides of Pontus on the 'breathless' condition
s: Extreme chilling makes breathing so small that it seems gone; Galen identifies this with the state Heraclides of Pontus called 'breathless'.
q: the condition which Heraclides of Pontus described as "breathless" is this one
n: Outside knowledge: Heraclides' lost dialogue Peri tes apnou (the woman without breath). Galen adds that neither breath nor pulse truly ceases while the animal lives.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Herophilus on rhythm in the pulses
s: The rhythm of breathing (inspiration compared with expiration) can be analysed with the same theory Herophilus wrote for rhythms of the pulse.
q: this topic will admit the same theory as that written by Herophilus concerning the rhythms in the pulses.
n: Herophilus' pulse-rhythm writings are lost; Galen is a main witness.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: The ancients called such patients 'struck' (blētoi)
s: Quoting Regimen in Acute Diseases: the ancients called pleuritics who died suffocated 'struck', partly because after death the side is found livid, as if from a blow.
q: The ancients very much called such persons 'struck' (blētoi), chiefly for this reason, and not least because, when they have died, the side is found livid, somewhat like a blow.
n: Hippocrates reporting earlier usage. The same passage has sputum held 'in the bronchi of the lung' (βρόγχοισι).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Most commentators read 'sleep after dinner'; Galen says after lunch
s: Galen disagrees with most earlier commentators, who took the advice to sleep 'as if passing the night' to mean after dinner. He argues from the context that it means after the midday meal and offers an emendation.
q: after dinner, as most of the commentators say, but, as the sense of what has been said requires, after the midday meal
n: In K15.557-558 he gives the corrected wording, 'one must sleep... after the luncheon'.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Empiricist 'syndromes' cannot capture degrees of illness
s: Galen argues that teaching by the Empiricists' syndromes cannot work, because the degrees of strength, fever and sputum cannot be written down. The physician has to weigh them himself in each case.
q: it is not possible to conduct the teaching according to what the Empiricists call syndromes.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Erasistratus' dictum on strong powers of food and drink
s: Galen quotes Erasistratus: strong foods and drinks bring the greatest benefit at the right moment and the greatest harm at the wrong one. He uses it to explain why physicians fall back on water.
q: for so Erasistratus used to say: strong powers of foods and drinks, when taken at the right moment, bring the greatest benefit, but when at the wrong moment, the greatest harm.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Erasistratus' On Fevers mocks Hippocrateans' wax cups
s: Galen says Erasistratus, in his books On Fevers, maliciously attacks Hippocrates through his pupils Apollonius and Dexippus. They supposedly made wax cups of one twelfth of a kyathos and gave fever patients one or two of them.
q: having made twelve waxen cyathi to the cyathus that is the sixth part of the cotyle, measured out one or two of these to those suffering from fever.
n: This is a fragment of Erasistratus' lost On Fevers. It also gives a measure: the kyathos is one sixth of a kotyle. K15.744 calls these 'wax cups' (κηρίνων κυλίκων).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Physician's book for Victor, prefect of Rome, excerpted Hippocrates
s: Galen says a physician gave Victor, the prefect of Rome, a book On Regimen according to Hippocrates. It included this passage and others, though some of them cut in half.
q: the physician who gave [723] to Victor, the prefect of Rome, the book On Regimen according to Hippocrates
n: Victor is a city prefect (praefectus urbi), possibly Aufidius Victorinus (city prefect under Commodus). The identification is uncertain. The book is a lost contemporary Hippocratic compilation.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Appendix already attached by Erasistratus' time
s: Even if the appendix is not by Hippocrates, Galen says it is ancient and was already joined to the genuine part in Erasistratus' day. That makes Erasistratus' mockery of the wax cups all the stranger.
q: This book, even if it is not a composition of Hippocrates, is at any rate ancient, so that already in the times of Erasistratus it had been appended to the genuine part.
n: This dates the joining of Acut. and Appendix before about 250 BC.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Thessalian Methodists: phlebotomy as a 'relaxing' remedy
s: Galen says the 'unmethodical Thessalians' declare phlebotomy a relaxing remedy without demonstration and explain 'relaxing' in different ways. He has examined this in his commentaries on the Methodic sect.
q: But the unmethodical Thessalians, just as they state everything else [764] simply and without demonstration, so too have declared phlebotomy to be a relaxing remedy
n: The Thessalians are the followers of Thessalus of Tralles. The phrase 'unmethodical' (ἀμέθοδοι) is a pun on 'Methodists'.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Galen read only the opening of Lycus, then was asked to reply
s: Galen swears he could not bear to read beyond Lycus' first expositions. He wrote this reply when a companion asked him to listen to Lycus' comment on this aphorism and many others urged him to answer.
q: having read the first expositions of his commentaries on the Aphorisms, I could no longer bear to read the rest of the book
n: The companion asked him ἐπακοῦσαι, to listen while the text was read aloud: a detail of group reading. Galen presents the work as written on request (ἀναγκασθεὶς).

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Galen wrote this work in one day at younger men's request
s: Younger men pressed Galen to write down the method he had taught them in jest, and he devoted a single day to it, unwillingly.
q: for their sake I have devoted a single day, not willingly, to this discourse as well.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Galen trained in arithmetic as a boy
s: Galen says that thanks to his education, exercised in numbers in boyhood, he answers type problems on the spot, while the untrained need years.
q: I for my part, in virtue of my education, answer each of these on the spot to those who put them to me, because I was exercised in numbers in my boyhood years

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Lost work defending solecisms against Atticist critics
s: Galen says he showed, in writings against people who censure those who commit solecisms, that the Attic writers themselves followed prevailing usage.
q: it has been shown [408] by me, in my writings against those who censure people who commit solecisms, that the Attic men themselves too followed the prevailing usage.
n: Outside knowledge: this polemic against hyper-Atticists does not survive; it appears in Galen's own lists of his writings.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Returned from Alexandria to Pergamum at age 28
s: Galen says he devised his treatment of nerve (tendon) wounds while still young, when he first came back from Alexandria to his native city in his twenty-eighth year.
q: I devised the regimen of treatment for those wounded in the nerves while still young, when I first returned from Alexandria to my native city, being in my twenty-eighth year.
n: Key autobiographical datum (c. AD 157). Greek γεγονὼς ἔτος ὄγδοον ἐπὶ τοῖς εἴκοσι. The automatic check failed on term recall, but the draft matches the Greek here.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Anatomical Procedures: first to describe cutaneous nerve branches
s: Galen says he described exactly, in his Anatomical Procedures, the small nerve branches that go only to the skin, which all earlier writers had omitted.
q: matters about which I wrote accurately in the Anatomical Procedures, since they had been omitted by all before me.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Galen lived in Rome after his thirtieth year
s: Galen says that after his thirtieth year he lived in Rome, a city so crowded that it explains how often he met rare injuries.
q: after my thirtieth year I lived in Rome, a city possessing so great a multitude of human beings
n: Chronological datum for Galen's arrival in Rome (outside knowledge: c. AD 162).

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Physicians brought Galen their unusual cases
s: Galen says all the physicians in Rome showed him unexpected cases for consultation, so such dislocations could not escape him.
q: since all the physicians seem (ἐοικέναι) to show me the unexpected cases [347] for the sake of consultation (συμβολῆς)
n: ἐοικέναι ('seem') is odd here; probably read εἰωθέναι ('are accustomed'). The draft keeps the transmitted word.

wt: On Plethora
t: Young Galen questions his Empiricist teacher
s: As a youth Galen asked his Empiricist teacher whether all signs of the plethoric syndrome must concur before phlebotomy; the teacher said all must.
q: what I myself, when I was a youth, asked my Empiricist teacher when he first taught me these things
n: Galen's Empiricist teacher is unnamed here (perhaps Aeschrion of Pergamum or another; outside knowledge, uncertain).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: A sophist disputes delirium breathing with Galen
s: Galen says one of the lecturing sophists once argued with him that large, rare breathing never occurs in delirium, because it did not fit his view that breathing is a vital (involuntary) function.
q: Indeed, one of such sophists once disputed with me about the breath's becoming large and rare in those who are delirious.
n: Personal anecdote from Galen's polemics (probably in Rome).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Opponent shows Galen a delirious patient and laughs
s: A man showed Galen a delirious patient who was not breathing large and rare, mocked Hippocrates and Galen, and left without hearing that the sign holds one way only.
q: One of such men, then, once showed us a patient who was delirious, yet breathing neither large nor
n: Galen's reply rests on the logic that large, rare breath implies delirium, but delirium does not imply large, rare breath.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: On the Causes of Respiration: diaphragm the chief organ
s: Galen cites his books On the Causes of Respiration, where he showed the diaphragm to be the first and most important organ of breathing.
q: which was shown by us in the books On the Causes of Respiration to be the first and most principal organ of these
n: Outside knowledge: De causis respirationis survives only as a short summary.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: On the Best Sect and Therapeutic Method on method of inquiry
s: Galen refers readers to On the Best Sect and the Therapeutic Method for how to investigate such problems, and says dull readers should give up, since a small nature cannot grasp a great man's thought.
q: It has indeed been stated both in the writings On the Best Sect and in those of the Therapeutic Method how one ought both to investigate and to discover all such things
n: Outside knowledge: Galen's own On the Best Sect is lost (the extant De optima secta is spurious).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Purgatives known by experience, need for purging by reason
s: Galen refers to his books On the Power of Simple Drugs: which humour a purgative draws is learned by experience, while the need to purge downward-tending humours was found by reason and confirmed by experience.
q: That the cathartic drugs are discovered through experience—both which humour each purges and whether it purges at all—you have learned in the books on the power of simple drugs
n: This is the De simplicium medicamentorum temperamentis ac facultatibus.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Galen's own thirst worsened by strong old wine after a summer walk
s: Galen recalls that once, thirsty from a summer journey on foot, he drank a single cup of old, rather strongly mixed wine. It increased his thirst rather than quenching it.
q: I myself, at any rate, know that once, having become thirsty from a summer journey on foot, and then having drunk a single cup of old wine that was a little too strongly mixed

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Galen read the book with his teachers
s: Galen admits that when he read this book with his teachers he never asked whom it calls 'private persons'; earlier commentators also left the question unexamined.
q: Nor indeed did I myself ever inquire into it during the reading of the book with my teachers.
n: Evidence of how Hippocratic texts were read with teachers in Galen's training.

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Galen's cures by purgation alone and the hatred they earned
s: Rivals hated Galen for curing by purgation alone alopecia, incipient cancer, elephas, phagedaena, scotoma, mania, epilepsy, melancholy, headache and sciatica.
q: another because I completely cured maniacal, epileptic and melancholic patients, and moreover not a few suffering from cephalaea, by purgations alone, just as I did sciatic patients too.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Perfumed akopon with lion's and crocodile fat
s: Andromachus' own perfumed akopon uses aromatised goose, bull, lion and crocodile fats with deer marrow, sal ammoniac, pepper, frankincense, cinnamon, Alexandrian malabathrum and opobalsam.
q: of aromatised lion's fat 2 ounces; of aromatised crocodile fat 1 ounce; of deer marrow 1 ounce

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Fire-free perfumed akopon for a king and Augustus
s: For 'a king and Augustus' Damocrates makes a perfumed akopon without fire: about 3 oz opobalsam, 15 oz malabathrum, 15 oz cinnamon and 10 dr of odourless white wax, worked in a silver bowl over hot water and kept in silver or thick glass.
q: But when making a myrakopon (perfumed akopon) for a king and Augustus, prepare this most easily and without fire, containing a measure of opobalsamum of about three ounces
n: Silver-bowl method at K13.1057.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Heras's white plaster for rabid-dog bites, also as pills
s: Heras's white plaster for hydrophobes: white Pontic wax 2 lb, chrysitis litharge 1 lb, white lead 1 lb, myrrh and deer marrow 2 oz each, frankincense 1 oz, old oil 1 xestes. For severe cases a pill the size of a Pontic nut is given for forty days.
q: one should also make from it a pill the size of a Pontic nut and give it, and [432] do this for forty days.
n: Galen will not test it on rabies (K13.435-436).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Caunian white plaster with hyena fat and deer rennet
s: A white plaster called Caunian: white wax, myrrh, frankincense, deer marrow, hyena fat, deer (or kid) rennet, nitre, galbanum, ammoniac, litharge, white lead, old oil and sea-water.
q: of hyena's fat, 2 ounces; of deer's rennet, 2 ounces, or of kid's

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Oily pitch in vinegar keeps rabid-bite wounds open
s: Galen's drug for rabid dog bites is oily pitch boiled in sharp vinegar (one Roman sextarius vinegar, one litra pitch, three ounces opopanax); it stops the wound closing and suits hard bodies such as diggers and reapers.
q: This drug does not allow the wound of those bitten by rabid dogs to cicatrize.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Costly fragrant nerve-wound drug made for a rich patron
s: For the rich man Galen made a nerve drug of cinnamon, dittany and maron (40 dr each), with a little amaracus because it was hard to get in Rome, in a cerate of the best opobalsam and Tyrrhenian wax.
q: Take of cinnamon, dittany and maron, forty drachms of each; for these are fragrant and fine-particled.
n: Shows luxury pharmacy for elite clients; compare the cheap rustic remedies in K13.582-584.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Halieus's tawny plaster against stingray and weever wounds
s: Asclepiades's tawny plaster of Halieus is for bleeding wounds, cut nerves, breast indurations, dog and human bites, and wounds from sea stingrays, weevers and other dangerous fish.
q: It works excellently also for the strikes of sea stingrays and weevers and the other dangerous fishes.
n: 'Weevers' renders δρακόντων (sea-dragons, i.e. weever fish).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Urine of an uncorrupted boy with nitron and lime for callous ulcers
s: For callous, bank-edged ('sweet') ulcers, Archigenes smears roasted nitron and unslaked lime mixed with the urine of an uncorrupted boy around them, or verdigris, frankincense, salt and honey.
q: smear around them roasted nitron and unslaked lime with the urine of an uncorrupted boy

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Cephalic dry remedy with silphium
s: A cephalic dry remedy with 50 dr of silphium, plus pine resin, pumice or roasted sory, iris, aristolochia, copper scale and frankincense, melts calluses and fills ulcer hollows. Some versions leave out the silphium.
q: The remedy with silphium. It melts away callused parts, cleanses foul parts, fills up the hollows of ulcers, and melts away the little tunics that remain.
n: Cyrenaic silphium was rare or extinct by Galen's day (outside knowledge), which may explain the versions without it.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Damocrates' Tyrian plaster takes on Tyrian purple colour
s: Damocrates' bandage-free Tyrian plaster (litharge 5 lb, wax 1, pine resin 3, verdigris, galbanum, burnt copper, scale, rich oil) takes on the colour of Tyrian purple when properly made. It checks eye fluxes when placed on the forehead.
q: I call it the Tyrian, for it takes on the colour of Tyrian purple, if it is made in the way it ought.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Galen's self-treatment: oil, linen, wool and a bath
s: Galen asked for oil, a linen bandage and wool, went to the bath, and lay in the tub with much oil poured over him while the supplies were fetched. He says most people would rather keep the deformity than suffer forty days of bandaging.
q: I needed oil and [404] linen bandage and wool; I myself went off to the bath and, having a great deal of oil poured over me, I lingered in the basin as long as was possible
n: Galen thinks the clavicle cannot be bent back in fewer than forty days.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Holding the breath cures yawning and hiccups
s: Holding the breath as long as possible ('retention of breath') cures continuous yawning, for the same reason it cures hiccups. Athletes also hold the breath after exercise to force moisture and vapour out of the pores.
q: For holding the respiration for as long as possible, which is called retention of breath, will cure yawnings by the same reasoning by which it cures hiccups.
n: The athletes' practice is in the same unit (σύμπαντες οἱ ἀθληταὶ).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Provoking anger to rouse innate heat
s: Galen notes that Epidemics II advises cultivating a sharp temper to restore colour and spread the humours, since anger stirs the innate heat. He would use it now and then, in moderation, for the chilled, pale and lean.
q: in the second book of the Epidemics too he advised making it a practice to induce sharpness of temper, both for the sake of the recovery of complexion and for the sake of the diffusion of the humours
n: Galen compares it to measured exercise. Frequent ('short') breathing heats and fans chilled parts.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Separating whey from ass's milk with a cold bronze vessel
