s: Instead of whole boiled ass's milk, Galen suggests using the whey alone. The milk is boiled with oxymel and a bronze vessel full of cold water is lowered into it again and again, which separates the whey from the curd.
q: once you have first boiled the milk with oxymel, by repeatedly lowering into the milk a bronze vessel full of cold water

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Twelve to sixteen kotylai of ass's milk: customary for the ancients
s: The appendix prescribes at least 12 kotylai of boiled ass's milk, and over 16 if the patient is strong. Galen says such quantities were customary with all the ancients. For the upward purge he would give white hellebore or another emetic.
q: do not be surprised at the quantity of the milk, for this was customary with all the ancients.
n: 12 kotylai is about 3.3 litres.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Winter regimen: much food, little and strong wine, roasts
s: In winter eat as much and drink as little as possible: wine as unmixed as possible, bread, all dishes roasted, few vegetables, to keep the body warm and dry.
q: The drink should be wine as unmixed as possible; the foods should be bread, and the dishes all roasted.
n: Galen: 'as much as possible' means relative to the other seasons, not to capacity (K15.178).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Slimming regimen: exercise fasting, eat while panting, sesame
s: To grow thin, do all exertion on an empty stomach, eat while still panting and not yet cooled down after a little mixed, not very cold wine, and season dishes with sesame and spices so that fatty food fills quickly.
q: Fat persons, and all who wish to become thin, must perform all their exertions while fasting, and set about their food while still panting and not yet cooled down
n: Galen warns this has caused liver obstructions in many (K15.193-194).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Emetic for the thin: warm bath, mixed foods, three wines
s: The thin vomit after food. Bathe in warm water, drink a kotyle of unmixed wine, eat many kinds of food, wait as long as it takes to walk four stades, then drink three wines (austere, sweet, sour), first strong and slow, then watery, fast and plentiful.
q: let them hold off for as long as it takes to traverse four stades. Then, having mixed together three wines, give them to drink, an austere, a sweet and a sour one
n: Time measured as a walking distance.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Infants: long warm baths and very watery wine
s: Babies should be bathed in warm water for a long time and given very watery wine that is not cold and does not cause wind, so that they have fewer convulsions, grow larger and have a better colour.
q: Infant children should be bathed in warm water for a long time, and should be given wine to drink that is most watery and not altogether cold
n: Galen: tense bodies are more prone to spasm (citing Hippocrates), and infants are prone because of weak nerves and greedy eating.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Physicians mistake two tertians for one quotidian
s: Galen often saw attending physicians take an interwoven double tertian for a single quotidian, convincing them only when the earlier tertian resolved and the severer remained.
q: often in the case of the sick we have seen the attending physicians supposing a complication of two tertians to be a single quotidian

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: An athlete of the xystos cured with the toad akopon
s: An athlete of the xystos used the toad akopon as both akopon and malagma and was freed of his whole condition. Large toads are sealed in a woven basket and boiled in the oil until they dissolve.
q: A man of the xystos (an athlete) used this both as an akopon and as a malagma, and was delivered from the whole condition.
n: The basket method is at K13.1023-1024.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Flavius Clemens' akopon: gout-crippled men walked again
s: Flavius Clemens' akopon (Sabine oil, wild cucumber root, wax, terebinth, deer marrow, galbanum, six frogs) is said to have made men contorted all over by gout of feet and hands walk about unmaimed.
q: We know of men contorted in the whole body by podagra and cheiragra who, having used this, were saved to such an extent that they walked about unmaimed.
n: Flavius Clemens is a name borne by Domitian's cousin, the consul of 95 (outside knowledge); the identification is not certain.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Fistulous thigh healed overnight under the phoinikine
s: A youth's thigh suppurated near the groin and became fistulous under the skin. Galen planned to cut it near the kneecap, but on the day of the operation it was found dry and closed, so he kept using the drug.
q: But when the thigh was unbound on the following day, on which I had resolved to cut it, everything was found to have fallen together, dry and without moisture.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Farmer's boy with a parotid fistula cured by litharge plaster
s: In the country Galen gave a 15-year-old farmer's son a litharge-vinegar-oil plaster for a six-month fistula left after a parotid swelling; he forgot the case, and two months later the boy came back healed.
q: For the boy was a farmer's son, about fifteen years of age
n: A pig's bristle was used as a probe; a second similar boy was then cured.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Pankratiast bitten on the index finger nearly lost it
s: Someone persuaded a physician to apply the Attalic white plaster to a young man bitten on the index finger in the pankration; putrefaction set in and the finger was agglutinated only with difficulty.
q: a young man who had been bitten on the index finger in the pankration, who was in such a bad state that the whole bitten part was in danger of rotting away
n: Biting was forbidden in the pankration, so this detail is notable (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Improvised verdigris cerate in a village without drugs
s: In a village with no drugs Galen found only verdigris and wax; he melted the wax with rose oil and added verdigris at one twelfth, and both 1/10 and 1/12 proved right for different bodies.
q: I myself once did in a certain village, in which I neither had any drug with me myself, nor was anyone else among the people there well supplied

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Asclepiades: 'the Best' plaster held loose bone fragments
s: Asclepiades reports using his black fracture plaster 'the Best' on fractures with many floating bone fragments; when everyone advised removing them, the plaster made them form callus with the rest.
q: I used this drug in the case of fractures in which many bones were floating loose, and when all were advising me to lift out the floating ones, 'the Best' accomplished something resembling a marvel.
n: The first person is Asclepiades, quoted verbatim by Galen.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Teachers' wet treatment of gladiators' knee tendons killed most
s: Galen saw his teachers treat gladiators wounded at the kneecap tendon with hot water and wheat-flour poultices in water-and-oil; very few survived, and those were lamed.
q: But perhaps it would be better to say not being treated, but perishing; for very few of them survived, and these became lame.
n: Unit failed the automatic check; the sense is clear in the Greek.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Euphorbium cerate invented for a chilled knee, sent to the bath
s: In a hard winter a man with a knee that hurt when chilled asked for a heating drug and said he would send for it from the bath. Galen improvised euphorbium ground in oil with melted wax, and the man was soon free of pain.
q: "Now then," he said, "I am going off to bathe, and I shall send for the drug from the bath."
n: Origin story of Galen's euphorbium cerate.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Contused middle finger: tendon thought rotten was preserved
s: A young man's contused middle finger was putrefying; Galen used lye with raw barley meal, then bitter-vetch. A half-rotten sinewy membrane came away, which onlookers took for the whole nerve, but the tendon was intact.
q: It seemed, then, to all those who saw it that this body was the whole nerve, rotted through, since they did not know how these tendons, clothed in sinewy membranes, both pass forward through the wrist
n: The troche of Polyeides dissolved in hepsema was used next.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Nerve-wounded man relapsed after going out in the cold
s: On day four, pain-free, a nerve-wounded patient went out in great cold on business and came home with the limb tense up to the neck. Galen bathed it in hot oil and applied liquid euphorbium with castoreum, and by evening the symptoms had stopped.
q: went out of the house in great cold for some necessary business, and having spent a longer time at it, came home with the whole limb strained with tension as far as the neck and feeling great pain.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Country improvisations for nerve wounds: propolis, leaven, spurge
s: On journeys and in the country Galen treated nerve wounds with what was at hand: a farmer's fresh propolis, old leaven, both mixed, or leaven with juice of spurge growing near the farmyard.
q: In the case of another countryman I mixed the juice of spurge with the leaven and applied it, having seen it growing near his farmyard; for I had judged the leaven deficient as being fresh.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Farmer copied Galen's pigeon-dung remedy for nerve wounds
s: Galen once used acrid dung of pigeons from country towers on a nerve-wounded young man; the farmer managing the estate, 'not unintelligent', copied it and has used it on nerve wounds ever since.
q: And the farmer who had charge of this estate, having observed this — for he was not unintelligent — imitated it and always uses it and treats those who have been wounded in the nerves.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Varix excised: old ulcer healed, new malignant ulcer at incision
s: After a varicose vein over an ulcer was cut out, the year-old ulcer healed at once, but a malignant ulcer that would not heal formed at the incision. Galen therefore advises bleeding, purging and lengthwise scarification of the vein first.
q: the ulcer was immediately cicatrized, even though it was a year old, but that in its place, at the incision from which the vein was excised, a malignant ulcer arose, which could not be cicatrized.
n: Galen does not say whether the patient was his own.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Heras: Halieus plaster cured a stingray wound
s: Heras says he once used the Halieus plaster (with Sinopian earth) on a man struck by a sea stingray who was in dreadful pain, and it worked marvellously; also on scorpion stings.
q: Indeed, I once used it on someone who had been struck by a sea stingray and was suffering most dreadfully, and it worked marvellously; likewise also on those stung by scorpions.
n: The first person is Heras, quoted by Galen, not Galen himself.

wt: On Plethora
t: Teacher bled a man thrown from a carriage, dragged by reins
s: Galen reminded the teacher he had bled a healthy, well-exercised man who fell from a carriage, was entangled in the reins and dragged, having only bruises; also an ophthalmia, a headache and a pleuritic.
q: the other having fallen from a carriage and then become entangled in the reins and dragged for a considerable distance, so that certain parts were bruised
n: The teacher was left 'in the greatest perplexity'.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Delirious patients forget the chamber-pot
s: Galen has seen many delirious patients ask for a chamber-pot and then hold it without urinating, or sit down to defecate and forget, until reminded. Breathing in delirium is likewise slow but large.
q: we know of very many who asked for a chamber-pot, but when it was given no longer urinated, but held it idly in their two hands
n: Clinical observation used to explain why breathing in delirium is large and rare.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Wife of Dealces in Thasos, on the Leion
s: Sick from grief with an acute shivering fever, she wrapped herself up, picked at hairs and swung between tears and laughter. Her breathing was mostly rare and large, sometimes short, and she died on day 21.
q: 'In Thasos the wife of Dealces, who lay sick on the Leion, was seized by an acute fever with shivering, arising from grief
n: Galen reads her drinking only when reminded, the parched skin and the drinks passing straight through as signs of the innate heat dying out (K7.866-867).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: The man from the mines
s: Epidemics IV: a man from the mines had a tense right hypochondrium, a large spleen, a tense and hard belly, and was 'full of pneuma' and colourless. Galen says the term could mean short of breath or bloated.
q: 'The man from the mines: right hypochondrium tense, spleen large, belly tense, somewhat hard, full of pneuma, colourless.'
n: Social detail: a mine worker as a patient.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Old man on watery wine; rival mocks 'he only looks at it'
s: Galen tells how he gave a sick old man water with a few drops of wine each day. A visiting physician laughed that the patient was not drinking wine but only looking at it. Galen explains that wine given for benefit is mixed differently from wine given for pleasure.
q: laughed and said that the sick man was not drinking wine [699] but only looking at it
n: Checks verdict is 'fail'.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Burning fever from wine mixed with sea-water and salted foods
s: Galen knows people seized by kausos after drinking a lot of wine mixed with sea-water, and others after eating too much salt-fish, salted meat and other salty foods.
q: I know of some who were seized by burning fever because of drinking a rather large quantity of wine mixed with sea-water
n: Wine treated with sea-water was a known style, for example Coan.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Surgeons opening muscle swellings found only scattered air
s: Some surgeons who cut into unnatural swellings in muscles, expecting pus, found only pneuma scattered through the flesh. Others found clots or a viscous, mucus-like fluid.
q: some have sometimes cut into swellings contrary to nature in muscles, expecting to find pus in the depth, and then found nothing other than pneuma scattered in small portions throughout the whole flesh
n: K15.770-771 continues with the clots and mucus.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Hiccup from pepper; feverish patients cured by vomiting acrid humour
s: Galen notes that hiccup can come from something pungent biting the stomach mouth, as when someone swallows too much pepper. Some febrile patients vomited a corrosive humour and were freed of hiccup at once.
q: as when someone swallows too much pepper or something of that kind

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: Hidden scirrhus of the liver revealed by dropsy and wasting
s: A scirrhous tumour in the concave liver may escape notice until dropsy follows; Galen saw many where a large tumour suddenly appeared once it reached the convex parts and the hypochondrial muscles wasted.
q: At any rate I have seen not a few who, along such a course of symptoms, in a short time brought to light a not small tumour in a scirrhous liver

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Layman with ulcerous eruptions refuses phlebotomy
s: A sensible layman with sudden ulcerous, discoloured eruptions demanded purging; told to be bled, he answered that the good would be evacuated with the corrupted.
q: 'Are you not mad?' he said, 'for it stands to reason that the good will be evacuated together with the corrupted.'

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Yearly melancholic purged in spring and autumn
s: A man who falls into melancholy every year unless purged is purged by Galen in both spring and autumn.
q: a certain man is seized by melancholy every year if he is not purged, and I purge him not only in spring but also in autumn.

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Incipient elephas controlled by yearly purgation
s: A man with beginning elephas (elephantiasis) was cured by phlebotomy and purgation; one purgation a year now suffices, and omitting it brings back signs of the disease.
q: In another man I cured an incipient elephas at first by phlebotomy and purgation, and each year thereafter a single purgation suffices for him too

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Summer tertians prevented by late-spring bile purge
s: A man always seized by tertian fevers in summer has had no fever for many years since Galen purged him of yellow bile in advance at the end of spring.
q: Another man, who was always seized by tertian fevers in the season of summer, has now for many years not had a fever, being purged of yellow bile by us in anticipation at the end of spring.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Killing a land tortoise for its blood with a two-edged reed
s: In the black-poplar akopon, saffron unguent is taken up in the blood of a land tortoise, killed at the collar-bone with a reed sharpened on both sides. More blood improves the drug.
q: The tortoise is slaughtered at the collar-bone with a reed sharpened on both sides.
n: Tortoise blood recurs in the Halieus and Valerius Paulinus akopa (K13.1025, K13.1026-1027).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Hernia surgeons apply the plaster right after operating
s: Many who operate on hernias apply the phoinikine immediately after surgery, without even moistening the wound first, to prevent inflammation.
q: many of those who operate on hernias also apply it immediately after the surgery, carrying through the treatment with it together with the affusions and the poultices.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Rectal injection by horn tube fitted with a pig's bladder
s: For inflamed swellings of the seat and rectum, the plaster is melted with more oil, in a water bath over smokeless coals, and injected through a straight-bored horn with a pig's bladder tied on.
q: so that it can be injected through a straight-bored horn having a pig's bladder fastened to it, as we are accustomed to use in such cases.
n: A simple clyster device; also used for sinuses (K13.499-500).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Storing gathered herbs: dry rooms with south-facing windows
s: Herbs should be watched through their fruiting stages to learn when to gather them, and stored in dry rooms, not underground, not under tiles, with windows facing south, away from sun-baking and damp.
q: This would come about if the rooms are neither underground nor προσχόρων (adjoining the ground?), nor under tiles, having, however, their windows turned toward the south.
n: The draft leaves προσχόρων untranslated with a guess; the word is rare and uncertain.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Letting the nerve-wounded bathe: oiled linen over the plaster
s: Since patients insist on bathing, Galen puts a plaster on the wound, several oil-soaked folded linens and a linen bandage over it, and pours oil on the bandage just before the patient steps into the tub.
q: I first pour the oil over the bandage, when the person wounded in the nerves is about to step into the tub
n: The Greek reads εἰς τὴν πτύελον (spittle), surely a corruption of πύελον (tub); the draft silently translates 'tub', correctly.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Bath test of euphorbium unguent strength
s: Galen's test unguent is euphorbium 1, wax 3, oil 12. Rubbed on the body it shows the drug's strength, especially in the bath, where fresh strong euphorbium makes the skin sting in the air and even more in the water.
q: And it becomes most evident in the bath; for people are stung strongly, by the air indeed, but still more by the water, when the euphorbium is hot and new and strong.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Exercise with halteres in place of bathing for leg ulcers
s: If the patient can safely skip bathing, he is rubbed with linen and oil and exercises with jumping-weights when the ulcer is on the leg, or by running when it is higher up. Bathers keep the bandage on and cool the sponge at once.
q: being rubbed down with linen cloths for a longer time, and next with oil, and then exercising with jumping-weights (halteres) if the affected part is a leg, or by running if it is in the parts above.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Boiling Heras' panacea outdoors because of fire risk
s: Heras' panacea ('Health') is made of herbs steeped overnight in oil, then litharge, ampelitis and asphalt boiled over a gentle fire. It must be boiled outdoors and never allowed to boil over, because once it catches fire it is hard to put out.
q: One must take care that it never boils over, and, as far as possible, boil it in an open space, for it becomes hard to extinguish if it catches hold of anything.
n: Ingredients at K13.766-767: chamaepitys, comfrey, chamaeleon, horehound, polion, centaury, elecampane, aristolochia and others.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Reduction of a forward dislocation with strap counter-extension
s: At the Smyrna wrestling school, a wrestler's arm spread out by his opponent threw the joint forward, and Galen reduced it on the spot. With the patient on his back, an assistant seated behind pulled a broad strap round the armpit over a pad. Galen pushed the head past the constricting muscles, then relaxed the extension so the muscles drew it into the socket.
q: Having laid the patient down on his back, we made the counter-extension similar to that performed by means of the heel, seating someone behind him and throwing a broad strap around the armpit
n: The general aims are counter-extension, levering and replacement, but the levering differs from that for an axillary dislocation.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Clavicle fracture: fourteen days' rest suffice
s: Customary bandaging with the right posture heals it quickly. Lying down helps greatly; fourteen days are enough if the patient keeps still, and twenty are very many. 'Customary' bandaging is like an unwritten law.
q: yet for the man to lie down makes a great difference, and fourteen days are sufficient, if he keeps still, and twenty are very many.
n: Hippocratic lemma; Galen adds the 'unwritten law' (ἄγραφον) gloss.

wt: On Leeches, Revulsion, Cupping, Incision and Scarification
t: Preparing newly caught leeches before use
s: Leeches kept by hunters are tamed and bite readily; newly caught ones are kept one day and fed a little blood so their venomous quality is squeezed out.
q: Those newly caught must be kept for one day, with a little blood thrown in to them for nourishment; for in this way their venomous quality will be squeezed out.
n: ἐκμειλίττουσαι ('tamed') describes leeches kept in captivity. Authenticity of this short tract is doubted; it is often assigned to Antyllus or a later compiler (outside knowledge).

wt: On Leeches, Revulsion, Cupping, Incision and Scarification
t: Applying leeches; snipping tails; salt or ash to detach
s: Leeches are placed in lukewarm water, handled with a sponge, and warm oil poured over the part; if they draw little, their tails are snipped so they keep drawing until salt or ash is sprinkled on their mouths.
q: If they should take hold only a little, one must snip off their tails; for as the blood pours out, they do not cease drawing until we sprinkle salt or ash upon their mouths.
n: Hands or feet are immersed in the water holding the leeches. After they fall off, a cupping-glass draws out the 'venomous' matter.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Colour change of blood as limit of venesection
s: Blood is let until its colour changes: redder if the body's blood is phlegmatic, livid or blackish if it is red. If the patient's strength cannot bear that much, Galen says it is better to stop than to break down the faculty.
q: it is more fitting to refrain from breaking down the faculty than from evacuating the excess blood

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Plethora reduced without bleeding in two or three days
s: Even when the plethoric syndrome is present Galen does not always bleed. Rubbing, more frequent baths and a reduced diet restore the patient in two or three days. He refers to On Plethora, On Phlebotomy and the Therapeutic Method.
q: by means of rubbing and more frequent baths and a deficient regimen we bring the patient back to the natural state in two or even three days

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Inspecting the throat by depressing the tongue
s: In the bilious kind of synanche, if the patient opens the mouth wide and the tongue is pressed down, the visible pharynx shows no swelling. The inflamed part lies out of sight.
q: And if you bid these patients open the mouth as wide as possible and depress the tongue, in order to inspect the parts about the pharynx

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Three kinds of dropsy; ascites tapped by paracentesis
s: Galen distinguishes ascites (thin fluid below the thorax, sometimes drained by tapping), tympanias (full of air) and hyposarkidios (phlegm throughout the body). Some physicians wrongly posit four kinds.
q: of the dropsies one kind gathers a quantity of fluid that is thin in consistency in the whole region below the thorax, and by tapping this we sometimes evacuate the fluid

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Preventive spring evacuation against gout, apoplexy, epilepsy
s: People liable to illness are evacuated at the onset of spring, by phlebotomy for plethoric diseases or purgation for corruption; Galen claims years of prevention of podagra and early arthritis before tophi formed, and of apoplexy, epilepsy and melancholy.
q: We, at any rate, have by means of such evacuation prevented, for many years indeed, both podagra and arthritis that was beginning and had not yet produced tophi about the joints from coming about.
n: Tophi = πώρους.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Dating: Galen first hears type-theory c. 161 CE
s: Galen first heard this theory just after Antoninus (Pius), emperor after Hadrian, had died, when the new emperor took the name Antoninus and made Lucius co-ruler.
q: Antoninus, who became emperor after Hadrian, had recently departed from among men, and at that time Severus was ruling, having renamed himself Antoninus
n: Antoninus Pius died March 161 CE; the accession of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus dates the episode (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Alexandria and Egypt: castor, radish and mustard oils abundant
s: If you are in Alexandria, melt the drug with castor oil and radish oil, which are most plentiful there and in all Egypt; mustard oil is also easily had there.
q: if you happen to be in Alexandria, with castor oil and radish oil, for these are most abundant in that city, as indeed throughout the whole of Egypt.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Natural cadmia from Cypriot torrents and mines
s: The naturally occurring cadmia, which needs no processing, is found in winter torrents, streams and the mountains of Cyprus, and elsewhere, especially near mines.
q: which, without undergoing any transformation, is found in the winter torrents and streams and in the mountains of the Cyprians, and in other regions too, but especially in those where the mines are.
n: Galen is known from other works to have visited the Cypriot mines at Soloi (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Cyprus: chief source of ladanum; a physician used it fresh
s: Ladanum is produced in greatest quantity in Cyprus. A physician there applied it fresh and soft to hard-to-heal ulcers, softening it with myrtle, henna or rose oil once it hardened.
q: In Cyprus, at any rate, where it is produced in the greatest quantity, a certain physician, kneading it while it was still fresh and soft, applied it to such ulcers

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Hermon the sacred scribe; recipe from the Hephaesteum in Egypt
s: The same plaster is called that of Hermon the sacred scribe, and others say it came from the inner sanctuaries of the Hephaesteum in Egypt, like the dittany plaster. Galen says these are all one drug.
q: He called it, as some others also do, the plaster of Hermon the sacred scribe. In others you would find it written that this one too is from the inner sanctuaries at the Hephaesteum in Egypt
n: Evidence that temple origins were claimed for recipes, with Egyptian priestly scribes as authorities.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Thasos woman lodging by the 'Market of Liars'
s: Epidemics III woman lying sick at the Market of Liars after a difficult first birth of a son, with rigors, delirium and later coma.
q: a woman who lay sick in the Market of Liars (ἐπὶ ψευδέων ἀγορῇ), having then for the first time given birth, with difficulty, to a male child
n: A Thasian place name in Epidemics III (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Galen's student years in Smyrna
s: Galen first saw a forward shoulder dislocation while still studying under his teachers in Smyrna, a city he says is many times larger than Hippocrates' home town.
q: In our Asia I first beheld such a dislocation while still being educated under the teachers there, in Smyrna.
n: Biographical: confirms Galen's study at Smyrna (outside knowledge: under Pelops).

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Ostia: Galen's network of physician friends
s: Not even at the harbour and the nearby city of Ostia could such a case escape Galen, because all the physicians practising there were his friends.
q: not even at the harbour and the city near it which they call Ostia, because all those practising medicine in those districts too were friends
n: Evidence of Galen's professional network around Rome and Portus/Ostia.

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Rome, 'this most populous city', full of jaundiced and dropsical
s: Galen challenges the sophists to a public contest of deeds in the city where countless jaundiced and dropsical patients can be found every day.
q: with the very deeds to which I summon them in this most populous city, in which countless jaundiced persons can be found every day, and countless dropsical ones.
n: The city is Rome (named at K11.340-341).

wt: Against Lycus
t: Bathhouse detail: heated stone for rolling on
s: In his analogy of well-mixed and ill-mixed baths, Galen mentions a well-tempered stone in the bath on which bathers can roll about.
q: So at any rate a stone too becomes well-mixed in the baths themselves, one on which it is possible to roll about
n: Bath faults are listed as too cold, too hot, full of vapour, and smoky (203). Smoke differs with the fuel: oak, fig, olive (203).

wt: Against Lycus
t: Every educated Greek is expected to have read the Philebus
s: Galen asks whether any Greek physician, grammarian, rhetor or philosopher could not have read the Philebus. He also says Lycus lacks the first lessons taught in the philosophers' schools.
q: Could there be any Greek man — physician or grammarian or rhetor or philosopher, or in general anyone else at all who lays claim to argument — who has not read Plato’s Philebus?
n: 'ἐν ταῖς φιλοσόφων διατριβαῖς', 'in the schools of the philosophers', is evidence of a common curriculum in dialectic expected of physicians.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Goldworkers use chaff fire (Lycus)
s: Lycus held that chaff fire is the weakest and is therefore suited to goldworking, since gold melts and runs in a stronger flame. Galen says goldworkers customarily use it.
q: thinking that the fire of chaff is the weakest, he says that it is serviceable for the working of gold; for the gold, he says, melts and flows away when it comes near a stronger flame.
n: The craft custom is stated at 222-223 (ὡς χρῆσθαι τοῖς τὸν χρυσὸν ἐργαζομένοις ἔθος). The draft's 'serviceable' renders ἐνταμίευτον, a rare and odd word that may be corrupt.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Books to Hephaestus or cut up for everyday use
s: Galen says such books should be given to Hephaestus (burned) or will perish with time, nobody copying them, and even being cut up for everyday needs.
q: let them, being ashamed, at last some day summon Hephaestus upon their books; or, even if they themselves do not summon him, time will destroy them.
n: Evidence for recycling of unwanted papyrus rolls.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Nychthemeron and a year of 365 and a quarter days
s: Here 'day' means day plus night, called by some nychthemeron, just as the year is said to be 365 and a quarter days.
q: Thus at any rate we also say that the year is of 365 days and a quarter.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: History of oils: castor oil ancient in Egypt; radish, mustard, sesame oils
s: Olive oil was once the only oil. Castor oil came later 'among you' but was ancient in Egypt, followed by radish, mustard and sesame oils; 'among us' lily, mastic and lentisk oils and perfumed unguents.
q: but later castor oil was added to it, among you at any rate. For in Egypt this too was ancient, and after castor oil again others, radish oil and mustard oil and sesame oil
n: Contrasts 'among you' and 'among us', apparently Italy/Rome against Galen's Greek East; the reference is not certain.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Fine wines for drugs: Ariousian, Lesbian, Tmolite, Falernian
s: Substitutes for Falernian: the Ariousian of Chios, the fragrant Lesbian (little at Mitylene, more and better at Eresos and Methymna), and the Tmolite, which resembles Falernian; a second Tmolite is dry and astringent.
q: the very fragrant Lesbian, which is produced in small quantity at Mitylene, but at Eresos and Methymna is at once both more abundant and better, and the Tmolite, which resembles the Falernian.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: 'Pontic' wax as a trade name for any white wax
s: Naturally white wax is called Pontic even when it comes from elsewhere, because Pontus produces the most; Tyrrhenian wax is not naturally white.
q: Naturally white is the so-called Pontic wax—for it is now customarily so named even if it comes from some other region, because white wax is produced in the greatest quantity in Pontus

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Roman litra: same name for weight and for horn liquid measure
s: At Rome the litra of weight for solids has the same name as the litra measure for liquids, a very common horn vessel found throughout the whole city.
q: For among the Romans the litra weight of solid bodies is called by the same name as the litra measure of liquids, which is very common throughout the whole city, being made of horn material.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Rhodian white lead imitated by makers at Puteoli
s: For a very white plaster use Rhodian white lead; some white-lead makers at Puteoli, formerly Dicaearchia, make theirs white in the same way.
q: in the city formerly named Dicaearchia and now Puteoli, some of those who prepare white lead are accustomed to make it white in the same way as the Rhodian.
n: Evidence for white-lead (cerussa) manufacture at Puteoli.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Old recipes' kotyle equals nine Roman ounces
s: Some say the mina has 20 ounces, others 16. From old recipes written before Roman dominance Galen infers that their kotyle equals nine ounces of the litra now used in Rome.
q: I have conjectured that what those authors call a kotyle is equal to nine of the ounces that make up the litra now in use in Rome.
n: Compare K13.429-430 (some say 16 2/3 ounces) and K13.434-435 (Roman xestes 20).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Roman xestes = 20 measure-ounces; horn measures with rings
s: The xestes name spread to all Greek-speakers under Roman rule, but the measure varies; the Roman xestes holds 1 2/3 litrai, i.e. 20 ounces, measured with horns marked with circular lines. Some wrongly say 18.
q: Among the Romans, at any rate, the xestes contains one litra and a half and a sixth, so that the ounces in all are twenty; and these they for the most part measure with the horns
n: Important metrological testimony.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Powerful patrons order plasters by colour
s: Because some very powerful men order a quince-yellow plaster for a given purpose, later physicians grouped plasters by colour and added their uses.
q: some of the very powerful men sometimes order us to make for them a quince-yellow plaster that is agglutinative of wounds, or cicatrizing, or emollient of parts that are becoming hardened
n: Explains the colour-based arrangement of recipe books such as Andromachus's.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Hard bodies of farmers, sailors and hunters need stronger drugs
s: Galen calls 'stronger' the drier bodies of farmers, sailors and hunters, and 'weaker' the soft bodies of women, eunuchs and children.
q: those that are drier in their temperaments, such as are those of farmers, sailors and hunters; by weaker, those that are softer by nature or by habit, such as those of women, eunuchs and children

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Colophonian frankincense-scented resin: scarce and costly
s: The frankincense-like Colophonian resin, which some call the only true Colophonian, smells pleasant and heats moderately; it is produced in very small quantity and is therefore expensive.
q: It is produced in very small quantity, and for this reason it is costly.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Menoetus's 'pugilistic' plaster used by boxers
s: Menoetus's first quince-yellow plaster is called 'pugilistic' because boxers in particular use it.
q: the one called the 'pugilistic' plaster, because boxers in particular use the drug
n: Confirms the label 'for boxers (πυκτική)' on Serapion's plaster in K13.509.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Ariusian wine once used for antidotes, now Falernian
s: The finest tawny wines 'among us in Asia' are the Tmolite, the Lesbian and the Ariusian of Chios, which everyone once used for the finest drugs and antidotes, as they now use Falernian.
q: the one most renowned among the ancients, the Ariusian, which is produced in Chios, which everyone used to use for the finest of the drugs and especially [514] for the antidotes, just as now they use the Falernian.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Oil measured by a horn litra marked in twelve ounces
s: Romans measure oil with a horn vessel incised with lines into twelve parts; the whole is a litra and each part an ounce, distinct from the weight ounce used on the balance for metals and wax.
q: There is among them a measure, with which they measure oil, incised with lines that divide the whole into twelve parts; and the whole measure is called by them a litra, and the twelfth part of it an ounce.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Roman name 'specularium' for transparent stone
s: The transparent stone that the Romans call specularium dries without biting when burnt; it suits hard-to-heal ulcers but is too mild for malignant ones.
q: the so-called transparent stone, which the Romans name specularium, is, when burnt, among the things that dry without biting
n: Latin lapis specularis (selenite or mica, used for window panes), transliterated in Greek. Burnt glass and copper-boiler deposits are said to have the same power.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: 'Unadulterated' wine means wine without added seawater
s: Galen explains that apárachytos (unadulterated) wine is wine with no seawater mixed in. It is poured hot over chalcitis and cadmia to take away the chalcitis's sharpness.
q: he pours the unadulterated wine—that is, one with which seawater has not been mixed—hot over the chalcitis and the cadmia
n: Evidence that seawater was routinely added to wine. Cf. 'wine free of sea-water' at K13.830-831 and K13.1014-1015.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Sardian earth, used by fullers, in a scrofula plaster
s: A plaster for scrofulous and parotid swellings contains beef suet, terebinth, manna, and five ounces of the Sardian earth that fullers use.
q: of the earth called Sardian, which the fullers use, five ounces.
n: Greek has 'σάρδης' (earth 'called sarde'), which the draft renders as 'Sardian'. Evidence that the earth was used in the fulling trade.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Jewish asphalt and pine-wood spatula in the black Hikesios
s: Heras' black Hikesios plaster calls for 100 dr each of litharge, Jewish asphalt and ampelitis earth, stirred with a pine-wood spatula. It treats wounds, dog-bites, indurations and dropsy.
q: Litharge 100 dr.; Jewish asphalt 100 dr.; ampelitis earth 100 dr.
n: Dead Sea bitumen (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Kotyle differs by city: Attic, Alexandrian, Ephesian
s: Andromachus, who lived in Rome, should have used litrai, xestai and ounces. The kotyle is used in Greek cities outside Italy and differs greatly between them, so the city (Attic, Alexandrian, Ephesian) must be stated.
q: he ought to have said either 'I mean the Attic cotyle' or the Alexandrian or the Ephesian or some other.
n: Most writers on measures say the physicians' kotyle is 9 Roman ounces; others say 12; Galen heard one claim 16.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Tasks possible with an unreduced shoulder
s: Adults with an unreduced dislocated shoulder cannot lift the elbow sideways, but can still draw a drill or saw, hew with an axe and dig, provided the elbow is not raised high.
q: for they could draw a drill (ἀρίς) and a saw, and could hew with an axe and dig, provided they do not raise the elbow very much upward
n: Hippocratic lemma; manual-labour detail.

wt: On Plethora
t: Laymen's words for stomach distress
s: Laymen describe being weighed down by food, being bitten and gnawed, or, unable to describe it, say they are nauseated (asasthai).
q: often, being unable to describe accurately what is happening, they say that they are nauseated (ἀσᾶσθαι).

wt: On Plethora
t: Trainers' three kinds of fatigue
s: Precise gymnastic trainers distinguish ulcerous, tensive and inflammatory fatigue; tensive fatigue means limbs 'filled up', inflammation adds throbbing pain.
q: the more precise of the gymnastic trainers too, when they call one of the fatigues ulcerous, another tensive, and another inflammatory

wt: On Plethora
t: Wine-jars bursting from must turned to pneuma
s: Not only sinews and ropes burst from tension but often wine-jars, from must that has turned to pneuma.
q: often also wine-jars, from must that has turned to pneuma.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Teachers lecturing from high thrones
s: Galen mocks teachers who sit on high, prominent chairs in their lectures to the young, ignore clinical practice and say whatever comes to mind.
q: But as many as, in their lecture-sessions with the young, seated upon high thrones, lofty
n: Detail of 2nd-century medical teaching. K7.828-829: such sophists 'sit indoors' and never see the sick.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Newly bought female house-slave as patient
s: Epidemics IV records a newly bought female house-slave with a large, not very painful hardness on her right side, who was 'not very dyspnoeic'.
q: "For the female house-slave, whom I saw when she was newly bought, [955] in whom the hardening (sklerysma) in the right parts was large, not very painful"
n: Evidence that physicians examined slaves, possibly at the time of purchase.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Synkomistos bread now called autopyros
s: Hippocrates' synkomistos bread, made with the bran left in, is what people of Galen's day call autopyros.
q: people nowadays call such bread autopyros, since the branny flour in it is not separated out but is kneaded up together with the pure

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Watery wines for fever patients: Sabine, Titacazene, Tibine
s: The best wine for the feverish is watery, white, thin and odourless. Galen's examples are the slack Sabine of Italy, which is given to fever patients, and the Titacazene and Tibine of Asia.
q: in Italy the slack Sabine, which they also give to those with fever; in Asia the Titacazene and the Tibine.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Dosage test: one kyathos of honey versus two of wine daily
s: To compare the nourishment in honey and wine fairly, Galen describes a trial: one kyathos of honey a day against two kyathoi of wine, each diluted as the patient likes.
q: he can, say, take one kyathos of honey either by itself or, mixing in as much water as he wishes
n: The kyathos is about 0.045 litre.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Holding back stool when no privy is near
s: Galen illustrates reverse peristalsis from ordinary life. When we hold back a bowel movement because of urgent business or because no privy is near, we feel the bile run back up.
q: or because there is no privy near at hand; for on such occasions we perceive the bile running back up in such a way that it is no longer excreted.
n: The same unit cites his commentaries On the Natural Faculties for peristalsis.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Bathing in tubs in army camps without a bathhouse
s: Galen notes that patients are still often bathed in a room with a fire and a tub of water in army camps, wherever there is no bathhouse.
q: which even now often happens in army camps, whenever someone needs to bathe but the place has no bathhouse

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Low pools at natural springs, level with the floor
s: The easiest tub to get in and out of is like the pools at natural hot springs. These are built so low that they hardly rise above the surrounding floor.
q: best and least fatiguing of all is the arrangement in the bathing-pools at natural waters, which nearly everyone makes so low that they do not project at all above the adjoining floor

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Wrestlers and pankratiasts strangled by an armlock
s: As an example of a manifest cause of sudden voicelessness Galen gives a wrestler or pankratiast nearly strangled by an opponent's forearms locked around him.
q: as if someone wrestling or competing in the pankration were brought into danger of being strangled from the encircling of the forearms

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Breads from emmer, einkorn, barley; peasants bake millet loaves
s: Explaining 'cereal foods', Galen lists the grains used for bread: wheat above all, then emmer (zeia), einkorn (tiphē) and barley. Country people even make loaves from millet.
q: zeia (emmer) and [876] tiphe (einkorn) and barley; and country people make loaves even from millet

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Goats are best in summer from feeding on tree shoots
s: Goat meat is best in summer and worst in autumn. Galen explains that goats then feed on the shoots and stalks of trees, which are plentiful in late spring and summer.
q: for goats the most suitable nourishment is the shoots and stalks of trees, which they have in abundance at the end of spring and during the summer

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Foxes and the beccafico taste best in autumn from grapes
s: To show that diet shapes meat quality, Galen notes that foxes have their finest flesh in autumn from eating grapes. The small bird called sykalis (beccafico) is likewise finest then.
q: you can learn also from foxes, which in autumn especially have the finest flesh on account of the grapes

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Homer's suitors: fattened hogs and blood-stuffed goat stomachs
s: Galen quotes Homer on piglets (choiroi) for servants and fattened hogs for the suitors. He mocks the suitors as undiscerning eaters who also ate goat stomachs stuffed with blood and fat, the hardest food to digest.
q: just as also in their eating the stomachs of goats stuffed with blood and fat, than which what food could you find harder to digest?
n: The lines are from Odyssey 14.80-81, and the goat-stomach sausages from Odyssey 18 and 20.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: 'Up in the air' (meteōros): current slang for absent-minded
s: Galen says the author was either forgetful or 'such a person as the one nowadays called by most people up in the air' (meteōros).
q: and such a person as the one nowadays called by most people 'up in the air'

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Soldiers, travellers and the 'circumstantial life'
s: People at war, travelling or fighting must eat whatever is at hand, as must those on hurried journeys, in civic business, or living the so-called 'circumstantial' life.
q: and in general for those who are engaged in civic occupations, or in what is called the 'circumstantial' life (περιστατικὸς βίος).
n: The Greek has the dative; the draft gives the nominative in brackets.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Clean clothes in winter, oil-soaked in summer: Galen objects
s: The author says to wear clean garments in winter and oil-soaked ones in summer. Galen disagrees: worn, dense-weave clean clothes cool better; oily clothes are dirty, no clean person tolerates them in summer, and they warm in time.
q: For the oil-soaked ones are in every case dirty, and no cleanly person tolerates dirty garments, especially in summer.
n: Detail on clothing and hygiene.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Trainers' 'body-fighting' exercises to build flesh
s: Trainers fatten clients with grappling exercises they call 'body-fighting', and avoid exercising them naked or without grappling. Those they want thin get fast exercise without the initial grappling.
q: For this reason, at any rate, the trainers also include the exercises performed with laying hold of one another and 'body-fighting' (σωματομαχεῖν)
n: Gymnastic jargon.

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: Prime of hunting dogs, racehorses and athletes
s: Hunting dogs and racehorses stay at peak strength two or three years; human athletes often four or five, illustrating an acme with breadth.
q: human athletes who have remained equal in strength, so far as perception goes, not for these three years only, but often for four and five.

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Laymen mock disputing physicians as 'logiatroi'
s: Hearing physicians contradict each other, the public laughs, condemns reasoning, and calls such men 'word-physicians'.
q: they call those who utter anything at all "word-physicians" (logiatroi).
n: Rare term λογίατρος; Galen adds that every layman is better than such a sophist.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Smoke and soot distinguished by Galen
s: Both are residues of flame. Soot (from many lamps or torches) is an earthy exhalation of over-roasted material. Smoke is from half-burnt material mixed of moist and earthy substance.
q: soot is an earthy exhalation of material that has been roasted through, whereas smoke is neither of over-roasted material nor earthy, but of material that is half-burnt
n: Rooms lit by many lamps (λύχνων) or torch-wood are called 'sooty' (λιγνυώδη): a domestic detail.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Galen's trilemma on Lycus and the Philebus
s: If Lycus never read the Philebus, Galen 'admires his education'. If he read it without understanding, he marvels at his intelligence. If he understood but was unpersuaded, he congratulates his judgement.
q: if Lycus did not read the book at all, I admire Lycus for his education; if he read it but did not understand it, I marvel at his intelligence
n: An ironic rhetorical trilemma typical of Galen's polemic.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Galen's physical account of why flames differ
s: Flame is an exhalation of particles torn from the fuel, with heated air caught between them. The particles differ in size, density and degree of burning, so flames vary.
q: a certain exhalation arises from the burning material in particles torn apart from one another, between which a certain air is caught
n: He presents this as what Lycus would have learned from the natural philosophers (φυσικῶν φιλοσόφων).

wt: Against Lycus
t: Embryo: blood-clot flesh with 'blood-weals'
s: The earliest embryo is unformed soft flesh like a blood clot, containing what Hippocrates called 'blood-weals'. Outlines of bone, cartilage, nerve and vessels form later, and the innate hot body shrinks relative to acquired parts.
q: For a certain unformed soft flesh, resembling a clot of blood, takes over the first appearance of the embryo, having within it certain things, as Hippocrates named them, like blood-weals
n: Hippocratic Nat. Puer. (outside knowledge). Greek οἶον is a misaccented οἷον. In extreme old age animals are nearly all bone, nerve, membrane and vessel; only flesh is bloody, and the old have little of it.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Galen's verdict: Lycus untaught, a corrupter of the young
s: Galen concludes that Hippocrates erred in nothing. Lycus was never introduced to the Hippocratic doctrines by teachers, contradicts himself, and corrupts the young who lack logical training.
q: you have not been introduced at all by teachers so as to understand anything of the Hippocratic doctrines
n: 'λυμαινόμενος τοῖς νέοις' echoes the charge against Socrates. Galen stresses formal instruction by teachers as the qualification for an exegete.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Types theory as dinner riddles; real fevers to learn
s: Type-books were exercises for the young like riddles at dinner; better to teach recognition of quotidian, tertian, quartan, semitertian and tertian-natured fevers by their own signs.
q: they wrote these things as exercises for the young, resembling riddles posed at dinner.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Mockers of organ-specific drugs quote a tragic verse
s: Critics mocked drugs said to act on particular organs by asking whether someone orders them about as in a tragedy: 'You, go to the streams of Inachus; and you, proceed around Cadmean Thebes.'
q: "You, go to the streams of Inachus; and you, proceed around Cadmean Thebes"?
n: The verse comes from an unnamed tragedy (outside knowledge: a fragment, sometimes attributed to Aeschylus or Sophocles); Galen does not name the author.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Sea-hare harms only the lung; cantharides only the bladder
s: Against people who mock organ-specific drugs, Galen notes that sea-hare ulcerates only the lung, cantharides only the bladder, and other drugs break kidney stones or ease expectoration.
q: by the sea-hare the lung alone of all the parts in the body is ulcerated, and the bladder alone, in turn, by cantharides

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Empiricists credit compound drugs to dreams and chance; 'cephalic' example
s: Galen says Empiricists refer nearly all compounds to dreams, chance and accident, admitting a few found by epilogismos, such as the novel 'cephalic' drug made by mixing all flesh-producing simples.
q: the contentiousness of the Empiricist physicians, who refer nearly all compound drugs to dreams and chance and accidental encounter
n: The draft also keeps an editorial note '(μίξωμιν, read μίξωμεν)' from the Kühn text.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Mixing a 5th-degree and a 3rd-degree drug gives the 4th
s: Galen's rationale for compounding: if no simple of the needed degree is available, mixing one hotter by five degrees with one hotter by three yields the mean of four.
q: if we have at hand two, of which the one is hotter by five degrees and the other by three, by mixing them we shall produce the mean, which exceeds the well-tempered state by four degrees.
n: Note: elsewhere Galen speaks of four orders; here he counts numerical degrees.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Twelve grades of drug action, against Dioscorides's 'by kind'
s: Galen insists drugs must be known not only by kind, as Dioscorides wrote, but by order (first to fourth) and position within each order (beginning, middle, end), giving twelve grades.
q: not simply by kind, as Dioscorides wrote in a different manner, but as we did in the books on simple drugs

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Euphorbium loses strength over years; thapsia within two
s: Thapsia is weak after a year and dead at two; good euphorbium keeps some power into the third or fourth year, weakens in the fifth and sixth, then dies. Age shows as a paler, yellower colour.
q: For the latter becomes quite weak after a year, and expires completely once it has become two years old.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen's nerve-wound treatment 'by providence of the gods', unrecorded before
s: Galen claims that none of the elders before him wrote down a whole course of treatment for nerve wounds, which he devised 'by a certain providence of the gods'.
q: The whole course of treatment of those wounded in the nerves, which I devised by a certain providence of the gods, none of the elders before me wrote down.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Against changing dressings often: wiping thrice daily is worse
s: Galen argues that a drug must stay on the skin a long time to work, since bodies in contact come to resemble each other. Most physicians wrongly wipe the ichor three times a day, and patients complain about once-daily dressing.
q: This very point too has escaped most physicians, and they think that, if they wipe away the ichors of the ulcer three times a day, they are doing something better than those who wipe them away twice.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Abbreviations in recipe books: 'unslaked', 'scale', 'split', 'terebinth'
s: Galen explains recipe shorthand: 'unslaked' means lime, 'scale' means copper scale, 'split' means split alum and 'terebinth' means terebinth resin.
q: when 'scale' is written simply, without 'of copper' being added, and 'split' without 'alum', and 'terebinth' without 'resin' being added, we supply in thought for them the words omitted
n: Useful for reading the shorthand in the many recipes that follow.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Verse recipes preserve proportions better than prose
s: Galen often says that recipes written in verse, like Damocrates', are more useful than prose because they aid memory and keep the proportions accurate.
q: It has often been said by me that metrical writings are more useful than those written in prose, not only for memory but also for the accuracy of the proportion of the ingredients that are mixed.
n: Compare K13.995-996, where Menecrates' spelled-out numerals are said to have been undone by copyists.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen claims priority: no predecessor wrote a general method
s: Galen says no predecessor wrote a general method of compounding, and none recorded a drug just for nerves pricked by needles or children's styluses, whereas he set out a great many.
q: For the general method was written by none of my predecessors, neither accurately with distinctions nor deficiently without distinctions
n: The Greek names needles and 'τὰ γραφεῖα τῶν παιδίων' (children's writing styluses) as causes of nerve punctures. Refers back to book III of this work on nerve wounds.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Altering a recipe slightly to claim it as one's own
s: Damocrates notes that some people, wanting the drug named after them, change it slightly, dropping steel scale and using sixteen drachms of copper scale.
q: But some, wishing this drug to be called their own, remove the one [922] of the one scale and put in the sixteen
n: The draft's 'remove the one of the one scale' is garbled; the sense seems to be swapping steel scale for copper scale.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Fats follow animal temperament; pig's fat for soft bodies
s: Fat takes on its animal's temperament: lion's is strongest, then leopard's, goose's and hen's. Pig's fat is softest and suits women, children, eunuchs and soft-living men raised in the shade.
q: so that it suits tender bodies, such as those of women and children and eunuchs and of delicately-living men, bodies made effeminate by rearing in the shade, by lack of exercise, and by rather frequent baths of fresh waters.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: How tophi and kidney stones form
s: Strongly heating and drying drugs disperse the thin part of a thick, viscous flux and leave the rest hardened. Galen says this is how tophi form in arthritis and stones in kidney disease.
q: And it is in this way that in arthritic affections the tophi (poroi) come about, and in nephritic affections the stones.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Physicians' ignorance turns erysipelas into scirrhus
s: Violently cooling and astringent drugs produce scirrhi. Galen says many patients have scirrhous tumours left from erysipelas because their physicians treated it ignorantly.
q: And we see many people who, from erysipelas that have suffered these things immoderately, have scirrhous [994] tumours, through the ignorance of the physicians who treated them.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Galen's rule for the good exegete
s: A good interpreter must show not only that an explanation is plausible or true but that it fits the author's own opinion, drawn from the author himself.
q: I do not think that the good exegete should consider this alone, whether he has spoken plausibly or truly, but also whether it adheres to the opinion of the author

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Hippocrates never uses epithets idly, unlike Homer
s: Homer says 'liquid oil' and 'white milk' with no distinction, but with Hippocrates every word and syllable signifies something real.
q: nor does he say, as Homer does, 'liquid oil' and 'white milk' for the sake of no distinction at all

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Hippocrates' graded vocabulary for derangement
s: Galen lists Hippocratic verbs for derangement (παρελήρει, παρηνέχθη, παρέκοψε, παρεφρόνησε, ἐξέστη, ἐμάνη, ἐξεμάνη, οὐ κατενόει, παρέλεγε), each marking a degree.
q: for each magnitude of the species of derangement he has devised a proper name.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Drunkenness as model for sleepless coma
s: Drunk people are heavy-headed, cannot lift their eyelids yet cannot sleep; similarly an unconcocted fullness of the head at disease onset makes patients comatose and sleepless, ending in recovery, phrenitis or lethargy.
q: So too, then, when an unconcocted plenitude has taken hold of the head, they are at the same time both sleepless and comatose.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Causes: wrestling schools and badly trained physicians
s: Galen blames falls in the wrestling schools and physicians who lever joints clumsily. Today's physicians learned briefly or not at all, while wrestling holds now twist limbs in many ways.
q: but those of today have either not learned at all or have learned in an altogether short time. Then too, in the practice of wrestling-holds there has been an astonishing advance
n: Polemic on contemporary medical training.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Thinness from famine, siege or grief makes flesh moister
s: People thinned by famine, siege, grief or loss of appetite do not get dry flesh, as those reduced by the art do. Their flesh partly melts and becomes moister and mucous.
q: Those who, through famine or through siege or grief or distress or loss of appetite, taking in nourishment insufficiently, have been made thin
n: Social detail: siege starvation as a medical category.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Acromion avulsion mistaken for dislocation
s: When the acromion (acromioclavicular junction) is torn away, the shoulder top looks hollow. Physicians mistake it for a dislocation and do harm trying to reduce it; the right treatment is bandaging with compresses over the projecting bone.
q: I know, then, many physicians, not bad in other respects, who have already done much harm in trying to reduce such shoulders, supposing them to have been dislocated in this way
n: Hippocratic lemma; it sets up Galen's account of his own injury.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Hippocrates and Xenophon mix rare words into plain style
s: Like Xenophon, Hippocrates writes in ordinary language but inserts figurative and rare words, more often than Xenophon does, such as kinklismos and ploōdēs ('floating', i.e. unsupported).
q: Hippocrates is accustomed to use figurative (tropical) and glossematic words for his notions, even though he employs the ordinary (civil) mode of expression; Xenophon has undergone something similar to this.
n: Ancient stylistic comparison.

wt: On Plethora
t: Liver parenchyma lacks nerves
s: The flesh of the convex liver, called parenchyma, has no nerve implanted; nerves at the portae are so short they only weave its membrane.
q: For the nerves implanted in the liver at the portae are so short that they appear to interweave only its membrane.

wt: On Plethora
t: Crude humour: bean-soup sediment in gluttons' urine
s: The crude humour, thicker than phlegm, settles in urine like bean-soup sediment, especially in gluttons who avoid exercise, eat much and bathe after meals; it brings white pallor.
q: such as settles in the urines, especially in those of people who, from gluttony, have a copious sediment resembling bean-soup
n: Only leucophlegmatic dropsy phlegm can abound through the whole body.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Breathing is voluntary, moved like the legs
s: Since breathing is a psychic (voluntary) work, an inflamed thorax breathes as an inflamed leg walks, with smaller and slower movements. Arteries cannot do this, because the pulse is a vital work.
q: But in fact it is one of the psychic works, as has been demonstrated elsewhere; it is clear, then, that it will be moved in the same way as the legs.
n: This is the core argument of the treatise against those who held breathing to be involuntary.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Signs of weak respiratory faculty: nostrils, shoulder muscles, collapse
s: When the breathing faculty is weak and chilled, the wings of the nose move, the muscles about the shoulder-blades work, and the thorax collapses all at once on breathing out.
q: he will have the movement of the wings of the nose, and the activity of all the muscles about the shoulder-blades, and the sudden collapse of the thorax.
n: Early description of nasal flaring and use of the accessory muscles as signs of failing breathing.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: The Epidemics are notes, not finished treatises
s: Hippocrates wrote about dyspnoea both in his treatises and in his notes; most or all of the Epidemics should be counted as notes (hypomnemata).
q: For most of the Epidemics, if indeed not all of them, one would rightly consider to be notes.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Authorship of the seven Epidemics books
s: Book 7 is plainly spurious and later. Book 5 is by the younger Hippocrates, son of Draco. Books 2, 4 and 6 are variously given to Hippocrates' son or to Hippocrates himself as notes; only books 1 and 3 are agreed to be by the great Hippocrates.
q: the fifth is not by the great Hippocrates, the son of Heraclides, but by the younger one, the son of Draco
n: Key testimony on how the Hippocratic corpus was judged in antiquity.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Copyist's error in Epidemics II preserved in all copies
s: The division of dyspnoeas in Epidemics II lacks the fourth pairing that Epidemics VI has. Galen blames an ancient copyist: the faulty book was published, and earlier scholars only noted the gap without daring to fix it.
q: Rather, one of the ancient copyists erred; then the book, being in this condition, had already been published, and this very error was understandably preserved down to the present day
n: Galen's textual-critical principles: rewriting the text is rash, small additions are allowed (K7.893-894). A copyist who removes phrases makes himself 'a corrector of Hippocrates, not a servant'.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Hysterical suffocation and apnoeas in barren women
s: Hysterical suffocation and all the apnoeas often affect women, especially the barren, and rarely men. The innate heat is smothered by cold matter like a flame choked by wet wood, and can be rekindled.
q: Among these belong also the so-called hysterical suffocation and in general all the apnoeas, which befall women continually, and especially those who are barren, but rarely on occasion men as well.
n: K7.958-959 adds childless women who are not properly purged and long-term widows.

wt: On Leeches, Revulsion, Cupping, Incision and Scarification
t: Leeches draw only superficial blood
s: Leeches do not draw the blood that lies deep but suck the blood next to the flesh; they are used in place of cupping-glasses and removed when half the intended blood is drawn, since they are cold by nature.
q: leeches do not draw the blood that lies in the depth, but suck in that which lies next to the flesh.

wt: On Leeches, Revulsion, Cupping, Incision and Scarification
t: List of the powers of the cupping-glass
s: The cupping-glass evacuates matter, resolves pain, reduces inflammation, disperses wind, restores appetite, tones a slack stomach, relieves fainting, transfers deep fluxes, checks haemorrhage and promotes menses.
q: The cupping-glass is able to evacuate the matter, to resolve pain, to diminish inflammation, to disperse flatulence, to restore the appetites, to make a slack stomach toned, to deliver from faintings
n: At the very beginning of an affection repellents (ἀποκρουστικοῖς) are used instead.

wt: On Leeches, Revulsion, Cupping, Incision and Scarification
t: Against frequent venesection: loss of vital pneuma
s: The author will not open a vein many times a year, because vital pneuma is evacuated with the blood, chilling the body and worsening psychic functions; removal should be from less important parts like the legs.
q: For I have not considered it suitable to open a vein many times in the year; for together with a great quantity of blood the vital pneuma is evacuated along with it
n: First-person statement; if the tract is not Galen's, this is the compiler's view.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Galen contrasts his useful exegesis with other commentators' sophistry
s: Galen says other exegetes fill their commentaries with sophistical questions that are useless for practice. He chooses instead to add useful teaching that follows from Hippocrates' doctrines.
q: for they sow their exegeses with sophistical questions that are of no use to learners toward the end of the art

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Azygos vein origin differs between animals and humans
s: Galen says the unpaired vein that feeds the lower eight ribs branches off above the heart in some animals. In others, humans included, it branches off where the vena cava meets the right auricle.
q: a single unpaired (azygos) vein, which in some animals grows off above the heart
n: This comparative anatomy comes from Galen's own dissections.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Contemporary physicians overfeed after evacuation
s: Galen says most physicians of his day feed patients abundantly after evacuating them. Hippocrates gives less ptisan after purging, because the exhausted faculty cannot work up much food.
q: For these, whenever they have evacuated, feed abundantly

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Bile duct sometimes has a branch into the stomach
s: Galen explains why yellow bile rises in some people: the duct from the liver to the outgrowth of the stomach is built differently in some, with a branch reaching the stomach.
q: For sometimes in some people a branch from it reaches the stomach; in these, then, the bilious residue floats up above
n: This is an anatomical variant of the bile duct based on dissection.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Book found in drafts; notes on front and back of sheet
s: Galen explains the book's disorder: it was found in draft form after Hippocrates' death. Examples he added on the front and back of the sheet were put in the wrong places by the copyist.
q: the examples that he had found were written in addition into the book by Hippocrates himself, for the confirmation of the universal statement, some on the front of the sheet and some on the back
n: The Greek is ἐπὶ τοῦ μετώπου / κατὰ τοῦ νώτου. This is evidence for ancient ideas about how texts were transmitted. Checks verdict is 'fail'.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Five differences of wine: colour, taste, consistency, smell, power
s: Galen faults Hippocrates' list of wines as disordered and incomplete and sets out five kinds of difference. The colours are white, black, tawny, yellow and red.
q: another is the quality according to taste, a third according to consistency, a fourth according to smell, and a fifth according to power.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Cough as a 'hand'; viscous phlegm clings like birdlime
s: Galen says the breath of a cough acts like a hand that carries thick humours up, but viscous humours stick in the bronchi like birdlime. So melikraton suits thick sputa and oxymel viscous ones.
q: And for this reason melikraton is most suitable for the thick humours with a view to expectoration, and oxymel for the viscous ones

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Melikraton can stretch survival from four days to five or six
s: Melikraton is not a weakener but a light nourishment. Galen says a fasting man who would die in four days could reach the fifth or sixth on melikraton.
q: if someone who had fasted were going to die in four days, this person, using melikraton, could arrive not only at the fifth day but even at the sixth.
n: This answers the lemma (K15.665) that melikraton got a reputation for causing swift death through people who starved themselves to death on it.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Hippocratic treatments of individual acute diseases lost or never written
s: Galen says Hippocrates' books on treating each acute disease either do not survive or were never written. Those in circulation are not worthy of him, though they contain much of his thought.
q: It is therefore evident either that the books written by him on the treatment of each of the acute diseases in particular are not preserved, or that they were not written at all

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Dogmatist versus Empiricist readings of Hippocrates against the Cnidians
s: Those who think Hippocrates was a Dogmatist say he meant affected places, conditions and causes. Those who think him an Empiricist say seasons, regions, ages, habits and air. Galen accepts both but says this book uses other indications.
q: Those who consider Hippocrates to be a Dogmatist said that these things are the affected places and their conditions and the causes

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Appendix perhaps by a pupil, or Hippocrates' preparatory notes
s: Physicians suspected the section after the baths. Galen says its thought fits Hippocrates, so a pupil may have written it, or Hippocrates may have written it in preparing the promised book on each acute disease.
q: so that one would suspect that some pupil of his wrote it.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Galen refuses to divine 'attractive gruels'
s: Galen admits he cannot tell what the author means by 'attractive gruels', since neither oxymel nor ptisan draws anything. He declines to guess and censures fondness for obscure expressions.
q: am unable to divine what he can possibly mean by "attractive gruels"

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Children and old men not bled; children's evacuation is innate
s: The indications for phlebotomy are magnitude of disease, strength and prime age. Children are not bled because their moist, hot temperament disperses their substance, and old men are not bled because of weakness.
q: they therefore have no need of phlebotomy, since they possess as something innate the evacuation that arises from their temperament.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: List of powerful critical days in acute and chronic disease
s: Galen lists the powerful critical days: in acute diseases the 3rd, 5th, 7th, 9th, 11th, 14th and 17th, and in chronic ones the 60th and 80th, with the 20th, 34th and 40th between them.
q: In acute diseases these are the 3rd and the 5th and 7th and 9th and 11th and 14th and 17th; in chronic ones, the 60th and 80th.
n: The numbers are Greek numeral letters in the text and could easily be corrupted.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: From experience garlic is not flatulent, no hotter than onion
s: Judging foods by experience, Galen denies that garlic is flatulent or gives more heat than onion, especially briefly boiled. It dries and heats and, given to a prepared body, cures heaviness of the head.
q: garlic would not rightly be said to be flatulent, nor to bring to those who have eaten it a sensation of greater heat than in the case of onion

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Some say chickpea's 'flatulence' means it distends the genitals
s: Galen reports that some interpreters read the chickpea's flatulence as distending the genitals. He refers the 'pain' instead to pain from inflation.
q: Some write that the chickpea is flatulent for this reason, as distending the genitals
n: This alludes to the chickpea's reputed aphrodisiac effect.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Exertions are occasions (prophaseis), not causes, of disease
s: Running, wrestling, sex, chilling and the like only expose a disease the body is already close to. Alone they cause at most an ephemeral fever, so Galen calls them occasions rather than causes.
q: each of such things becomes not the cause of the disease but its occasion
