wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Authorship: Polybus; title 'On the Nature of Man and Regimen'
s: Galen treats Regimen in Health as a separate book from On the Nature of Man. With the interpolated material between them removed, some titled the whole 'On the Nature of Man and Regimen'. He accepts the common attribution to Polybus.
q: Let it be assumed to be the work of Polybus, as has seemed right to many.
n: Galen calls On the Nature of Man faultless, the interpolated part entirely faulty, and Regimen in Health mostly faultless.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Who are the 'private persons' (idiōtai)?
s: Galen argues that the regimen is not for everyone. It excludes athletes, whose diet is fixed to bread and meat, and soldiers, travellers and men in public life; it is for those 'minding their own affairs'.
q: he seemed to me to separate the athletes outright from the rest of human beings, since those men have one regimen, defined in bread and the eating of meats.
n: K15.176-177 names the ἰδιοπραγοῦντες.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Germans called 'yellow' but are really red
s: Galen says writers who use colour words loosely confuse the teaching; for example, some call the Germans yellow (xanthoi), though strictly they are red.
q: Thus, at any rate, some call the Germans yellow, although they are not yellow, if one wishes to name them accurately, but red.
n: Ethnographic aside. The same unit cites On Temperaments (περὶ κράσεων) for the signs of temperament.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Galen faults the author for two ages instead of four
s: The author divides life into only two ages. Galen holds there should be four, matching the four temperaments: children moist and hot, those in their prime dry and hot, those past their prime dry and cold, the old moist and cold.
q: calling that of children moist and hot, that of those in their prime dry and hot, that of those past their prime dry and cold, and that of the old moist and cold.
n: He puts the best temperament between childhood and prime (youths and lads, K15.186-187).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Galen: water before wine after exercise, as athletes do
s: Galen says wine should not be drunk straight after exercise or the bath, because it goes to the head. Water comes first, as athletes have learned from experience, and cold water should follow warm.
q: one does not at all deem it right to drink wine immediately after exercises, but water first, just as the athletes too do these things, having been taught by experience.
n: Galen cites his own treatise on hygiene for the distinctions.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Dogmatists issue precepts like royal commands
s: Galen repeats to his companions and friends that dogmatist physicians err by giving orders without reasons, like royal decrees. Hippocrates did better in giving the properties of ptisan.
q: The men who champion the dogmatic sect seem to me to err in no small way when, without stating the reasoning behind what they recommend, they issue pronouncements as if they were royal commands.
n: Quotes Regimen in Acute Diseases on ptisan's viscous part as smooth and soothing.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Galen rejects drying regimen for women
s: The author prescribes a drier regimen for women, for their soft flesh and for the womb and embryo. Galen objects that women's moistness is natural and should be preserved unless it goes beyond healthy proportion.
q: but since this is in accordance with nature for them, one ought to preserve it, except if it should at some point exceed the healthy due proportion.

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: Periods of an inflammation: filling, putrefaction, pus, decline
s: An inflammation begins while the part fills with blood; it increases as contents putrefy, generating heat and pneuma; the acme is while pus forms, with greatest pain; decline follows suppuration or dispersal.
q: For the pains and the fevers occur around the generation of the pus rather than once it has been generated

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: No disease attacks at its acme; synochos needs 3-4 hours
s: Even the synochos fever takes at least three or four hours to reach full acme, and apoplexy and epilepsy pass quickly through beginning and increase; even a beheading has successive moments.
q: from the first onset to the most complete acme it arrives in four or three hours at the very least

wt: Against Lycus
t: Lycus had partisans who held his views
s: Galen twice refers to a group who share or champion Lycus' opinions and imagines their objections.
q: those who champion Lycus’s views will perhaps say
n: Also at 214-215 (οἱ τὰ τοῦ Λύκου φρονοῦντες). This implies that Lycus had a following or readership in Galen's day, though it may be a rhetorical construct.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Agathinus slipped into type-theory teaching
s: Even Agathinus, 'a man of no ordinary stature', fell into this sort of teaching, which is still tolerable compared with seven-hour periods.
q: for even Agathinus, a man of no ordinary stature, slipped into such a form of teaching
n: Agathinus of Sparta, Pneumatist, teacher of Archigenes (outside knowledge).

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Philistion invoked to mock seven-hour period theorists
s: Those who posit seven-hour periods need not Galen but Philistion, or someone like him, to make sport of their drivel.
q: those who make periods of seven hours had need not of us but of Philistion, or of someone of that sort to make sport of their drivel.
n: Almost certainly Philistion the mime-writer (Augustan era), not the physician of Locri (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Themison used Asclepiades' first akopon
s: Asclepiades' first akopon, from book 4 of External Remedies (marjoram, libanotis, fenugreek, cardamom, savin, sweet wine, Venafran oil, wax), is said to have been used by Themison.
q: Themison used it. The drug is exceedingly good.
n: Themison of Laodicea, founder of Methodism (outside knowledge). The akopon is finished with Venafran oil (K13.1009-1010).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Mnasaeus's plaster: oil, litharge and fat in equal parts
s: The drug compounded by Mnasaeus has oil, litharge and fat in equal amounts and is very well suited to beginning and increasing inflammations; Galen's phoinikine adds astringents to it.
q: At any rate the drug which Mnaseas compounded has the oil, the litharge and the fat in equal amounts to one another
n: The Greek spells the name Μνασαῖος (Mnasaeus); the draft writes 'Mnaseas' here and 'Mnasaeus' elsewhere.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Xenocrates used the Ariobarzanian white plaster on a tarsus abscess
s: Heras records 'the white Ariobarzanian, with which Xenocrates dispersed the abscess around the tarsus when it had already undergone change.'
q: The white Ariobarzanian, with which Xenocrates dispersed the abscess around the tarsus when it had already undergone change.
n: Name of the plaster probably honours a king Ariobarzanes (Cappadocia); Xenocrates possibly Xenocrates of Aphrodisias. Both identifications are outside knowledge.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Pamphileion: Asclepiades renamed the Attalic plaster after its user
s: Asclepiades calls the white pepper plaster not Attalic but Pamphileion; Galen thinks he did not know its inventor and named it after the man who used it and gave it to him.
q: does not call it Attalic but Pamphileion, being ignorant, as [447] I think, of the one who first discovered it, and having added instead the name of the man who used it and gave it to him.
n: Shows how recipe names drift between collections.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Rusticus, pupil of Isidorus, variant of Heraclides's plaster
s: For Heraclides's quince-yellow plaster dispersing internal abscesses, Galen gives a variant 'according to Rusticus, the pupil of Isidorus'.
q: But according to Rusticus, the pupil of Isidorus
n: These two physicians are otherwise obscure.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Lucius 'the Teacher' used Asclepiades's cadmia plaster
s: In Asclepiades's list of cicatrizing plasters the cadmia plaster is noted as used by 'Lucius the Teacher', who elsewhere is called 'our teacher Lucius'.
q: The cicatrizing plaster through cadmia. Lucius the Teacher used this.
n: The words are Asclepiades's, so Lucius was Asclepiades's teacher, not Galen's (compare K13.538-539).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Pythion's fracture plaster used by Helenus; bathe with it on
s: Asclepiades records the fracture plaster of Pythion, used by Helenus, so adhesive that it must be loosened with a hot wet sponge; the patient should bathe with the drug on.
q: Another, the fracture-plaster of Pythion. Helenus used this.
n: Contains Judaean asphalt and Bruttian pitch.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Claudius Philoxenus the surgeon: 'Egyptian' plaster
s: Asclepiades gives the Egyptian plaster of Claudius Philoxenus the surgeon, with litharge, wax, ammoniac, propolis, copper and steel flake, burnt greasy wool and castor oil.
q: The Egyptian of Claudius Philoxenus the surgeon, for the aforementioned conditions.
n: Outside knowledge: Claudius Philoxenus was an Alexandrian surgeon also cited by Celsus. Another plaster of his is at K13.538-539.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Demetrius the Bithynian used chrysocolla in hot wax
s: Heraclides reports that Demetrius the Bithynian used chrysocolla alone, taken up in very hot wax. Galen approves and says he often uses single drugs in soft wax himself.
q: Demetrius the Bithynian said that he used the chrysocolla itself, taking it up in very hot wax.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Andreas' plaster, opening Asclepiades' first group
s: First in Asclepiades' list is the plaster of Andreas: litharge 3 lb; copper scale, chalcitis and verdigris 3 oz each; vinegar 1 cotyle; old oil 8 lb. Drugs of Aster and Amphion follow.
q: The plaster of Andreas, repressive of every excrescence.
n: Probably Andreas of Carystus, Ptolemy IV's physician (outside knowledge). An emollient of Andreas appears at K13.982.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Turpilianus' plaster 'of the philosophers'
s: A plaster attributed to Turpilianus is called 'of the philosophers'. It is good for rheumatic and chronic ulcers and brings up corrupted bones.
q: Turpilianus', the one called "of the philosophers".
n: Turpilianus is a Roman name; who this was is unknown.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Herodotus, source of Criton's Hicesius recipe
s: Criton records that he received his recipe for the Hicesius plaster from Herodotus. A 'simple willow plaster as Herodotus gives it' appears later.
q: I received this recipe from [789] Herodotus.
n: Probably the Pneumatist physician Herodotus (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Aristarchus of Tarsus' troches, also taken by mouth
s: Asclepiades' first troche is Aristarchus of Tarsus' polychrest, for ulcers, fistulas and womb conditions. It is also swallowed, 3 obols in a suitable drink, for early phthisis, spleen, coeliac and dysentery patients.
q: it works [825] for incipient phthisics, splenetics, coeliacs, dysenterics, being given in the weight of three obols with the appropriate drink.
n: Aristarchus' name is in the heading at the end of K13.824. The troche is taken up in Falernian wine.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Agathinus: troche with boiled egg yolks
s: A troche from Agathinus' writings combines white lead, manna, frankincense, crocomagma, unburnt sulphur and the yolks of boiled eggs, taken up in sweet wine.
q: From the (writings) of Agathinus. Take white lead 6 drachms; manna, frankincense, 1 drachm each; crocomagma 2 drachms; unburnt sulphur 2 drachms; yolks of boiled eggs 6 drachms
n: Agathinus, Pneumatist teacher of Archigenes (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Musa's remedy in Andromachus' pastilles
s: Andromachus lists a remedy (iatreion) of Musa: split alum, aloe, myrrh and chalcanthum 6 dr each, saffron and krokomagma 3 dr, kytinoi 4 dr, taken up with honeyed Falernian wine.
q: The remedy (iatreion) of Musa.
n: Possibly Antonius Musa, Augustus' physician (outside knowledge). The same unit gives the 'pastille of Darius'.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Dioscorides of Tarsus gave Areius the Asclepiadean a styptic
s: A haemostatic that checks bleeding marvellously (chalcitis, manna, dry resin, gypsum) was given by Dioscorides of Tarsus to Areius the Asclepiadean. Gypsum is added at the time of use.
q: And as Dioscorides of Tarsus gave it to Areius the Asclepiadean, checking haemorrhages marvellously
n: Areius is presumably the dedicatee of Dioscorides' Materia Medica, so this Dioscorides may be the pharmacologist himself (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Antonius the root-cutter's black emollient
s: A black drawing plaster for scrofula, parotid swellings and joint complaints is given 'as Antonius the root-cutter used it': mined salt, litharge, 4 lb of pure strigil-scrapings and galbanum.
q: It is also a good emollient (malagma), [935] as Antonius the root-cutter used it.
n: This unit's automatic check failed. Strigil-scrapings (gloios) from bathers were a drug ingredient.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Ulpianus, a gifted young man, used Damocrates' lime plaster
s: Damocrates' discutient plaster with quicklime disperses scrofula, reduces oedema, treats watery liver and spleen, increases urine and relieves chronic sciatica. Ulpianus, a naturally gifted young man, helped very many with it.
q: Ulpianus, a naturally gifted young man, by using this benefited very many.
n: The Greek spells the name Οὐλβιανός, which the draft normalises to Ulpianus. Damocrates' verse; the 'father of the drug' in the next unit (K13.944-945) is presumably Ulpianus.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Marcus Telentius Asclepiades; 'Asclepiadeion' after Asclepiades of Bithynia
s: A malagma of Marcus Telentius Asclepiades for swellings of the womb is called 'Asclepiadeion' because it is traced back to Asclepiades the Bithynian.
q: the drug is inscribed 'Asclepiadeion' because it is referred back to Asclepiades the Bithynian.
n: The Greek may show a different first name or spelling than 'Telentius'; check the unit.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Aquilia Secundilla: patient of Neapolites
s: Asclepiades records a malagma 'of Neapolites prepared for Aquilia Secundilla'. A perfumed akopon composed for her appears later (K13.1030-1031).
q: Another, that of Neapolites; it was prepared for Aquilia Secundilla.
n: A named Roman woman, otherwise unknown.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Callinicus' malagma from the writings of Paccius
s: A malagma of Callinicus, taken from Paccius' writings, contains henbane seed, poppy juice, white poppy seed and pine nuts.
q: Another malagma, of Callinicus, from the writings of Paccius, for all conditions.
n: Paccius Antiochus, a pharmacologist under Tiberius (outside knowledge).

wt: On Plethora
t: Philippus and Archigenes touched on faculty theory
s: No one before Galen defined the faculties scientifically; Philippus and Archigenes and their followers touched the theory only slightly; arterial plethora signs are in Galen's pulse treatise.
q: For Philippus and Archigenes and their followers touched to a small extent upon the theory of them, but none even of these worked it out completely.
n: Philippus is probably the Empiricist/Pneumatist physician also named elsewhere by Galen; identity uncertain (outside knowledge).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Apollonius and Dexippus, pupils of Hippocrates
s: Apollonius and Dexippus are named as Hippocrates' pupils who restricted drink in fevers. Galen says Erasistratus could produce no book of theirs.
q: Erasistratus, who mentions Apollonius and Dexippus while having no book of theirs to show
n: Dexippus of Cos is known from other sources (for example Plutarch) as a pupil of Hippocrates.

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: Archigenes mixes logical inquiries into medical treatises
s: Archigenes is criticised as one who brings everything into everything, mixing inquiries about names and logical matters into strictly medical treatises.
q: as those do who bring everything into everything, one of whom is Archigenes. For this man mixes into the most strictly medical treatises sometimes an inquiry about names
n: Archigenes of Apamea, Pneumatist, active under Trajan (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Asclepiades: 'openly shameless' opponent of attraction
s: Asclepiades is named as one who, unlike anyone in Hippocrates' time, shamelessly fought the truth that purgatives attract their proper humour.
q: Asclepiades, who was openly shameless and stripped, as it were, for some prize (ἔπαθλόν τινα) against the truth
n: Asclepiades of Bithynia (fl. c. 100 BC), corpuscular theorist who denied natural faculties (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Erasistratus never recognises the attractive power
s: Erasistratus, more modest, still overturns the main point: nowhere in his writings does he know the attractive power, substituting 'following toward what is being emptied'.
q: the attractive power, Erasistratus knows nowhere in his own writings, but rather employs in its place the following toward what is being emptied.
n: Refers to Erasistratus' principle of horror vacui (πρὸς τὸ κενούμενον ἀκολουθία; outside knowledge).

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Unnamed sophist: drugs draw like sucking things, thinnest first
s: A sophist, when cornered, claimed each drug simply draws like a sucking creature, the thinner humours following first, then thicker, then thickest.
q: each of them simply draws, like the things that suck (βδάλλοντα); and that what is thinner among the humours follows the attraction first, next after it the thicker, and then in this way the thickest.
n: Probably an Erasistratean or Asclepiadean contemporary in Rome; unnamed.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Lycus' commentaries expounding Hippocrates' Aphorisms
s: Lycus wrote exegetical commentaries (hypomnemata) on the Aphorisms; Galen says he distorts Hippocrates both where he praises and where he censures.
q: commentaries expounding the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, but he does violence to the man's doctrines from both sides
n: Lycus of Macedon, pupil of Quintus (outside knowledge; not named here). The commentary is lost; this treatise is a main witness to it.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Lycus' thesis: hot does not differ from hot
s: Galen quotes Lycus' claim that the hot, insofar as it is conceived as hot, has no variation from another hot. He refutes it by asking what the qualifier 'insofar as' adds.
q: ‘The hot, insofar as it is conceived as hot, has no variation with respect to another hot.’
n: A verbatim fragment of Lycus' commentary on Aph. I.14. A longer form is quoted at 215-216 (κατ’ αὐτὴν λέγω τὴν θάλψιν).

wt: Against Lycus
t: Lycus himself wrote differences of diseases, including pleurisy
s: Galen turns Lycus' own practice against him: Lycus wrote many differences of diseases and symptoms, including kinds of pleurisy, though 'disease does not differ from disease insofar as disease'.
q: But Lycus himself also writes down a great many differences of diseases
n: Pleurisies differ by pain ending at the collarbone or at the hypochondrium, and by coloured sputum versus the kind some call ἄπτυστος. At 222-223 Lycus 'elsewhere writes of differences of fevers' too. Evidence for other lost Lycus writings.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Theophrastus wrote a whole treatise on juice (chylos)
s: Galen says that on Lycus' view Theophrastus wrote a whole treatise on chylos (juice/flavour) in vain.
q: in vain wrote a whole treatise on juice (chylos)
n: Diogenes Laertius lists a Theophrastean Περὶ χυλῶν, and CP book 6 treats flavours (outside knowledge). 'Juice' may better be 'flavour' here, since the treatise concerns χυμοί/χυλοί.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Lycus thought vinegar has a styptic quality
s: Galen mocks Lycus for holding that vinegar is styptic (astringent) rather than sour: a sign that he ignored flavour distinctions known to materia medica writers.
q: who has reached such a degree of lack of education as to think that there is a styptic quality in vinegar
n: A specific doctrinal fragment of Lycus. Galen adds sour dock (oxylapathon) and sorrel (oxalis) as sour but not styptic (220-221).

wt: Against Lycus
t: Lycus' three senses of 'much heat'
s: Lycus distinguished three senses of 'much heat': by substance, by intensity of the quality, and by strength of its proper activity. He granted growing bodies only the third, and called that usage improper.
q: he says that ‘much heat’ is understood in one way in respect of substance, in another in respect of the intensification of the quality, and in another in respect of the strength of its proper activity.
n: The core of Lycus' exegesis. Galen later turns all three senses against him (240-241).

wt: Against Lycus
t: Structure of Lycus' comment: two inquiries
s: In a verbatim quotation Lycus says he set out two questions: whether Hippocrates was right to add 'innate', and whether he was right that heat is greatest in growing things.
q: one, whether Hippocrates was right to add 'innate', the other, whether he was right to say that the heat is greatest in those who are growing.
n: The quotation seems to run from 226 to about 234. It is the longest surviving piece of Lycus' Aphorisms commentary; the draft's quotation marks should be checked for where it ends.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Lycus attacks the proof in On the Nature of Man
s: In the quotation, Lycus calls 'utterly foolish' the proof in the treatise On the Nature of Man that heat is greatest in the young, because nourishment is carried upward against its weight during growth.
q: For what is said by him in the treatise On the Nature of Man, as a proof that heat is greatest in those who are growing, is utterly foolish
n: The speaker is Lycus, and 'him' is Hippocrates. At 233-234 Lycus grants the same passage 'would have been well said' in the third sense. The Ionic βίην there suggests a verbatim Hippocratic quotation, which needs locating in the extant text.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Diagnosis by 'antapodoseis' (correspondences of paroxysms)
s: Some recognise the three types not by their nature but by correspondences of paroxysms, and so remain ignorant until day four or five.
q: but from the correspondences (antapodoseis) in the paroxysms—for this is what they themselves are accustomed to call the analogies of the paroxysms.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: A whole book on finding kind and number of types
s: Galen learned that someone wrote a whole, not small, book teaching how to find the kind and number of types for any period; he says the method fits in a few words.
q: I learned that a certain person has even written a whole book, and not a small one, teaching how one might, for each paroxysmal period proposed, discover both the kind and the number of the types.
n: Author unnamed; lost.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Type-theorists disagree on the longest type
s: Some extend types to fifteen days, some to monthly ones, some to two or three months; Galen notes he has treated Hippocrates on what lies beyond the quartan in other writings.
q: Some of them suppose that the periods of the types proceed as far as fifteen days; some as far as monthly ones; and there are also those who go as far as two or three months.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Criton's Cosmetics book 2: gleukinon; Andromachus' unclear keramion
s: Criton gave gleukinon (must-oil) in book 2 of his Cosmetics. Galen notes that Andromachus' 40-day gleukinon gives no method and does not say how many Italian litrai or xestai his keramion holds.
q: Preparation of gleukinon, as Criton gives it in the second book of the Cosmetics.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Heras's drug book titled Narthex or Tonos of Remedies
s: Heras recorded the Attalic plaster in his book of drugs, which some entitle Narthex and others 'Tonos of remedies'; he wanted old oil and an equal or half amount of water.
q: Heras too mentions it in his book of drugs, which some entitle Narthex, others Tonos of Remedies
n: Heras of Cappadocia's work is lost and known mostly from Galen's quotations.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Andromachus's white plaster quoted from 'Remedies for External Conditions'
s: Galen quotes Andromachus's own white plaster: litharge and white lead one mina each, wax and resin a quarter, oil three kotylai, water two kotylai, with no uses or boiling given.
q: The white plaster which I use: litharge, one mina; white lead, one mina; wax, a quarter; resin, a quarter; oil, three kotylai; water, two kotylai.
n: Andromachus the Younger's work survives only in Galen's quotations.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Menecrates's book 'Autokrator hologrammatos' of noteworthy drugs
s: Galen cites one book by Menecrates titled 'Autokrator hologrammatos of noteworthy drugs' and says he will also include drugs used by his own teachers.
q: And there is also one book of Menecrates entitled [503] 'Autokrator hologrammatos (The Emperor, written out in full letters) of noteworthy drugs'.
n: Outside knowledge: Menecrates (Ti. Claudius Menecrates) wrote quantities in full words to prevent copying errors; the work is lost.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Criton's fourth book of Drugs: 'boxwood-coloured' plasters
s: Criton calls quince-yellow plasters 'boxwood-coloured' (pyxinai) and wrote others in the fourth book of his Drugs.
q: Criton has also written certain other plasters in the fourth book of his Drugs, 'boxwood-coloured' as he himself names them, but 'quince-yellow' according to the [517] others

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Asclepiades Pharmakion, External Remedies book 3: drug for Chironian ulcers
s: Galen quotes Asclepiades Pharmakion's third book of External Remedies: flake of copper 1 oz, scraped verdigris 1 oz, wax ½ litra, larch resin 1½ oz, laid on the ulcer only and undone every third day.
q: Take: flake of copper, one ounce; scraped verdigris, one ounce; wax, half a litra; larch resin, one and a half ounces.
n: Asclepiades Pharmakion's work survives only in Galen's quotations (outside knowledge). Galen works out that the metallics are one third of the wax.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Andromachus' twelve cicatrizing plasters listed without distinction
s: Galen faults Andromachus for listing twelve 'cicatrizing' plasters one after another without saying which is strongest, so that physicians use them hit-or-miss. Galen then grades them himself.
q: One might, however, find fault with him for having written out the drugs without distinction.
n: Galen's main source for compound drugs; the work survives only through these excerpts (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Primion's remedy 'for desperate cases'
s: Andromachus took from Primion's writings a cicatrizing remedy for ulcers others had given up as incurable: sory 24 dr; split alum, pomegranate rinds and quicklime 16 dr each; frankincense and oak-gall 32 dr each; wax 120 dr; calf's fat 160 dr; old oil 1 kotyle. Galen trusts it as tested by experience.
q: Cicatrizing remedy from the writings of Primion, for desperate cases.
n: Primion is otherwise very obscure (outside knowledge). The ingredients follow in K13.695-696. Galen adds that old unsalted pig's fat (axoungion) may replace calf's fat, and he explains the proportions at K13.705-706.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Criton's fourth book: five remedies, the ladanum plaster
s: Galen quotes five remedies from the fourth book of Criton. The ladanum plaster for callous and hollow ulcers, left in place four days: dry pitch 100 dr, verdigris 24 dr, burnt copper 15 dr, red scale 24 dr, ladanum 9 oz, litharge 3 lb, oil and wine 1½ xestai each.
q: among which remedies are also these written in the fourth book of Criton, being five in all.
n: Criton, physician at Trajan's court; his drug books are lost apart from Galen's excerpts (outside knowledge). Galen made this plaster himself (K13.708-709).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Heraclides' book 'The Soldier' (Stratiotes)
s: Heraclides wrote the same drugs in another book titled The Soldier, differing only in the third drug: 'wax 40 drachms' with 'but some, 16 drachms' added, which Galen thinks better.
q: Heracleides also, in another book entitled The Soldier (Stratiotes; printed στατιώτην), wrote the same drugs, disagreeing with himself only in the one that is third among them in order.
n: The printed Greek has στατιώτην; the draft emends it to Stratiotes, which is plausible but not certain.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Heraclides' writings addressed to Antiochis
s: Heraclides repeated these drugs in writings to Antiochis, adding there that the ulcer should first be washed with cold water. Galen also says Heras followed Heraclides' Antiochis text for the Hicesius plaster.
q: Heraclides mentions these same drugs also in the writings addressed by him to Antiochis
n: Antiochis, a woman to whom Heraclides addressed medical writings (outside knowledge: possibly the Antiochis honoured at Tlos).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Heras' praised plasters: Aribarzaneios, Isis, panacea, Hicesius
s: Heras' book includes several much-praised plasters: the Aribarzaneios for malignant, spreading ulcers, the Isis for gangrenes, a good-coloured one, his panacea, and that of Hicesius.
q: For all have praised both the plaster called by him Aribarzaneios, as curing malignant, spreading [751] and hard-to-heal ulcers, and the Isis, as circumscribing gangrenes
n: The name presumably honours a King Aribarzanes of Cappadocia, fitting Heras' Cappadocian origin (outside knowledge).

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Homer uses 'coma' for sleep
s: Galen cites two Homeric lines where coma seems to mean sleep, contrasting Hippocratic usage.
q: "Truly a soft coma enfolded me, suffering terribly as I was."
n: Odyssey 18.201 and Iliad 14.359 (outside knowledge).

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Prorrhetic: sleepless comatose patients, 'are they phrenitic?'
s: Hippocrates' Prorrhetic asks whether those comatose at the start, with pain of head, loins, hypochondrium and neck and sleepless, are phrenitic.
q: "Those who become comatose at the beginnings, with pain of the head, loins, hypochondrium, neck, being sleepless — are they phrenitic?"
n: Prorrhetic I.1 (outside knowledge).

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Commentators derive 'comatose' from kōmazein (revelling)
s: Some commentators said the comatose are named from revellers, who stay awake, have moist red unsteady eyes and uncontrolled movements.
q: some of the commentators say that the comatose are named from revelling (kōmazein); for those who revel are awake, and the comatose are awake as well.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: 'Typhomania' as a supposed mixture of lethargy and phrenitis
s: Uneducated physicians and self-styled Hippocrateans called phrenitics who lie still like lethargics 'typhomania', a mixture of lethargy and phrenitis.
q: while some suppose it to be a mixture compounded of lethargy and phrenitis, and name it typhomania.
n: Typhomania is a term otherwise found in later authors (outside knowledge).

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Two readings of the Prorrhetic: with or without 'are they'
s: The Prorrhetic sentence circulated in copies with and without εἰσίν ('are they'), i.e. 'are they then phrenitic?' versus 'then phrenitic?'.
q: This saying is written in two ways: in some copies thus, but in some without the "are they", "are they then phrenitic?"
n: Evidence of textual variants in Galen's copies; returned to at K7.664-665.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Commentators read ἆρα as syllogistic, not aporetic
s: Some interpreters said Hippocrates' ἆρα is syllogistic ('therefore'); Galen argues from word order and Greek usage that the preposed ἆρά γε is interrogative.
q: The word ἆρα, he says, is syllogistic, not aporetic.
n: Galen's grammatical argument continues K7.660-662.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Hippocratic parallels for interrogative ἆρα
s: Galen cites Epidemics I (dysentery after watery urine), Epidemics VI (sediment after urination in children, because warmer?) and Prorrhetic (white evacuation in phrenitics, as in Archecrates).
q: 'In phrenitics a white evacuation is bad, as also in Archecrates. Does torpor, then, also occur in these cases?'
n: Archecrates is a patient named in Prorrhetic I.

wt: On Plethora
t: Asclepiades and Methodists deny faculty; plethora only relative to vessels
s: Asclepiades, many Asclepiadeans and Methodists said there is no faculty in animals, so they measure much and little only against vessel space and take indication only from 'constriction'.
q: the things written [515] by Asclepiades and by many Asclepiadeans and Methodics to the effect that there is no faculty at all in animals
n: 'Constriction' = στέγνωσις, the Methodist common state (outside knowledge).

wt: On Plethora
t: Contemporary Herophileans on the cohesive cause
s: Self-styled Herophileans pronounce on a cohesive faculty binding stones and wood without knowing whether it is air, fire or both, and call their questioners sophists when refuted.
q: some of those who nowadays call themselves Herophileans, having not even in a dream heard these things, boldly make pronouncements about the cohesive faculty

wt: On Plethora
t: Erasistratus' signs of plethora quoted
s: Erasistratus: with moderate filling people seem better-toned and stronger; with more, upper arms, shins and hands fill out; when advanced, they are sore, sluggish, tense, with lassitude, near disease.
q: when the plethora advances far, these parts are sore, slower and harder to move, and the whole body is tense to the touch, since a lassitude (kopos) appears.

wt: On Plethora
t: Erasistratus' On Fevers: plethora causes paremptosis
s: For Erasistratus plethora causes paremptosis of blood into arteries, on which inflammations form and fever follows; he ignores faculty-plethora in this book and On Fevers.
q: For plethora, according to him, is the cause of paremptosis, upon which inflammations are formed and fever follows

wt: On Plethora
t: Those who make arteries and nerves 'pipes' for pneuma
s: Galen rejects the view that faculties do not pervade solid bodies and that arteries and nerves are pipes or conduits for pneuma, refuted in PHP and Natural Faculties.
q: who set up the arteries and the nerves as pipes or conduits for pneuma.
n: Target is Erasistratean physiology (outside knowledge).

wt: On Plethora
t: Nicarchus and Praxagoras: arteries without blood
s: Galen denies that the arterial pulse clearly shows venous plethora when thick humours block transfer, against Nicarchus and Praxagoras, who give arteries no share of blood.
q: however much Nicarchus and Praxagoras may think so, even though they do not grant [574] the arteries any share of blood.
n: Nicarchus is obscure, perhaps a follower of Praxagoras of Cos (outside knowledge).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Archigenes' counter-argument against Magnus on the rapid pulse
s: Galen recalls Archigenes' objection to Magnus that a rapid pulse comes from weakness, not strength, of the faculty, and says he refuted it in his work on causes in the pulses.
q: the counter-argument of Archigenes against Magnus, to the effect that the rapid pulse does not arise from strength of the faculty but rather from weakness
n: The refutation is placed in the treatise on the causes in the pulses (De causis pulsuum).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Erasistratus' definition of phlegmone
s: In Erasistratus and the later physicians 'phlegmone' means a hard, hot, painful swelling, whereas the ancients used the word for burning heat (phlogosis).
q: "inflammation" (phlegmone) being understood here as the hard, hot and painful swelling, as Erasistratus is accustomed to call it and all the more recent physicians
n: K7.910-911 adds that nearly everyone before Erasistratus called phlogosis 'phlegmone'.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Regimen in Acute Diseases, also called Against the Cnidian Sentences
s: The Prognostic, Aphorisms, Airs Waters Places, and Regimen in Acute Diseases (titled by some Against the Cnidian Sentences) are believed genuine. Other works are assigned to Euryphon, Thessalus and Polybus.
q: On Regimen in Acute Diseases, which some entitle Against the Cnidian Sentences, are not unreasonably believed to be writings of Hippocrates himself.
n: Outside knowledge: the Cnidian Sentences are a lost work of the Cnidian school (associated with Euryphon).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Ancient Empiricists' term syndromē; ancients said synedreuonta
s: Galen notes that 'concurrence' (syndromē) is the ancient Empiricists' name. The ancients called such symptoms 'sitting together with' (synedreuonta) the affections.
q: the 'concurrence' (συνδρομή), as it is named by the ancient Empiricists—though the ancients used to call such symptoms things 'sitting together with' (συνεδρεύοντα) the affections

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Dioscorides' edition read 'spring' instead of 'summer'
s: Galen reports that Dioscorides and others wrote 'the spring season' instead of 'summer' in the dropsy passage. They feared summer would dissolve the faculty and winter would add chill.
q: Some people, however, like Dioscorides, wrote not 'the summer season' but 'the spring'
n: This is Dioscorides the Hippocratic editor (Hadrianic era), not the pharmacologist.

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: Hippocratic maxims on beginnings and acme
s: Quoting Hippocrates: at the beginning of diseases move what needs moving, at the acme keep quiet; and around beginnings and ends all things are weaker.
q: "When diseases are beginning, if anything seems to need moving, move it; but when they are at their acme, it is better to keep quiet."
n: Hippocrates, Aphorisms II.29 and II.30; purging maxims from Aph. I.22-24 follow (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: Hippocrates on shoulder dislocation: 'I do not insist'
s: Galen imitates Hippocrates' reserve on the shoulder dislocation and declines the logical question whether the acme has duration.
q: "I, for my part, do not insist upon this, although I have something I could say."
n: Hippocrates, On Joints 1 (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: Archigenes' two books on the periods in diseases
s: Galen says Archigenes turned aside into prolixity, in all his writings and in the two books he wrote on periods in diseases, burdening readers with useless matters.
q: as did Archigenes both in all his other writings and in the two books which he wrote on the periods in diseases.
n: A lost work of Archigenes; also K7.461-462.

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Opponents' theory: purgatives transform humours into their own kind
s: The opponents hold that a purgative changes any humour it touches into its own form: cholagogues make yellow bile, phlegmagogues phlegm, hydragogues water, another black bile.
q: The purgative drug alters whatever humour it touches into its own form: the one they name cholagogue producing yellow bile, just as the one they call phlegmagogue produces phlegm

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Asclepiadean and Erasistratean views of phlebotomy vs purgation
s: For the Asclepiadeans phlebotomy removes all humours equally while purgation removes the others to leave the blood pure; for the Erasistrateans both evacuate equally, purgation adding corruption of what is evacuated.
q: According to Erasistratus and his followers, the evacuation of all the humours is equal, as in phlebotomies, so also in purgations
n: Greek has τοὺς Ἀσκληπιάδας and in K11.326-327 οἱ Ἀσκληπιάδαι, rendered 'Asclepiadeans'/'Asclepiadae'. Whether this means followers of Asclepiades or the Asclepiad guild is unclear; context suggests followers of Asclepiades.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Cites his On the Elements according to Hippocrates
s: Galen refers readers who want a scientific proof that hot, cold, dry and wet are the principles of generation to his book On the Elements according to Hippocrates.
q: This book is entitled On the Elements according to Hippocrates.
n: Extant De elementis secundum Hippocratem (Kühn I). Useful for relative chronology: it predates Against Lycus.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Cites On Mixtures as following On the Elements
s: Galen says the books On Mixtures follow On the Elements and show which bodies have more or less of the hot element, and why some are hotter or colder by nature.
q: And following it there are others, those On Mixtures, in which I show which bodies have in themselves a greater share of the hot element
n: Extant De temperamentis (3 books). 'Following it' (ἐφεξῆς) gives a reading or composition order.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Cites his commentaries On Seed
s: Galen says he showed in his commentaries On Seed that seed, made of serous moisture and pneuma, is least in the old and greatest in the young.
q: as we demonstrated in the commentaries On Seed.
n: Extant De semine (Kühn IV). The reference gives a relative date: On Seed predates this text.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Treatise already circulated among Galen's companions
s: Galen notes these things had already been written and given out to some companions before he added the finger method.
q: These things having already been written and given out to some of my companions
n: Evidence for informal circulation (ἔκδοσις) of Galen's texts.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: On the Power of Simple Drugs cited as eleven books
s: Galen refers readers to his commentaries On the Power of Simple Drugs and gives their number as eleven.
q: all such matters have been defined by us in the commentaries On the Power of Simple Drugs, which are eleven in number
n: The extant De simplicium medicamentorum temperamentis ac facultatibus has eleven books, which fits.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Reading list of Galen's pathological and therapeutic works
s: Galen lists works his companions already have: on the differences of diseases, of symptoms, on causes of diseases, three on causes of symptoms, On Plethora, On the Differences of Fevers and the Therapeutic Method.
q: You also have my writing On Plethora and that On the Differences of Fevers; and after these, the books of the Therapeutic Method
n: A useful internal cross-reference list for dating; all these works are extant.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen's own phoinikine plaster used as liquid drug
s: Around the ulcer Galen applies a liquid drug made from his own phoinikine plaster melted with astringent wine, using myrtle or quince oil if the area is hot and old or castor oil if it is hard.
q: a liquid drug made from my phoinikine, not simply melted, but having taken up as much astringent wine as possible.
n: Phoinikine is Galen's date-palm plaster, described elsewhere in his works (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen's teacher added dracontium to the Isis
s: Galen always adds 8 dr of dracontium root to Heras' Isis, following one of his teachers. The teacher also used colophony instead of terebinth and kneaded the plaster at length with sharp vinegar in a bronze vessel.
q: I myself have always used it in this way, since one of my teachers too used it, putting into the proportion written by Heras 8 drachmas of dracontium.
n: The teacher is not named.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen uses Sicyonian oil or improvises one with roots
s: Galen often used Sicyonian oil in discutient plasters. When none was available he made a similar oil by boiling roots of wild cucumber, bryony and marshmallow in it.
q: I myself have often put Sicyonian oil into the discutient plasters, and when that too was not available, I improvised another oil
n: Castor oil may be replaced by old oil (same unit).

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Galen saw five non-axillary shoulder dislocations
s: Hippocrates says he saw the humerus dislocate only into the armpit. Galen says he has seen other dislocations five times, once in Asia and four times in Rome.
q: we ourselves too have seen them five times up to now, once in Asia, and four times in Rome.
n: The unit's checks failed, but the Greek confirms the figures (πεντάκις... ἐν Ῥώμῃ δὲ τετράκις).

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Commentaries on In the Surgery and the treatise on hygiene
s: Galen says rubbing is discussed in his commentaries on the Hippocratic In the Surgery and most fully in his treatise on hygiene.
q: matters about which it has been spoken both in [366] the commentaries on that book and, indeed, most completely in the treatise on hygiene.
n: The hygiene work is De sanitate tuenda; the In the Surgery commentary is In Hipp. de officina medici.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Commentaries on On Fractures
s: Galen refers to his commentaries on On Fractures, where fracture-type (circular) bandaging is treated, as opposed to the distributive bandaging of the present book.
q: For it has been shown by me also through the commentaries on that book, and it has been recalled even now
n: Galen's commentary on De fracturis is extant.

wt: On Plethora
t: PHP, On the Elements, Natural Faculties cited on faculties
s: Galen refers to On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato (heart, brain, liver as sources of arterial, nervous and venous faculties), On the Elements according to Hippocrates, and On the Natural Faculties.
q: I also taught that the heart is, as it were, a kind of source of the faculty of the arteries, the brain of that of the nerves, and the liver of that of the veins.
n: 'A certain other treatise' on mixture as substance of faculties: perhaps Quod animi mores (outside knowledge).

wt: On Plethora
t: On the Natural Faculties: four faculties
s: Citing On the Natural Faculties: attractive, alterative, retentive and expulsive faculties; heaviness alone cannot signal plethora relative to each.
q: one faculty is attractive of what is proper, another alterative of these same things, another a retentive faculty, and a fourth expulsive of what is foreign
n: Unit ends with a garbled clause '(κατὰ τὰ νεῦρα)'; the draft sentence is incomplete.

wt: On Plethora
t: On the Movement of Muscles cited
s: Whether the limb weighs on the muscle only when moving or also at rest was settled in Galen's writings On the Movement of Muscles.
q: which has been determined by us in the writings On the Movement of Muscles

wt: On Plethora
t: Cross-references: Causes of Symptoms, Hygiene, Mixtures, Simple Drugs
s: For biting things Galen refers to book 2 of On the Causes of Symptoms, book 4 of the Hygiene, On the Power of Drugs, and On Mixtures.
q: what has been said in the second book of On the Causes in the Symptoms and in the fourth of the Hygiene is sufficient
n: 'On the Power of Drugs' is presumably De simplicium medicamentorum facultatibus (outside knowledge).

wt: On Plethora
t: Planned discourse on phlebotomy
s: Galen defers the full set of indications for bleeding to his discourse on phlebotomy, which no one has yet written precisely.
q: I, since I have at present no leisure for idle talk, have decided not now, but in the discourse on phlebotomy
n: Probably De curandi ratione per venae sectionem (outside knowledge).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Cross-references to Galen's pulse treatises
s: Galen says he showed in On the Use of the Pulses that breathing and the pulse give the same benefit to the heat; he also cites Causes in the Pulses (books 1-3) and On the Differences of Pulses.
q: if indeed we did not wrongly show, in the work On the Use of the Pulses, that the same benefit comes from respiration to the heat in the heart
n: Other citations: Causes in the Pulses I (K7.768), III (K7.771), II (K7.799, K7.803-804); Differences of Pulses (K7.806-807).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: On the Movement of Muscles and commentaries On Respiration
s: Galen refers to On the Movement of Muscles for the difference between collapse and relaxation of a part, and to his commentaries On Respiration, where the diaphragm only slackens its tension in breathing out.
q: It has been stated at greater length in the books On the Movement of Muscles in what respect the collapse of a part differs from its letting-down and relaxation
n: K7.839-840 cites book 2 of On the Movement of Muscles for his proof that breathing is voluntary.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Commentaries On the Innate Heat (lost work)
s: Anyone puzzled by the different kinds of heat is referred to Galen's commentaries On the Innate Heat.
q: rather to refer him to the commentaries On the Innate Heat
n: Outside knowledge: Galen's De calore innato is lost.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Promised fourth book on Thessalus, Polybus and Euryphon
s: Galen plans, if he has more time, a fourth book on what the other works under Hippocrates' name say about dyspnoea, including those of his son Thessalus, his son-in-law Polybus, and works thought to be by Euryphon.
q: if ever I come to have more leisure, I shall add another, fourth book, expounding what is said about dyspnoea in the remaining works inscribed with the name of Hippocrates.
n: Polybus is called Hippocrates' son-in-law (Πολύβου τοῦ γαμβροῦ). No such fourth book is known.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Galen cites On the Elements according to Hippocrates and Causes of Symptoms
s: For his account of how pain arises Galen refers to two of his own works, On the Elements according to Hippocrates and the Causes of Symptoms.
q: it has been stated by me both in the work On the Elements according to Hippocrates
n: Galen's De elementis ex Hippocrate and De symptomatum causis. The draft points out that the Greek title has its words in a disturbed order.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Anatomical Procedures book III and Anatomy of Veins and Arteries
s: On the elbow veins cut in venesection Galen refers to the third book of his Anatomical Procedures and to a separate single book on the anatomy of veins and arteries.
q: these have been sufficiently discussed both in the third book of the Anatomical Procedures and in the Anatomy of the Veins and Arteries, written separately in another single book
n: De anatomicis administrationibus III and De venarum arteriarumque dissectione.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Therapeutic Method gives the orderly teaching Hippocrates lacked
s: Galen refers readers to his Therapeutic Method for the ordered treatment of quantity of food. He excuses Hippocrates' disorder because Hippocrates was the first to discover these things.
q: All such matters have been stated in the treatise on the therapeutic method, in sequence and in order
n: This is the Methodus medendi.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Galen promises commentaries on On Diseases and On Affections
s: Galen says he will settle whether On Diseases and On Affections are authentic in commentaries written on those works.
q: we shall define this same point and decide it in the commentaries written on them
n: No Galenic commentaries on these works survive. They may have been planned only or are lost.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Books On Difficulty of Breathing cited
s: Galen refers to his books On Dyspnoea, where he set out the causes of all kinds of laboured breathing with demonstrations.
q: in which we have written out the causes both of these and of the other dyspnoeas together with their proper demonstrations
n: This is De difficultate respirationis in three books. It is cited again at K15.793-794.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Prognostic, On Humours and Aphorisms commentaries written earlier
s: Galen says that before this commentary he had already expounded the Prognostic, On Humours and the Aphorisms. He also refers to his books On Crises.
q: For we have already expounded, before this book, both the Prognostic and the work On Humours and the Aphorisms
n: This is evidence for the relative order of Galen's Hippocratic commentaries.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Pungent substances: pepper, mustard, pellitory (Simple Drugs IV)
s: Galen cites book IV of On Simple Drugs: pepper, mustard, pellitory and other hot substances taste pungent. Salty things dry even more than pungent ones but heat less.
q: pepper and mustard and pellitory, and all the other things that are hot in their powers, also appear pungent to those who taste them

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Two books by Galen on phlebotomy
s: Galen says the most persuasive views on venesection are set out in two of his books. One is titled On Phlebotomy and teaches everything useful; the other was written for physicians, Empiricists and Dogmatists.
q: the one of them is entitled On Phlebotomy, in which everything useful is taught; the other has been written, as I said, for the physicians, both the Empiricists and the Dogmatists
n: These are probably De curandi ratione per venae sectionem and one of the anti-Erasistratean venesection books. The description of the second book ('as I said', 'for the physicians') is odd and may be corrupt.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Galen's commentaries on the Methodic sect
s: Galen refers to his own commentaries examining the Methodic sect.
q: as has been shown by me in my commentaries when examining the Methodic sect
n: This is perhaps the lost work in six books On the Methodic Sect (listed in On His Own Books).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Phlegmone's old broad sense; Galen's book on swellings
s: In Hippocrates phlegmainein covered all hot swellings (erysipelas, herpes, anthrax), while recent physicians restrict it. Oedema too once meant any swelling. Galen refers to his single book on unnatural swellings.
q: we have spoken elsewhere, in a single book, about swellings contrary to nature
n: This is De tumoribus praeter naturam.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: On the Faculties of Foodstuffs in three books
s: Galen says the whole range of foods is set out item by item in his three books On the Faculties of Foodstuffs.
q: The whole material of foodstuffs, taken item by item, is set out in three treatises bearing this title: On the Faculties of Foodstuffs.
n: De alimentorum facultatibus (extant, 3 books).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Commentaries on the Aphorisms: athletes' peak condition is precarious
s: Galen recalls showing in his Aphorisms commentaries that athletes' peak condition, full of blood and flesh, is precarious. In dense-fleshed bodies it comes and goes quickly.
q: For it was shown in the commentaries on the Aphorisms that the good condition of athletes, along with repletion of blood and of flesh, is one that preserves the strength of the natural faculties.
n: The unit's checks failed. The draft's 'preserves the strength' may misread the Greek; Aph. I.3 is about extreme good condition being dangerous.

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: On Crises, book 1: recognising the beginning
s: Galen refers to the first book of On Crises, where he showed how to recognise the first period, chiefly by lack of concoction.
q: Many things, then, have been said by me about this beginning also in the first book of On Crises
n: Also argues the beginning cannot be the same for diseases resolved by day 7 and a quartan lasting a year.

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: On Uneven Dyscrasia and On Tumours contrary to Nature
s: Galen cites these treatises for the theory of inflammation, listing rival mechanisms: paremptosis, wedging-in of vessels, blocking of masses in pores.
q: as we taught both in the treatise On Uneven Dyskrasia and in that On Tumours contrary to Nature
n: Paremptosis and sphenosis are Erasistratean concepts (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: On the Differentiae of Diseases
s: Galen says the genera, differentiae and species of diseases are set out in a single treatise titled On the Differentiae of Diseases.
q: have been set out in a single treatise, which is entitled On the Differentiae of Diseases.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Menecrates' 'dia chylon' with mallow, fenugreek and linseed
s: Menecrates' plaster 'through juices': oil 7 litrai in summer (9 in winter), litharge 6, plus a decoction of fresh wild mallow root (3 litrai), fenugreek and burnt linseed (½ xestes each) in 8 xestai of water, boiled until quince-yellow.
q: Of fenugreek he said a half part of a xestes, and the same of burnt linseed. And of wild mallow he said three litrai by weight, of the root still having its fresh juice
n: Ancestor of the long-lived diachylon plaster (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Salve for Domitius Nigrinus with seal fat
s: A gout salve compounded for Domitius Nigrinus uses many perfumed oils, mandrake and colocynth, and six ounces of seal fat, with very old deer marrow as the substitute.
q: of seal fat six ounces—if this is not available, one must use very old deer marrow
n: Domitius Nigrinus is named at the start of the unit.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen's phoinikine (date-palm) plaster: exact quantities
s: Galen's own chalcitis plaster: old unsalted fat (sellers call it axoungion) 2 litrai, old oil 3 litrai, litharge 3 litrai, chalcitis 4 ounces, stirred with a fresh palm-wood stick.
q: Of the old fat, which those who sell it call axoungion, let there be 2 litrai; of the old oil, 3 litrai; and of litharge, 3 litrai; and of chalcitis, 4 ounces.
n: Outside knowledge: the 'diachalciteos' plaster became the medieval diapalma. 'Axoungion' is Latin axungia, a trade term.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Attalic white plaster with white pepper: full composition
s: Litharge and white lead one litra each, oil two litrai by measure, wax half a litra, terebinth 3 ounces, frankincense half or equal to that, split alum 6 drachms, white pepper 3; the metals are boiled in the sun first.
q: In addition to these, half a litra of wax by weight, three ounces of terebinth resin, of frankincense either half of this or an amount equal to it, and six drachmas of alum and three of pepper.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Asclepiades's 'Rhodian' plaster for hard breasts, with egg yolks
s: Asclepiades's Rhodian plaster, discutient for hardnesses of the breasts: litharge and Pontic wax one litra each, white lead and pig's fat half a litra each, myrrh 4 ounces, two roasted egg yolks, 1.5 kotylai oil.
q: of myrrh four ounces, of roasted eggs two yolks, and one and a half kotylai of oil.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Green plaster of Gallus, first of Andromachus's green series
s: Andromachus's first green plaster, of Gallus: pine-cone resin 300 dr, wax 100 dr, scraped verdigris 50 dr, frankincense 25 dr, vinegar as needed. Galen judges it drying, for large wounds and hard ulcers.
q: Green plaster of Gallus. Rx: pine-cone resin, 300 drachmas; wax, 100 drachmas; scraped verdigris, 50 drachmas.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Isis green plaster as recorded by Epigonus, with dracontium
s: The plaster others call Isis, written by Andromachus as Epigonus's green plaster: equal parts burnt copper, ammoniac salt, copper scale, verdigris, ammoniac, aristolochia, frankincense, with aloe, myrrh, galbanum, round alum, Colophonian resin and wax. Epigonus added dracontium root.
q: He added this at the end, since it is not carried in the recipe of the Isis; for Epigonus added it, and in this respect the Isis of Epigonus differed.
n: The Isis is one of the 'Egyptian' sacred plasters (K13.517-518).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen's tawny plaster of metals only, with old Sabine oil
s: Galen's own tawny plaster without resin or wax: 4 litrai of oil (the older the better, especially Sabine), 3 litrai litharge, 2 of sharpest vinegar, and 2 ounces each of black copper scale, verdigris and chalcitis.
q: I put in four litrai of oil—and the older it is, the better it will be, and all the more if it is Sabine—and three litrai of litharge.
n: Continues in K13.519-520 with uses: glues bleeding wounds, closes fistulas.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Moschion's fracture plaster: dropsy, bronchocele, corns
s: Moschion's fracture plaster claims to form callus on bones, help incipient dropsy and testicle contusions, shrink piles, dissolve bronchoceles and remove 'nails' (corns) without ulceration; the mina is set at 160 drachms.
q: It is effective also against the callus-like outgrowths on the feet and hands, which we call "nails" (hēloi), so as to remove them without ulceration

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Heras's three-ingredient cephalic troche ground in the dog-days
s: Heras's 'trimigma' troche for skull fractures: erythrias earth, red copper scale and Pontic fish-glue, ground with sharp vinegar for 20 days in the dog-day heat, then sunned 8 days in a red-copper vessel.
q: Do this in the heats of the dog-days for 20 days. Then take the fish-glue, crush it, pour on 1 kotyle of vinegar and melt it over a gentle fire

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Heras's black barbaros spread on two leathers for blood-spitting
s: Heras's black plaster for bleeding wounds also stanches blood in those who bring up blood: spread on two pieces of leather, one on chest and sides, one on the back. Change it every 7 days in winter, 5 in summer.
q: Having spread it onto two pieces of leather, apply one [558] to the chest and the sides, and the other to the back; it checks the blood remarkably.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen's barbaros plaster for the greatest wounds
s: Galen gives his own barbaros: pitch 8 litrai, wax 6 litrai 8 oz, pine resin 5 litrai 4 oz, asphalt 4 litrai, oil, plus litharge, white lead, verdigris, frankincense, alums, opopanax, aloe, opium, myrrh, terebinth, mandrake juice and 6 cotylae vinegar.
q: They are two: one for the greatest wounds, another for the smaller ones.
n: For the oil quantity see the doubt item on σι΄.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Strongest and weakest metallic drugs for nerve punctures
s: Strongest: raw chalcitis 1, raw misy 2, copper scale 3 parts. Weakest: burnt misy and chalcitis 1 each, scale 4. Middle: burnt misy, chalcitis and verdigris 1 each, scale 3. Wax is added at 2 to 2.5 times the metals.
q: let it have one part of raw chalcitis, two of misy, likewise raw, and three of scale of copper; and the weakest, likewise one of misy and of chalcitis, but both burnt, and four of the scale.
n: The worked example gives 12 parts of wax for both the strongest and the weakest, though the rule (double vs two and a half) needs 15 for the weakest; the Greek has the same ιβ΄, so the numeral is corrupt in the text, and the following 'between eighteen and twelve' is also confused.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Burnt river-crab for cancerous ulcers; polion for worm-infested ulcers
s: Archigenes treats cancerous and malignant ulcers with burnt river-crab and cadmia, or crab ash in cerate. Ulcers with worms get white lead and polion in liquid pitch.
q: For cancerous and malignant ulcers, sprinkle on burnt river-crab and cadmia, in equal parts, finely ground; or apply the ash of the crabs with cerate
n: The same unit mentions malignant black ulcers (melantria) of the shins and malignant ulcers of the breasts.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: 'Plaster of Galen, our own': wax, pitch, bitumen base
s: Galen's own plaster: wax, pitch and bitumen 1 litra each; manna, verdigris and white lead ½ litra each; pomegranate rind, oak-gall, Egyptian thorn, Illyrian iris, round aristolochia and chalcanthum 4 oz each; long aristolochia and burnt copper 2 oz each.
q: Of wax, of pitch [753] and of bitumen, one litra each; of manna, of verdigris, of white lead, half of the aforesaid amount, that is, half a litra of each.
n: The heading 'Plaster of Galen. Our own, a good one.' closes K13.751-752. The dry ingredients are ground with vinegar over several days.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen's wax-free plaster for fistulas and Chironian ulcers
s: Galen's own plaster without wax: litharge 3 lb, old castor oil 4½ lb, sharpest vinegar 2 lb, and 2 oz each of black copper scale, chalcitis and verdigris, boiled until it no longer stains. It closes callous fistulas.
q: Our wax-free plaster. ♃ litharge 3 pounds, old castor oil 4½ pounds, sharpest vinegar 2 pounds, black scale of copper and chalcitis and verdigris, of each of the three 2 ounces apiece.
n: Steel scale is preferred, then black scale, then Cyprian copper scale (K13.760-761).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Isis (Epigonus' plaster): uses against venoms and wounds
s: Heras' Isis, also called Epigonus' plaster, heals head wounds with cut bone without removal. It treats punctures, human and dog bites, and draws out venom of viper, scorpion, sea-dragon and stingray.
q: and it draws out the venoms of viper, scorpions, sea-dragons and stingray, and is good for fractures of the limbs with a wound.
n: The recipe (wax, terebinth, red copper scale, verdigris, aristolochia, myrrh, aloe, galbanum and others) is at K13.774-775.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Machairion's plaster for rabid-dog bites, also taken as pills
s: Criton's plaster of Machairion treats fresh wounds and bites of rabid dogs: applied widely, changed often, and taken as a bean-sized pill for 30 days.
q: In cases of those bitten by rabid dogs it is excellent, applied over a wider area and changed very frequently, and taken as a pill about the size of a bean for 30 days.
n: Notable for a plaster also swallowed as a pill.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Damocrates' Dysrachitis for fistulas and gout
s: The Dysrachitis (as Damocrates gives it, via Criton) is put into callused sinuses and fistulas. Spread widely at the start of a gout attack, it lets patients keep walking and working without bathing until the third day.
q: It also acts wonderfully on gouty patients when it is spread on as a plaster at the beginning of the paroxysm and applied around over a broad area
n: Damocrates (Servilius Damocrates) wrote recipes in verse (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Phanias' sitz-bath for haemorrhoids in a single man's urine
s: Phanias' sitz-bath: equal parts chalcanthum, split alum, chalcitis, raw misy and sandarach (12 dr) in two xestai of old stale urine of a single man, topped up, sat in for 7 days. The gluey sediment is smeared on the anus.
q: put old, stale urine of a single man, 2 xestai by measure, into an earthenware basin, and 12 dr. of the drug
n: 'Of a single man' may mean from one man only; the sense is uncertain.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Apelles' papyrus remedy, also infused for dysentery
s: Apelles' 'papyrus' remedy (burnt papyrus, burnt lead, burnt washed copper, arsenic, steel scale, sulphur) stops and prevents spreading sores. Infused with rose oil in dysentery, a biting sensation warns of a spreading sore.
q: And whenever, he says, on being infused into dysenteric patients it causes a biting sensation, the spreading sore is to be suspected.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Criton's whetstone plaster: chronic pain, menses, spleen
s: Criton's plaster 'with whetstone' is used for chronic pains, headache, gout, sciatica, toothache and liver or spleen hardness, and placed above the pubes to bring on the menses. It is very hot, containing mustard, adarke, sulphur and Cnidian berry.
q: The plaster with whetstone (ἀκόνη), which is in use among us, is effective against all chronic conditions, and specifically against headache when applied to the forehead
n: Left on seven days (five for delicate patients) until it raises pustules.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Criton's 'Invincible': prevents hidden abscesses of colon and peritoneum
s: Criton's 'Invincible' plaster (copper scale, pyrethrum, stavesacre, Cnidian berry, mustard, cachrys, pigeon's dung, cumin, rocket, nitron, bay-berries, fig decoction) is said to prevent hidden abscesses in the colon and peritoneum, or make them burst into the bowel.
q: it does not allow concealed abscesses to form in the colon and the peritoneum, provided at least that suppuration has not already taken place
n: The same unit names Criton's 'Mesiane' plaster.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Serapion's plaster, called Egyptian or Aphrodite, from Criton's Pharmakitis
s: Criton's book of drugs (Pharmakitis) gives the plaster of Serapion, also called Egyptian or Aphrodite, for wounds, punctures, parotid swellings, ulcers of the aged and Chironian ulcers. It is stored in a skin.
q: Crito wrote this one too, in his book of drugs (the Pharmakitis), in the following words: the plaster of Serapion, which some call Egyptian, others Aphrodite.
n: Possibly the Empiricist Serapion of Alexandria (outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Plaster with ash of asps for scrofula and gout
s: A discutient plaster for scrofulous swellings and gout contains 140 dr of ash of asps with terebinth, Asian stone, asphalt, aphronitron, bay-berries, pyrite, quicklime. The ash goes in last, once cooled, or the drug is ruined.
q: Another, the one made with asps, dispersive of scrofulous swellings and for gout.
n: This unit's automatic check failed.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Mnaseas' plaster: old oil, litharge, pig's fat
s: Everyone agrees Mnaseas' emollient plaster is made of old oil, litharge and pig's fat, but quantities and the age of oil and fat vary. Galen counts the resulting strengths, and many say Mnaseas used equal parts.
q: since all who have mentioned it agree with one another that it is made from old oil, litharge and pig's fat
n: Mnaseas was a Methodist physician (outside knowledge). Andromachus listed it as eleventh of his quince-yellow plasters, adding 'soft' (K13.964-965).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Regimen in Acute Diseases: ptisan timing in pleurisy
s: Galen quotes Hippocrates: if side pain persists despite hot applications and the sputum is not coming up, relieve the pain by softening the belly or bleeding before giving ptisan, or the patients die quickly.
q: either by softening the belly or by cutting a vein, whichever of the two of these is indicated, and yet gives the ptisans to those in such a condition, the deaths of such patients come quickly.
n: Also: giving gruel before clearing the bowels makes the breath more frequent (K7.914, K7.924-925).

wt: On Leeches, Revulsion, Cupping, Incision and Scarification
t: Dressings for leech bites and bleeding after leeching
s: Slight oozing is treated with cumin or flour and wool with a little oil; haemorrhage with vinegar-soaked linen, burnt oak-gall, or a sponge dipped in liquid pitch and burnt.
q: linen cloths soaked in vinegar are to be applied, or burnt oak-gall, or one must soak a sponge in liquid pitch, burn it, and apply it.
n: Liquid pitch = ὑγροπίσσῃ.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Barley or bitter-vetch fomentation: pound, boil in oxycrate, bag
s: Galen explains that the barley and bitter vetch of Hippocrates' fomentation are pounded before being boiled in vinegar and water and sewn into bags. Bran is prepared the same way, and bitter vetch cuts thick humours.
q: Both barley and bitter vetch he bids one boil in vinegar and water not as whole seeds, but having first pounded them
n: The lemma says the vinegar mixture should be 'a little sharper than one would drink it'. In K15.524-525 Galen explains this middle strength: inflamed parts cannot bear pungent oxycrate.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Hiera made with colocynth; best version has hellebore, no scammony
s: Among purgatives Galen names the colocynth preparation that people now call hiera. Of its several versions he judges best the one that contains hellebore but no scammony.
q: among which is also the one made with colocynth, which they now customarily call hiera.
n: K15.540 continues: 'the one that has received hellebore but does not contain scammony is the finest drug'.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Hepsēma and siraion: boiled-down must
s: Galen describes hepsēma and siraion, made by boiling down must. The sweeter it becomes, the blacker and thicker it is, and over-boiled must turns bitter.
q: what is called hepsēma and siraion, which is produced from must being boiled down
n: K15.632-633 adds that must boiled too long turns bitter, as honey does.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Raw melikraton more laxative, boiled more nourishing
s: As a side note Galen says raw melikraton loosens the bowels more, while well-boiled melikraton nourishes more.
q: raw melikraton is more laxative, while that which has been well boiled is more nourishing

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Oxymel is melikraton with a little vinegar, best boiled
s: Galen says proper oxymel is not simply vinegar and honey but melikraton with a small amount of vinegar. Boiling it is better, because boiling weakens the vinegar's harm while keeping its benefit.
q: For the composition of oxymel does not come about merely from a mixture of vinegar and honey, but from melikraton that takes on a small quantity of vinegar.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Pine-cone electuary: cone boiled with horehound, then honey
s: Galen gives his own electuary for chest expectoration. A fresh, resinous pine cone is boiled in water with horehound, honey is added to the decoction, and it is boiled again to the thickness of honey.
q: Boiling it fresh in water together with horehound, then mixing a moderate amount of honey into the decoction, and boiling this again to a honey-like consistency
n: The 'kokkalos' and myrrh electuary is the appendix's.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Cantharides drink for dropsy (appendix)
s: The appendix prescribes three blister beetles with head, feet and wings removed, ground in three kyathoi of water and drunk fasting, followed by a warm bath and oil-bread.
q: Three cantharides: having removed the head of each and the feet and wings, having ground the bodies in three kyathoi of water
n: This is the Hippocratic lemma; Galen's response is the case at K15.913.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Heating and drying foods: lentil, cabbage, game, salted meat
s: As further examples of warming, drying foods, Galen adds the lentil among pulses, cabbage among vegetables, and among meats those of wild animals and salted meats.
q: You, however, will select also among the pulses those that heat and dry, such as the lentil; and also among the vegetables those that possess this power, such as the cabbage

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Vomiting in the six winter months, enemas in summer
s: Use vomiting during the six winter months, which are more phlegmatic, and enemas ('washings-out') in hot weather, when the body is more bilious. Purging drugs are different, acting on the whole body.
q: to vomit during the six winter months; for this time is more phlegmatic than the summer one, and the diseases arise about the head and about this region above the diaphragm.
n: Per the Aphorisms, purge upward in summer and downward in winter (K15.198-199).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Enema materials: milk, chickpea water, brine, sea-water
s: Oily, thick enemas are made from milk or water in which chickpeas were boiled, and suit the thin, who are more bilious. Thin, salty ones of brine or sea-water are more cutting and suit the fat, who are more phlegmatic.
q: Among the clysters, the oily and thick ones are those made from milks and boiled chickpea-water and [200] the other things of that kind; the thin and salty ones are brine and sea-water and the like.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Hyssop emetic for the fat
s: The fat should vomit fasting, around midday, after running or walking fast. They drink half a kotyle of pounded hyssop in a chous of water, with vinegar and salt to taste, slowly at first and then faster.
q: Let there be a half-kotyle of pounded hyssop in a chous of water, and let him drink this off, pouring in vinegar and adding salt, in whatever way it is likely to be most pleasant.
n: Galen explains the cutting drink as suited to the thick, cold humours of fat people.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Athletes with diarrhoea: cut exercise by a third, halve food
s: Athletes who get diarrhoea with undigested stools should cut their exercise by at least a third and halve their food, eating very well-baked bread crumbled into wine, with little strong drink, one meal, and no walk after it.
q: Let the food for these be bread as thoroughly baked as possible, crumbled into wine, and let the drinks be as small as possible and as unmixed as possible
n: The author blames dense flesh and forced meat-eating (K15.213-214); Galen would treat the cause with gentle rubbing and much oil in the bath.

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Radishes with oxymel spiked with white hellebore
s: A weak hellebore purge: radishes with oxymel into which sprigs of white hellebore have been fixed for a whole day and night.
q: We have sometimes given radishes with oxymel, having fixed into them for a whole day and night sprigs of white hellebore; and such a purgation from hellebore would be a weak one.
n: A known mild hellebore preparation (cf. Hippocratic and later ῥαφανὶς ἐλλεβορισμένη; outside knowledge).

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Unmixed melikraton boiled with thinning herbs
s: When an acute disease must be purged early, preparation may use unmixed melikraton boiled with hyssop, thyme, origanum, goat's-origanum or pennyroyal to thin the humours.
