q: unmixed melikraton made and given, having boiled in it some hyssop, or thyme, or origanum, or goat's-origanum, or pennyroyal

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Best hiera: with hellebore, without scammony
s: Of the variously prepared hiera, the version containing hellebore but not scammony is the best laxative.
q: the version that has taken hellebore but does not contain scammony is the best laxative drug.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Galen's debate over a 7-hour period (5 h paroxysm, 2 h remission)
s: Asked what type a 5-hour paroxysm with 2-hour remission makes, Galen replied it cannot occur, since short paroxysms have long declines; the propounder said it was for exercise.
q: I answered him at once that this cannot even occur. For paroxysms of so short a duration make their declines long, and for the most part even arrive at apyrexia.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Bassus, paralysed, saved by his own akopon
s: Two akopa are linked to Bassus, who was paralysed for a long time and recovered after using them (myrtle and henna oils, chalcanthos, wax, terebinth, galbanum, bryony, verdigris, pepper, pyrethrum, kid's fat, euphorbium).
q: Another, a successful drug of Bassus. He himself, having used this, after having previously been paralysed, was saved.
n: A 'Bassus the Stoic' appears at K13.1033; whether he is the same man is unknown.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Halieus cured himself of a disabling condition; recipe passed to Valerius Paulinus
s: Halieus, so afflicted that his body was distorted, cured himself with his akopon (Sabine oil, black poplar shoots, perfumed oils, fats, sulphur, galbanum, blood of ten tortoises) and gave the recipe to Valerius Paulinus, who altered it.
q: in which Halieus, passing his time and being gripped by the affection to such a degree that his body was distorted, used the drug and was freed from the whole condition.
n: This unit's automatic check failed. 'Passing his time' is unclear and may hide a place name or occupation.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Arruntius Aquila cured with an euphorbium akopon
s: An akopon with opopanax, galbanum, castoreum, white pepper, euphorbium, oesypum, cassia, deer marrow and several oils is recorded as having cured Arruntius Aquila, for sciatica and sinew tension.
q: Another acopon, with which Arruntius Aquila was cured; effective for sciatica and for every tension of the sinews.
n: The same unit gives the akopon of Glytus 'as Philoxenus the grammarian' records it.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Clemens Sertorius cured of a bronchocele
s: Andromachus records a discutient plaster for bronchoceles and indurations 'with which Clemens Sertorius was cured' (litharge, pine resin, old oil, galbanum, burnt copper, ammoniac, alum, manna, wax).
q: Another discutient for bronchoceles, with which Clemens Sertorius was cured, and for indurations
n: A green akopon 'according to Clemens Sertorius, which I use' appears at K13.1037. The draft marks a 'wax 50 pounds (?)' figure in this unit as doubtful.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Slave's wife after miscarriage at five months
s: Epidemics III: a household slave's wife, after miscarriage at about five months, had fever; at first comatose, then sleepless.
q: "Another woman, after a miscarriage at about the fifth month, the wife of a household slave, fever seized; at the beginning she was comatose, and then again

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Parotid swellings that never suppurated
s: In the constitution described, swellings by the ears came in feverless, ambulant people, on one or both sides, and subsided harmlessly without suppurating or inflammation.
q: they subsided in all without harm, and did not suppurate in any, as do those arising from other causes.
n: The mumps constitution of Epidemics I (outside knowledge), though Galen says it is from the 'same book'.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Pythion: comatose on the ninth day
s: Epidemics III, Pythion: on the ninth day comatose and nauseated when roused; here coma means a kind of kataphora.
q: in the case of Pythion, he says, "on the ninth day comatose, nauseated when he was roused"

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Axillary dislocations wedged forward by unskilled levering
s: Two of Galen's patients said the shoulder had first gone into the armpit, but physicians levered it clumsily and wedged the joint among the muscles.
q: For two of those I saw said that the dislocation had occurred into the armpit, but that, when the physicians levered it unskilfully, the joint had been wedged
n: Doctor-caused injury.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Galen's tally: four cases at the shoulder-vein region, one outside
s: The head of the humerus lodged four times in the region of the shoulder vein, where the pectoral and deltoid meet, and once outside the middle region.
q: where the two muscles come together, the great one from the sternum and the one named deltoid, has been seen by us four times to receive the dislocation
n: ὠμιαία φλέψ: the cephalic vein.

wt: On Plethora
t: Tin vessel of viper theriac swells and bursts its wrapping
s: Recently a tin vessel holding the drug made from vipers swelled so much that the leather wrapping and the tying cord burst and the lid bulged.
q: Recently, at any rate, a tin vessel was so greatly inflated by the drug contained in it, the one prepared from vipers, that both the leather wrapped around it and the cord with which it had been tied burst
n: The viper drug is theriac; fermentation in storage. Unit flagged 'fail' by checks but this passage reads soundly.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Philiscus (Epidemics I, case 1): breath rare and large
s: Philiscus, the first patient after the three constitutions in Epidemics I, breathed throughout 'as of one recollecting himself, rare and large'. He was delirious, and his spleen was swollen but not painful.
q: For in this man, he says, the breath throughout was, as of one recollecting himself, rare and large.
n: K7.871-872: the swollen spleen was neither painful nor pressing on the diaphragm, so delirium set the form of breathing.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Wife of Dromeades: rigor after childbirth, delirium, convulsion
s: After childbirth the wife of Dromeades had a rigor on day 2, then delirium and rare, large breathing. Galen later notes she died seized by convulsion, matching the 'drawn up' (uneven) breath.
q: "The wife of Dromeades," he says, "having given birth, and all the other things having gone according to reason, being on the second day, a rigor seized her."
n: The Greek name form is Δρομάδεω (Dromades). For the death by convulsion see K7.931-932.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Anaxion: pleurisy described by its symptoms
s: Anaxion had acute fever, constant right-side pain and a dry cough, then delirium on day 6 and dyspnoea on day 7. Galen explains why Hippocrates lists the symptoms rather than writing 'pleuritic'.
q: let us mention Anaxion, whom, as he himself says, an acute fever seized; continuous pain of the right side; he coughed dry, and did not spit during the first days.
n: Galen says four things are necessary in pleurisy: side pain, fever, dyspnoea and cough (K7.856-857, πλευριτικοῖς).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Young man in Meliboea: quiet delirium to madness
s: The young man in Meliboea became quietly delirious on day 10, talked much nonsense on day 14 and went mad on day 20. His orderly, silent character made the delirium more serious, and his breath stayed large and rare.
q: "on the tenth of the days he became delirious quietly, on the fourteenth he talked much nonsense, on the twentieth he went mad," he says.
n: His hypochondrium was 'somewhat slack' (ὑπολάπαρος, 'somewhat empty', K7.863-864), so it did not override the delirium.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Criton: great-toe pain, raving, death on day 2
s: A man going about his normal business got violent pain in his great toe, became slightly warm on day 1, raved, and died on day 2. Galen thinks Hippocrates could not have watched his breathing.
q: a man who was going about and doing his customary activities, and then had violent pain in the great toe of his foot, should on the first day become slightly warmed and on the next day die.
n: The patient is named Criton at K7.875-876.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Hipposthenes in Larissa: wrestling fall mistaken for peripneumonia
s: Hipposthenes fell on his back on hard ground while wrestling, with his opponent landing on him. He bathed in cold water, then had fever, a dry cough, pain on coughing and frequent breathing. Physicians thought it peripneumonia, but he had no stertor.
q: 'In Larissa, Hipposthenes seemed to the physicians to be gripped by peripneumonia; but it was not so at all. The beginning: while wrestling he fell on his back on hard ground, and [his opponent] fell upon him;
n: Epidemics V, case 14.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Daughter of Agisis: lifted a heavy load after childbirth
s: Short of breath since girlhood, after childbirth she carelessly lifted a great weight, felt a noise in her chest, then had asthma, pain in the right hip and frothy sputum. Galen infers an old lung growth had burst.
q: being in distress not long after childbirth, she carelessly lifted a great weight, and immediately there seemed to be a noise in her chest; on the following day she had asthma
n: Epidemics VI. Galen uses the case to separate frequent breathing from asthma.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Stool frequency of Eudemus versus Paulus
s: Galen reports that Eudemus went to stool two or three times a day, while Paulus sometimes passed nothing at all. He explains this by where each man's bile went.
q: Hence Eudemus went to stool twice each day, and sometimes even three times, whereas Paulus at times did not excrete at all.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Burning fever after bath plus strong wine, anger or sleeplessness
s: A man came home from a hot journey on foot, bathed, then drank wine with a high wine-to-water ratio and fell straight into burning fever. Others fell ill after violent anger or sleeplessness.
q: Another man, coming from a journey on foot and from burning heat, first bathed, and then, having arrived [740] home and drunk wine which had the larger share in the mixture
n: Checks verdict is 'fail'.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Causi resolved by parotid swellings, but not genuine causi
s: Galen says resolution of kausos through an abscess is extremely rare. He knows cases resolved by parotid swellings, but they were not genuine causi.
q: For I know of some causi that were judged by parotid swellings, but not the genuine ones

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Galen purged on day one, two, four or five, not by number
s: Against the author's 'purge on the fourth day', Galen says purging must follow the state of the humours. He himself has purged on the first, second, fourth and fifth days.
q: so that we too have purged around the first day, sometimes also on the second and the fourth, and sometimes also on the fifth

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: Scirrhous leg swellings growing over three or four years
s: Galen has often seen scirrhous swellings of the legs form without prior inflammation and grow slowly over three or four years before hindering walking.
q: I have often observed scirrhous swellings in the legs forming right from the beginning without an inflammation having preceded them, and increasing little by little over three and sometimes even four years

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Supposed colic patient cured by purgation after three months
s: A man treated three months as a colic case and worsening was cured by Galen with purgation alone after discarding the other remedies.
q: that man recently who had already been treated for three months by the physicians as a colic patient and was progressing toward the worse

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Female flux in a prominent Roman woman cured by purgation
s: Galen cured a uterine flux in a not inconspicuous woman at Rome, and in many obscurer women, by purgation alone.
q: I also cured a female flux, in a certain not inconspicuous one of the women at Rome, by purgations alone

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Stirring the plaster with a fresh palm branch
s: The phoinikine is stirred with the thick end of a fresh palm branch, and thin peeled pieces are thrown in at the cerate stage to add their juice; the branch is cut the day before in winter, the same day in summer.
q: So, if it is winter, let it be removed on the previous day; but in summer the branch must be removed from the tree on that very day on which you boil the drug.
n: The palm juice is the 'date' (φοῖνιξ) element of the plaster's name.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Teacher smeared wild pigeon blood on wounds before plastering
s: One of Galen's teachers smeared sinuses and large fresh wounds with the blood of 'grazing' pigeons living in field towers, not domestic ones, before applying the wine plaster.
q: smearing beforehand with the blood of a pigeon, not of the domestic ones, [515] but of those called by some boskades (the 'grazing' ones), which go into the towers that people in our country construct in the fields.
n: 'In our country' means Galen's Asia Minor.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Nerve-wound regimen: warm oil, never water, dressing changed twice daily
s: Galen keeps water away from nerve wounds altogether, washing off blood with oil; he unbinds and foments with sufficiently warm oil two or three times a day, at dawn and evening, and at night when nights are long.
q: I guard against the use of water throughout the whole treatment, to the point that it does not even touch the wound

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Cross-incision to keep a narrow nerve puncture open
s: For narrow punctures over a nerve, keep the opening open so the hot drug can draw out the moisture; if needed enlarge it with two skin incisions crossing at right angles.
q: with two incisions through the skin cutting one another at right angles.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Making hepsema/siraion: last-run must from sweetest grapes
s: Siraion (boiled must) for dissolving troches should be made from the sweetest grapes and the last-flowing must, boiled to half; must of another kind is boiled down to a third.
q: And it becomes such when the must is neither from austere grapes, [613] but from grapes as sweet as possible, nor from what flows first, but from what flows last.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen sun-grinds cadmia for days with vinegar or wine
s: To make cadmia more drying Galen grinds it in the summer sun for several days in a row with vinegar or tawny wine, then dries and stores it to sprinkle on ulcers turning malignant.
q: I am accustomed to prepare it so as to be more drying, in the season of summer, by grinding it in the sun for several days in succession with vinegar or with wine that is tawny in colour
n: The same method is repeated for cadmia with sharp vinegar in the next unit (K13.659-660).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Ulcer dressing: dry powder, platysma, linen and cold sponge
s: A malignant ulcer is wiped with soft clean dry linen and its hollow filled with powder. A flat piece of lip-thinning plaster goes on top, then linen, then a sponge from water or wine, kept cold.
q: The bandage itself should be applied and wound round as Hippocrates taught in the books On Fractures, holding that the greatest harm would result from a bandaging that excels in fine appearance rather than in benefit.
n: Dressings undone every third day; linen bandages, not rags; water never applied to the ulcer itself.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Lucius' quince-yellow escharotic moistened with fasting saliva
s: Lucius the teacher's escharotic: raw chalcitis 8 dr and cadmia 4 dr, barely moistened with saliva while fasting, covered until quince-yellow, dried in the shade and pressed in with the olive-tip of a probe.
q: fasting, take it up with saliva to such an extent that the drug is only just moistened, then gather it together and, having covered it, let it become quince-yellow
n: Fasting saliva was valued as a remedy (outside knowledge: Pliny NH 28).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Galen's rule: weight-litra of litharge to measure-litra of oil
s: From much boiling, Galen finds the right mixture is equal weight-litra of litharge and measure-litra of oil. More oil boiled longer makes it more drying. For white plasters, white lead is added and less oil used because long boiling blackens litharge.
q: the well-proportioned mixture of it comes about when the weight-litra of litharge is set equal to the measure-litra of oil

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Equal-tension nooses and the Hippocratic bench
s: Extension can be done by hand, by the heel, or by a noose of equal tension such as the double karchesios knot or one made of two diantees. For a chronic dislocation Galen needed the Hippocratic bench.
q: The noose must be of equal tension, such as is the double karchesios knot and the one made of two diantees (διαντέων).
n: Technical knot names; διαντέων is obscure (compare the knots in Oribasius' Book 48/49 on nooses).

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Bandaging after shoulder reduction: cerate, compresses, wool pad
s: Treat with cerate, compresses and many linen bandages; fill the armpit with a roll of soft clean wool as a counter-support; keep the upper arm inclined upward; then bind the arm to the side with a band round the body.
q: Such patients, then, one must treat [362] with cerate and compresses and many linen bandages, binding them underneath. And one should place in the armpit soft, clean wool rolled up together
n: Hippocratic lemma (De articulis).

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Rubbing the shoulder in every direction
s: Rub gently with soft hands, top to bottom and bottom to top, obliquely, in circles and across, to soften all the muscle fibres. Galen notes that 'anatripsis' covers every kind of rubbing, not only upward strokes.
q: It must be performed in many forms, the hands being carried around from above downward and from below upward
n: Galen defines rubbing more fully elsewhere.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Cautery irons: elongated, not thick or 'bald'
s: Use glowing irons that are elongated, not thick or rounded at the tip, so they pass through quickly and leave small eschars. Galen identifies 'bald' irons with the pyrenes (diapyrina) and spathomelai.
q: One must cauterize such parts with irons that are not thick, nor too bald, but elongated; for they pass through more quickly
n: Instrument names. The Greek has σπαθομίλαι for 'spathomelai'.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Lead weight bandaged onto a broken clavicle
s: Some have devised the refinement of binding on a heavy piece of lead to press down the projecting fragment. Hippocrates judges this useless, since the projecting part cannot be pushed down that way.
q: There are indeed some who have already devised the refinement of binding on in addition a heavy piece of lead, so as to force down the projecting part.
n: Hippocratic lemma reporting a rival technique.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Girdle and perineal bandaging for clavicle fracture rejected
s: Some tie a girdle round the patient and run the bandage from it over the clavicle, or round the perineum, seat and spine. These seem sound in theory but slip when the patient moves and are troublesome.
q: carrying the bandage in a circle round the perineum and alongside the seat itself and along the spine, in this way they compress the fracture.
n: Hippocratic lemma. Galen adds that porous bones form callus quickly.

wt: On Plethora
t: Trainers' treatment of over-exercised athletes
s: Trainers treat those who exercised too much with abundant oil, soft rubbing and warm baths of sweet water to disperse biting humours formed from melted fat and flesh.
q: the gymnastic trainers treat those who have exercised too much with more abundant oil and soft rubbing and warm baths of sweet waters that are precisely well-tempered

wt: On Leeches, Revulsion, Cupping, Incision and Scarification
t: Preparing the skin for leech application
s: The part to be leeched is first rubbed with natron and smeared, or scratched with the nails, so the leeches take hold more readily.
q: let the part that is to be leeched be first rubbed with natron and smeared over, or scratched with the nails, for so they will take hold more readily.
n: Greek προεκνιτρούσθω = 'be rubbed beforehand with natron (nitron)'.

wt: On Leeches, Revulsion, Cupping, Incision and Scarification
t: Revulsion: cupping at the hypochondrium for nosebleed and uterine flow
s: Revulsion diverts humours away from a part: towards the hands for thorax and belly, vomiting for downward flows, sharp clysters against vomiting; cupping beside the breasts or pressed on the hypochondrium checks nosebleed and excessive menstrual flow.
q: with those pressed firmly upon the hypochondrium you will revulse the rush of blood towards the nostrils, just as also the immoderate flow through the womb.
n: Breasts = τιτθούς (παρὰ τοὺς τιτθοὺς προβαλλομένη σικύα).

wt: On Leeches, Revulsion, Cupping, Incision and Scarification
t: Scarifying the legs after suppressed haemorrhoids
s: When haemorrhoidal bleeding has been suppressed, the legs are scarified after bathing or fomentation; scarification also helps chronic eye fluxes, head conditions, chest and upper back affections, quinsies.
q: when haemorrhoids have been suppressed, we scarify the legs, having first bathed the patient, or fomenting (πυριᾷν) either in hot water or
n: 'Impactions' at the end renders σφηνώσεις (wedgings, obstructions).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Frothy, intensely bilious stools mean colliquative fever: stop melikraton
s: Frothy, intensely bilious stools show that the fever is colliquative. Galen says to stop melikraton, move to ptisan juice, and give cold water at the right moment for the greatest benefit.
q: know that the fever is colliquative, and on this account desist from the use of melikraton and proceed to the juice of ptisane

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: After the bath: three graded lukewarm affusions
s: Healthy people plunge into cold water after the hot bath, but the sick cannot bear it. Galen advises at least three lukewarm waters, each cooler than the last, poured over the patient.
q: those will do better who prepare no fewer than three lukewarm waters for after the hot bath, differing from one another
n: K15.710-711 says physicians of Galen's day pour lukewarm water instead of using the cold basin.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Galen bleeds at once instead of fomenting first, with rubbing
s: Where the author fomented before venesection, Galen always cuts the inner elbow vein at once to save time. Many attendants rub the body meanwhile, and if blood will not flow he rubs and foments until it does.
q: it is better to do what we ourselves have always written: to cut at once the inner vein at the elbow

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Treating synanche: sublingual venesection and attractive neck plasters
s: Treatment combines whole-body evacuation (venesection, purging, clysters), astringent and hot pungent local drugs, incision of the veins under the tongue, and attractive drugs on the neck to draw the humours outward.
q: and, without drugs, the veins beneath the tongue, when incised, evacuate the inflammation in the pharynx

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Venesection only for anasarca from suppressed haemorrhoids or menses
s: Only the dropsy throughout the flesh sometimes needs phlebotomy at its start, when it began from suppressed haemorrhoids, suppressed menses or plethora. No one has dared bleed tympanites or ascites.
q: when at any rate it is formed having begun from a suppression of a haemorrhoid, or of the menses in women

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Eyelid trichiasis surgery called anabrochismos
s: Galen summarizes the appendix's closing prescriptions and names its suture operation for ingrowing eyelashes: anabrochismos.
q: next he wrote the surgical procedure for hairs on the eyelids, which they call anabrochismos
n: The Greek spelling here is ἀναβρογχισμόν (with gamma), a variant of ἀναβροχισμός.

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: Feeding by disease period; remission defined
s: Treatment is soothing at the acme and combative at beginning and end; if strength will last, food is withheld until decline, otherwise the patient is fed from the start in remissions.
q: if it will hold out until the time of the acme even without taking nourishment, it is best to abstain from food until the decline has begun
n: Refers to 'the treatise on the therapeutic method' (Methodus medendi).

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Preparing a patient for hellebore
s: Before hellebore, thick humours are thinned and passages opened; the patient's response to vomiting is tested with moderate emetics, he is habituated to vomit, and the body is moistened with abundant bland food and rest.
q: In those who are about to take hellebore, one must first make trial of their nature, to see how it stands with regard to upward purgations, that is, those through vomiting.
n: Neglect brings griping, vertigo, nausea, bad pulse and faintness.

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Purging regimens for three kinds of dropsy and jaundice
s: Phlegmatic dropsy: phlegm-drawing drug via lower belly, then vomits, then apophlegmatisms; ascites: a hydragogue; jaundice: a cholagogue, with bile expelled up, down, by urine, palate and nostrils.
q: in the case of the ascitic dropsy we shall give one of the hydragogue drugs, just as in the case of the icteric one of the cholagogue drugs.
n: Apophlegmatisms = ἀποφλεγματισμῶν (errhines/masticatories drawing phlegm from the head).

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Purge upward in paroxysms, downward in remissions
s: Evacuations should be made from the upper parts during paroxysms and from the lower parts during remissions, imitating spontaneous vomiting and nosebleeds in paroxysms and urine and stools in remissions.
q: making the evacuations from the upper parts during the paroxysms, and from the [350] lower parts during the so-called remissions.

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Sipping ptisane after a cathartic (Hippocrates)
s: After the cathartic is drunk the patient sips ptisane juice to wash residue from gullet and stomach and temper the drug; once purging begins ptisane is stopped so as not to dissipate it.
q: After the cathartic has been taken it is beneficial to sip ptisane afterwards, as Hippocrates says.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Thasos: the Parian lodging above the Artemision
s: Epidemics III case of the Parian at Thasos who lay sick above the Artemision, seized by acute, continuous, burning fever.
q: "In Thasos the Parian, who lay sick above the Artemision, an acute fever seized
n: Temple of Artemis on Thasos (outside knowledge).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Galen found watery wines in Cilicia, Phoenicia, Palestine, Scyros, Crete, Egypt
s: Galen says he found thin watery wines in Cilicia, Phoenicia, Palestine, Scyros and Crete, and even in Egypt, though hot regions usually make thick strong wines. In Italy, Bithynia and Asia such wines are common.
q: I at any rate have found wines of this kind in Cilicia and Phoenicia and Palestine and Scyros and Crete
n: This is evidence for Galen's travels (compare his journeys to Palestine and Cyprus mentioned in Simple Drugs). Checks verdict is 'fail'.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Wine quality: styptic is noble, sour means turning
s: In wine, stypticity marks excellence. No wine is sour by nature, and any sourness at once raises the suspicion that it is turning to vinegar.
q: for the styptic wines are of noble quality, whereas none is sour by nature, but if even a little of such a quality comes upon them, we at once suspect their change into vinegar.
n: The same passage notes that apples and pomegranates are popularly called sour, styptic or sweet.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Galen excerpts long quotations rather than copying in full
s: Galen says Lycus' passage is very long, so, as with the previous one, he copies only the most pertinent part.
q: for that one too, being extremely long, I did not write out in full, but selected only the most pertinent part of it.
n: Evidence of Galen's quotation practice: the Lycus fragments are selective excerpts.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Wine-mixing measures: kotyle, pithos, kyathoi
s: To illustrate proportion, Galen contrasts a kotyle of water thrown into a jar (pithos) of wine with a small cup of three kyathoi, one of water and two of wine.
q: having thrown a cotyle of water into a jar of wine, he says that the water in the jar is more than that in a small cup, when, as it happens, there are three cyathi in the latter
n: A 1:2 water-to-wine cup is mentioned in passing. Drinkers judge the mix by proportion, not volume.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Olympic and Pythian periods as model of 'period'
s: The ancients used 'period' for any same event recurring at equal intervals, as in the Olympic and Pythian periods.
q: they used to call certain periods Olympic [476] and Pythian.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Pythian precept: be sparing of time
s: Galen closes recalling the Pythian precept that one should be sparing of time.
q: remembering the Pythian precept, that it is fitting to be sparing of time.
n: Delphic maxim (χρόνου φείδου; outside knowledge).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Limnesion sold in Italy as 'adarke'
s: Damocrates says the rough limnesion is what sellers and buyers of ingredients in Italy call adarke.
q: and equal to these of rough limnēsion—those who sell the ingredients in Italy, and those who buy them, call this adarkē
n: Evidence of trade names in the Italian drug market.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Emplastron with rho; kentrion and melotris etymologies
s: Galen notes that recent physicians write emplastron with a rho, as with kentrion (from kentein, to prick) and melotris (from mele, probe, and ous, ear), and he follows the prevailing usage.
q: the kentrion having been named from kentein (to prick), its final syllable not having the rho, and the melotris being compounded from mele (probe) and ous (ear).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Andromachus at Rome still wrote kotylai, not local litrai
s: Galen wonders why Andromachus, living in Rome, wrote kotylai instead of the local units litra, xestes and ounce.
q: And yet one might wonder how, while residing in Rome, he named kotylai instead of litrai; for these are the local names: that of the litra, that of the xestes, and that of the ounce.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Alexandrian mina of 20 ounces = 160 drachms
s: Where Asclepiades says the mina has 160 drachms, Galen infers the Alexandrian mina of 20 ounces at 8 drachms each.
q: It is quite evident, then, that he means the Alexandrian mina, which has 20 ounces, so that each of the ounces has 8 drachmas

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Regional resin names: Laconian 'first-flowing', Cilician kapnelaion
s: Self-flowing resins are called 'first-flowing' in Lacedaemon and elsewhere, and kapnelaion in Cilicia; unrefined pine resin is shipped in cases and jars full of wood and stones.
q: In Lacedaemon and in certain other places they call these 'first-flowing' (πρωτόρρυτοι), while in Cilicia they name such a resin kapnelaion (smoke-oil)
n: Unit failed the automatic check. The Greek spells the word πρωτοῤῥύτους. 'Smoke-oil' is the draft's gloss.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Black amaracine perfume once made with Pontic pitch
s: Oily fragrant pitch from Bruttium and from Pontus was put into the black amaracine unguent, as all of it used to be made; nowadays they make a whitish amaracine without it.
q: that brought from the regions about Pontus, which is at once oily and fragrant, and which they put into the black amaracine unguent, such as formerly all of it used to be prepared.
n: A change in perfume manufacture within Galen's lifetime (continues in K13.630).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Roman perfumed oils 'spicatum' and 'foliatum' and perfumers' wax
s: For bared nerves Galen made a cerate of perfumers' wax with the perfumes the Romans call spicatum and foliatum, adding a twelfth of washed pompholyx.
q: I compounded the cerate from the wax called perfumers' wax and from the perfumed oils named among the Romans spicatum and foliatum.
n: Latin perfume names written in Greek.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Most drying wines: Falernian, Tmolite, Ariusian, Lesbian of Eresos and Methymna
s: Galen grinds cadmia with tawny, translucent wine and names the most drying wines: Falernian (Italy), Tmolite (Asia), Ariusian (Chios) and the fragrant Lesbian of Eresos and Methymna.
q: such as the Falernian is in Italy and the Tmolite in Asia; and such a wine is the most drying of wines. Of the same class are the Ariusian, produced in Chios, and the fragrant Lesbian at Eresos and Methymna.
n: A useful regional wine list from a pharmaceutical point of view.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Alexandrian mina 20 ounces; ounce 7, 7½ or 8 drachms
s: Writers on weights disagree: the mina is 16 or 20 ounces (some say the Alexandrian mina is 20 and the other 16), or 100 drachms or more, and the ounce is 7½ drachms, 7 or 8.
q: some also making a distinction and asserting that the Alexandrian mina is twenty ounces and the other sixteen
n: Galen uses these figures to show Criton wrote the Hicesius at double Heras' quantities.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Attic kotyle = 9 Italian ounces = 60 drachms; graduated horns
s: Galen explains that Heras' 180 drachms of oil equal three kotylai. The Attic kotyle is 9 Italian ounces measured on graduated horns, which weigh 7½ weight-ounces, or 60 drachms at 8 drachms to the ounce.
q: for the Attic one at any rate does weigh that, being of nine Italian ounces. For the nine Italian ounces, those marked on the graduated horns, weigh seven and a half weight-ounces, which come to sixty drachms
n: Distinguishes volume ('measure') ounces from weight ounces; graduated horn measures were used for oil. Asclepiades' version of the Hicesius in External Remedies book 2 is fourfold.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Melanteria prepared from nails
s: Andromachus' golden powder for spreading sores calls for melanteria 'of the kind prepared from nails'. When fresh, as Philinus says, it works better on spreading sores.
q: melanteria, the kind prepared from nails, 5 dr.
n: Implies melanteria made artificially from iron nails, beside the mined kind.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Scythian bdellium better than Arabian
s: For softening, Scythian bdellium is far better than Arabian, especially fresh and soft, which recent physicians call 'fatty' or 'moister'.
q: that the Scythian is far better for these purposes than the other, the Arabian, and especially when it is fresh and soft, which they also call "fatty" (λιπαρόν).

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Plough-oxen suffer most in winter (Homer)
s: Homer rightly saw that oxen suffer most of all grazing animals in winter, and plough-oxen most of all, because they work through the winter and cannot crop short grass.
q: For Homer had well observed that of all grazing beasts oxen suffer most at this season, and of oxen the plough-oxen, because they work during the winter.
n: Lemma text (Hippocrates), not Galen's own words; Galen notes Homer's 'welcome spring' line for the crumple-horned oxen (K18a.356-357).

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Recurrent shoulder dislocation ends athletic and military careers
s: Hippocrates says many men, otherwise capable, have been kept from athletic contests by a shoulder that keeps dislocating, and many became useless in war and died because of it.
q: For many men have already been prevented from athletic contest by this misfortune, though in all other respects fully capable, and many have become useless in matters of war
n: Hippocratic lemma; the unit's checks failed, but the Greek matches.

wt: On Plethora
t: What makes blood hotter, moister, colder, drier
s: Idleness and moist regimen make blood moister; anger, exercise, sun exposure, rubbing, heating drugs or food, and stronger older wines make it hotter; recent chill colder; dry foods drier.
q: from anger and exercises, from exposures to scorching heat and from rubbings, from a heating drug, from nourishment of that kind, and from wines less diluted and older, hotter

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Asian Greeks still say 'greenish' for pale-yellow
s: To explain Hippocrates' 'greenish' urine, Galen cites a usage still current among the Greeks of Asia. They call a sallow person chlōros, using it the same as ōchros.
q: by 'greenish' he speaks according to a certain usage of the Greeks in Asia, which is preserved even now
n: This is evidence for spoken Greek in Galen's home region of Asia Minor.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Potainia: Ionic word for fresh barley-groats
s: Galen notes that Hippocrates calls fresh barley-groats potainia, in the dialect of the Ionians and the older writers.
q: he called the fresh ones potainia in the dialect of the Ionians and of the older writers

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Theraean and Scybelite: outstandingly sweet, thick, black wines
s: Galen's examples of sweet wines are the Theraean and the Scybelite, both thick and black.
q: At any rate the Theraean and the Scybelite are sweet wines to an outstanding degree, both being thick and black

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Maeonian sweet wines: Therinos and Karyinos
s: Sweet wines are also made in Maeonia, the Therinos and the Karyinos. They are less sweet, thick and black than the Theraean and the Scybelite.
q: sweet too are those produced in Maeonia, the Therinos and the Karyinos

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Greek terms stryphnos (harsh) versus austēros (dry) wine
s: Galen notes that the Greeks call an excessively astringent wine stryphnos and a more moderate one austēros.
q: which the Greeks also call stryphnos (harsh), while they call the more moderate one austēros (dry)

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Dark austere wines near Pergamum, Perperina and Aegae
s: Not all dark wines are sweet. Galen's examples are the austere dark wines of his home region in Asia, near Pergamum and around Perperina and Aegae.
q: some of them are austere, such as those among us in Asia near Pergamum and around Perperina and Aegae.
n: Checks verdict is 'fail'.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Cilician Anabates wine: sweet and austere at once, bad
s: Galen says the Anabates of Cilicia combines austere and sweet qualities. For that reason it is a bad wine that lingers in the upper belly and causes wind.
q: The Anabates in Cilicia is at once both austere and sweet, being compounded of opposite qualities
n: Checks verdict is 'fail'.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Modern practice: no strigil; patients wrapped in linen or unfulled cloaks
s: Galen reports that physicians of his day use neither strigil nor sponge on the sick. After the bath they wrap them in linen or in cloaks, especially unfulled ones, to make them sweat.
q: Nor do physicians nowadays use strigils on the sick, nor indeed a sponge either, but after the bath they wrap them in a linen cloth

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: In Asia people call all swellings 'systrophai'
s: Galen explains 'gatherings of diseases' by current usage: he still hears many people in 'our Asia' call all unnatural swellings systrophai.
q: for even now I hear many people in our Asia naming in this way all the swellings contrary to nature

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Kokkalos = konos (ancients) = strobilos (recent physicians)
s: Galen notes that the pine cone the author calls kokkalos was called konos by the ancient Greeks and strobilos by nearly all recent physicians.
q: the kokkalos spoken of by him was not so named by the ancient Greeks, but rather konos (cone), just as by nearly all the more recent physicians it is called strobilos

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Young wines are never tawny
s: Galen calls the author's diet of hot bread in dark wine and oil 'layman's and archaic', because dark wine makes melancholic blood. Tawny, thin, older wine is better, since no young wine is tawny.
q: for of young wines none will be tawny, but either white or red or dark, whereas as they age they become both tawny and yellow

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: Black bile as the lees of blood, like lees in wine
s: Black bile is described as a sort of sediment of the blood, as lees are in wine.
q: although it is, as it were, a kind of sediment of the blood, as the lees are in wines.
n: Greek ἰλύς (sediment) and τρύξ (wine lees).

wt: Against Lycus
t: Commentators of opposing sects should not expound the Aphorisms
s: Galen holds that neither those enrolled under opposing doctrines nor those ignorant of the basics of the art are fit to expound the Aphorisms.
q: For it is not reasonable that either those who have been enrolled under opposing doctrines, or those who do not even know the first useful things of the art, should expound the Aphorisms
n: ἐνεγράφησαν, 'were enrolled', is the language of sect membership; it implies that Lycus belonged to a rival school.

wt: Against Lycus
t: The aphorism at issue: growing things have most innate heat
s: Galen states the lemma under dispute: those who are growing have the most innate heat (Aphorism I.14).
q: growing things have the most innate heat
n: Hippocrates, Aph. I.14 (outside knowledge for the numbering).

wt: Against Lycus
t: Physicians disputed whether bodily heat comes from cardiac motion
s: Galen reports that physicians disagree on whether heat arises from the motion of the heart and arteries or is innate in the heart, as its motion is.
q: is a matter of dispute among physicians
n: A doxographic note on a real controversy; no names are given.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Innate heat comes from seed and menstrual blood
s: Everyone has the hot element innately from the first beginning, drawn from seed and menstrual blood. Individuals differ in degree within a latitude of health; beyond it they fall ill or die.
q: For in all of us the hot element is present innately from the first beginning, which we possess from the seed and the menstrual blood.
n: The latitude (πλάτος) of health is a characteristic Galenic idea.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Galen's own definitions of wet and dry fevers
s: Wet fevers: the patient sweats from day one with little or no benefit. Dry fevers: violent thirst, dry tongue, skin hard as hide. Kausoi are given as dry and 'typhodeis' as wet.
q: The patients sweat from the first day, yet are benefited by these sweats either moderately or not at all: these fevers I call wet
n: He offers his own definitions in case others use the names differently, which signals that fever nomenclature was unstable.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Galen reduces Lycus' argument by swapping 'hot' for 'sound'
s: Galen rewrites Lycus' sentence word for word with 'sound' in place of 'hot'. The result would abolish grammar, the art of the 24 letters, and music, so Lycus' argument is invalid too.
q: it is carried through by means of those very words of his, all of them, with only one, the name of ‘hot’, changed into that of ‘sound’
n: A clear example of Galen's parody-by-substitution method. Musical examples follow: mese, lichanos of the mesai, paramese, parhypate, trite of the diezeugmenai.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Catalogue of named fevers
s: Galen lists fever kinds that physicians had written about: kausos, leipyria, epialos, typhodes, pestilential, semi-tertian, quotidian, tertian, quartan.
q: the burning fever (kausos) and the leipyria and the epialos and the typhoid and the pestilential and the semi-tertian, the quotidian and the tertian and the quartan.
n: 'Typhoid' renders τυφώδης and should not be read in the modern sense. The same unit says Lycus 'elsewhere writes of differences of fevers' (ἑτέρωθι γράφει πυρετῶν διαφορὰς).

wt: Against Lycus
t: 'Innate' means primordial: the body from seed and menses
s: Galen glosses 'innate' as 'primordial' (archegonon): the body present from the beginning, from which the animal was first generated, namely menstrual blood and seed.
q: having considered what sort of thing among the bodies in us is innate, that is, primordial.
n: At 235-236 he invokes Hippocrates' 'six-day seed' (τὴν ἑκταίαν γονὴν), in which only the innate hot body exists before bone, vein or nerve form.

wt: Against Lycus
t: Tetrapharmakon recipe: wax, fat, pitch, resin in equal parts
s: Galen uses the tetrapharmakon, equal parts wax, fat, pitch and resin, to show that 'more pitch' means more by proportion, not by the size of the vessel.
q: the preparation called the tetrapharmakon, composed of wax and fat and pitch and resin, all put together in equal amounts
n: 'δύναμις' here means a compound drug. The recipe matches standard ancient tetrapharmakon (outside knowledge).

wt: Against Lycus
t: A common drug of iris, aristolochia, vetch flour, frankincense
s: Galen describes a very customary drug of iris, aristolochia, bitter-vetch flour and frankincense in equal weights. Doubling the aristolochia makes it 'more' in substance, quality and activity.
q: this drug, which is among the most customary, and which is composed of iris and aristolochia and the flour of bitter vetch and frankincense, all equal to one another in weight
n: Here the ingredients are not wholly blended, unlike the tetrapharmakon.

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Galen's table of type-hours (24 to 1176)
s: A diagram lists hours per type in steps of 24: quotidian 24, tertian 48, quartan 72 up to the fiftieth-day type at 1176, to be kept on a sheet of papyrus.
q: either by memory or written down on a sheet of papyrus: for the quotidian that of 24, for the tertian that of forty-eight
n: Table continues in K7.490-491, K7.492 and K7.493; values check arithmetically (nth-day type = (n-1) x 24).

wt: Against Those Who Wrote on Types or on Periods (of Fever)
t: Inclusive naming of types
s: Types are named from the return of the paroxysm, not completed days: a period of four days is called a quintan.
q: when you find a period of a type of four days, you will call it quintan, for it is not the same thing to suffer the paroxysm on every fifth day and to have a period of five days.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Rheumatic conditions come from weakness and cold, not heat
s: Against those who think fluxes come from much heat, Galen says weakness of parts, mostly from cold dyscrasia, causes rheumatic conditions; relaxants alone make them slack, strong astringents make them scirrhous.
q: Rather, it is the weakness of the parts that produces the rheumatic conditions, a weakness which for the most part is brought about in accordance with a cold dyscrasia.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Andromachus arranged plasters by colour, writing 'another' sixteen times
s: Galen faults Andromachus for listing sixteen green plasters headed only 'another', grouped by colour rather than power and without their uses.
q: prefixing to each of them only this one word, "another", writing them all as differing from one another in power

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Cold is hostile to nerves, so dry, near-neutral drugs are best
s: Since putrefaction comes from moisture and heat, and Hippocrates rightly said cold is hostile to the nerves, Galen concluded that the best drug for nerve wounds dries and is neutral or somewhat hot.
q: But reflecting again that cold has truly been said by Hippocrates to be hostile to the nerves

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: 'Chironian' ulcers means extremely malignant ones
s: Galen explains that 'Chironian' ulcers are not moderately malignant ones but the most extremely malignant.
q: for they call thus those ulcers that are not moderately malignant, but very extremely so.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Definitions: 'austere' moderate astringency, 'harsh' intense
s: Galen defines 'austere' as moderately astringent and 'harsh' as violently astringent. Astringents seal the surface, so fine-parted sharp drugs are added to carry their power into the depth.
q: For by the word 'austere' is signified, among the Greeks, that which is moderately astringent, and by 'harsh' that which is violently and intensely so.

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Manna is the shaken-off residue of frankincense
s: Galen explains that 'manna' in recipes is the aposeisma (shaken-off residue) of frankincense, which carries a little bark and is therefore more astringent.
q: For that is what they call [784] the shaken-off residue (aposeisma) of frankincense, which partakes also to some small degree of the bark.
n: The term is important for reading every recipe in the work.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: 'While being heated, dined': Hippocrates' gradation of fever
s: Hippocrates would not call 'fever' a heat during which one can dine, and wrote 'fire seized him' for great fever.
q: For "a man," he says, "while being heated, dined": he did not venture to call "fever" a heat of such a degree during which one is able to dine.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Sluggish (nōthra) wakeful kataphora distinguished from lethargy
s: Wakeful kataphora has two species, one called sluggish; such patients rave and want to get up, react to voices and touch, and move spasmodically, unlike motionless, voiceless lethargics.
q: for they readily get up on hearing a voice or any sound at all, and if you touch some part of the body, they at once raise their eyes and look toward the one touching them.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Physicians cauterise recurrent dislocations in the wrong places
s: Many physicians burn the top of the shoulder, the front or behind. Since the humerus dislocates downward, these burns rather encourage the dislocation by closing the space above.
q: For many physicians have already cauterised dislocating shoulders both at the epomis and in front, where the head of the humerus bulges out, and a little behind the epomis.
n: Hippocratic polemic, endorsed by Galen.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Hippocratic 'cords' (tonoi) are nerves
s: The 'most critical cords' under the armpit are the nerves. Galen mocks recent physicians who limit the word to the paired nerves from the brain on the strength of an Epidemics passage.
q: He says that beneath the part under the armpit lie critical cords, naming the nerves in this way.
n: The nerves to the hand come from the spinal cord in the neck (K18a.380-381).

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Most copies wrongly read 'posterior eschar'
s: Galen says most copies wrongly read 'and again another posterior eschar', because the site is on the outer side of the joint, not behind it.
q: But in most of the copies the wording is not correctly written thus, 'and again another posterior eschar'; for this place is not behind the articulation, but on the outside.
n: Galen's evidence on the manuscripts of De articulis.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Galiankones: weasel-armed from birth
s: People born 'galiankones' (short upper arms) result from a dislocation in the womb or from deep suppuration at the humeral head in infancy. Galen leaves open whether the name comes from weasels (γαλαῖ).
q: Whether the galiankones were so named from their resemblance to weasels (γαλαῖ) or from something else, one must leave it to those who busy themselves with such matters to investigate carefully.
n: Congenital or early-acquired shortening of the humerus.

wt: On Plethora
t: Four grades of biting: squill to rigor
s: Biting substances grade into itch-producing (like squill), biting (like onion, ulcerating with time), shivering, and rigor; biting humours act the same four ways.
q: for those that bite moderately are itch-producing, like squill; those that bite more vehemently are biting, like the onion

wt: On Plethora
t: Euexia, eusarkia, polysarkia; euaimia vs polyaimia
s: Good nourishment of solids is euexia, increase of flesh eusarkia or polysarkia; good-bloodedness is natural in quality and quantity, much-bloodedness excess in quantity; in athletes faculty and blood rise together.
q: in the case of blood there is on the one hand what is, as it were, a kind of good-bloodedness (euaimia), and on the other much-bloodedness (polyaimia).

wt: On Plethora
t: Skin colour reveals the predominant humour in plethora
s: Blood plethora is deep red, yellow bile pale-yellow, phlegm whiter and black bile darker; bile in excess by itself, as in icterus, is cacochymia, not plethora.
q: For the plethos of blood is deep red, that of yellow bile somewhat pale-yellow; and the colour turns toward whiter than the natural when phlegm predominates

wt: On Plethora
t: Sweet, sour and salty phlegm and their effects
s: Sweet phlegm makes people somnolent, sour phlegm hungry, salty phlegm thirsty; the crude humour removes appetite; moist, cool sensory principle brings coma, dry hot brings sleeplessness.
q: people become somnolent when the sweet kind is in excess, hungry when the sour kind is in excess, just as they become thirsty when the salty kind prevails
n: Greek: ὑπνώδεις ... ἐπὶ τοῦ γλυκέος, πεινώδεις ... ἐπὶ τοῦ ὀξέος, διψώδεις ... τὸ ἁλυκόν; draft matches.

wt: On Plethora
t: Melancholic humour vs true black bile
s: Black bile with acid quality makes people hungry; while it is only like a sediment of blood and not yet acid, Galen prefers to call it 'melancholic humour' rather than black bile.
q: it is perhaps better (so far as it is called a melancholic humour) not yet to call such a humour black bile either, but, as I am accustomed, melancholic

wt: On Plethora
t: Ranking of plethora signs; season, region, skin density
s: Scientific signs (tension, heaviness, vein swelling, colour, pulse) outrank causes (suppressed excretions, idleness, rich food, baths after meals); winter, spring, cold regions and dense skin favour plethora.
q: for in winter and spring, and in cold and temperate regions, people accumulate plethora more, but in hot and dry seasons and regions less

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Causes of small, rapid, frequent breathing
s: Tumours of the stomach, liver, spleen or colon press on the diaphragm. In dropsy, pregnancy, over-filling, pot-belly, orthopnoea, lung growths and spinal deformity the breath is likewise small, frequent and rapid.
q: in dropsical patients and in pregnant women and in [782] those who have been over-filled and in those with protruding bellies, the form of respiration becomes of this kind
n: Spinal deformities are named as kyphotic, lordotic and scoliotic. A narrow thorax can be present from the womb.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Four diagnostic pairings of dyspnoea
s: Large and frequent breathing shows increased need; small and rare, decreased need; large and rare is proper to delirium; small and frequent, to pain. Unevenness is a fifth sign.
q: it was found that the large and frequent respiration indicates increase of the need, and its opposite, the small and rare, indicates diminution; and that the large and rare is peculiar to delirium
n: These pairings are the core diagnostic result of Book 1 (summary at K7.823-824).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Count of patients in Epidemics I and III
s: Galen counts sixteen patients in Epidemics I, with rare, large breathing mentioned four times. Later he counts fourteen patients in book I, and in book III twelve before and sixteen after the pestilential constitution.
q: In the first book of the Epidemics, then, Hippocrates, having described sixteen patients in all, is seen making mention of rare and large breathing four times.
n: Inconsistency: K7.879-880 says 'These fourteen patients' (τεσσαρεσκαίδεκα ἄῤῥωστοι) from book I, perhaps counting only those after Philiscus and Silenus. Worth checking against the Greek.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Rejected reading 'as those who breathe in cold upon hot'
s: Some editors join 'hot, cold' to the previous phrase and read 'as those who breathe in cold upon hot'. Galen rejects this as senseless and keeps hot and cold breath as a separate pair of dyspnoeas.

n: A variant reading of Epid. VI (and II) recorded only by Galen.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: Prognostic: cold breath from nose and mouth is deadly
s: Galen quotes the Prognostic on three dyspnoeas: frequent breath signals pain or inflammation above the diaphragm, large and slow breath signals delirium, and cold breath from the nose and mouth is already very deadly.
q: and breathed out cold [902] from the nostrils and the mouth it is already exceedingly deadly.
n: K7.928-929: chilled respiratory organs mean death because the heart, source of the innate heat, lies there.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing

s: Some call Regimen in Acute Diseases 'On Ptisan'. No critic has denied it to Hippocrates, but many remove the final part after the section on baths.
q: For the parts at the end, those after the use of the bath, many remove, but the parts up to that point all preserve.
n: Ancient testimony that the appendix (Acut. Spur.) was regarded as not genuine.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing

s: Galen quotes On Joints: people with a hump above the diaphragm grow a pointed chest, are short of breath and wheezing, and often have hard, unripe lung growths.

n: Galen equates κέρχνος (On Joints) with ῥέγχος (Regimen in Acute Diseases).

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing

n: Lexical dispute over a Hippocratic term.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV

n: This explains the lemma (K15.692-693) that vinegar is hostile to women because it pains the womb.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: 'He had a crisis' implies survival; deaths are specified
s: Galen notes a usage of unqualified terms for the better case. A good crisis is called simply 'he had a crisis', but a fatal one is 'having had a crisis, he died'. Likewise 'bile' means yellow bile and 'cloudy urine' means white clouds.
q: when the one who has had the crisis dies, they do not say it simply, but say the whole thing: 'having had a crisis, he died'

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: The chous varies by place; Galen finds the Attic chous too much
s: Galen cannot fix the quantity, because the chous is not the same size everywhere. If the Attic chous is meant, he thinks it too much, though the ancients gave whey and washing-out drinks in very large amounts.

n: Evidence on regional variation in ancient measures (K15.200-201).

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Liver pain after exercise or bathing after meals
s: In people without fever, exercising or bathing after a meal causes pain in the viscera, especially the liver, from thick humours blocking the narrow vessel ends. They should rest and take diuretics that open the liver, or growths and fevers follow.
q: Such people must rest during the time in which they are in pain, and drink some one of the remedies that are diuretic and that unblock the liver.
n: A physiological account of blood passing from the concave to the convex parts of the liver.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Brain-disease and strangury passage suspected spurious
s: A passage on brain diseases with numbness and strangury, ending when water or mucus breaks out of the nose or ears, has rightly been suspected. Some reject it as neither Polybus' nor Hippocrates', and Galen agrees its claims are untrue.
q: With good reason people have regarded this passage with suspicion, and some have even condemned it outright, on the grounds that neither Polybus wrote it, nor, still less, Hippocrates.
n: The passage (K15.221-222) describes nine days of strangury and sight being 'stolen' afterwards.

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: Concoction signs in ophthalmia and nasal catarrh

q: the eyelids of those who have slept are even glued together by the rheum (lēmē) that has formed

wt: On the Periods of the Whole Disease
t: Good and deadly urines
s: Best urine is well-coloured, moderately thick, with good suspended matter, cloud or sediment; water-like urine is unconcocted; black cloud or sediment, dusky, bran-like, foul-smelling or oily urine is deadly.
q: urine that is strongly foul-smelling, and that which is fatty, which they call oily, is deadly.

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Which humour to purge for which chronic disease
s: Elephas and similar need purging of black humours; epileptic, apoplectic and asthmatic diseases of phlegm; hot arthritic diseases of yellow bile, cold-swelling ones of phlegm.
q: epileptic, apoplectic and asthmatic diseases, of the phlegmatic humours; arthritic diseases, those accompanied by much heat, of the bitter-bilious humours

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Narrow-chested patients and emetics: vessel rupture
s: People with a narrow, compressed thorax are most unsuited to emetic purges, especially white hellebore, because a vessel in the respiratory organs ruptures.
q: Those who have a narrow (στέρνον ἔχοντε) thorax, and for this reason also a compressed one, happen to be most unsuited to purgations by means of emetic drugs
n: Same unit: bile is evacuated upward, phlegm downward (sometimes reversed), melancholic humour always downward.

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Hippocratic Aphorism on seasonal direction of purging
s: Citing the Aphorisms: in summer purge the upper cavity, in winter the lower; analogous reasoning applies to regions, ages and habit (those used to vomiting tolerate upward purges).
q: It is written in the Aphorisms of Hippocrates concerning the seasons: in summer purge
n: Hippocrates, Aphorisms IV.4 (outside knowledge).

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: Definition of humours 'in turgor' (orgân)
s: Humours are said to be in turgor when, in violent motion and flowing between parts at the start of a disease, they cause pain, nausea and restlessness; only these may be purged early.
q: The humours are said to be in turgor when, having come into a more violent motion and flowing across from parts to parts, at the beginning of the disease they trouble the person
n: Gloss on Hippocratic ὀργᾶν (Aph. I.22).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind
t: Numeral δ΄ ambiguous: 'four parts' or 'a quarter'
s: Galen warns that in the copies the verdigris figure δ΄ is written either with a point or with a long overline, so it means either four parts or one quarter. The difference changes the drug's strength greatly.
q: in some of the copies the δ΄ is written marked off with a point (ἀπεστιγμένον), but in some having a long line above it, so that it signifies either four parts or a fourth of one.
n: Galen's own warning about corruption of numerals in recipes, of direct use to editors. He settles on one quarter (K13.726-727).

wt: On the Composition of Drugs by Kind

wt: Against Lycus
t: Lycus on the works of heat in the body
s: Within the quotation, Lycus lists heat's works: melting, setting, transforming, and in our bodies digesting food in the stomach and intestines, distributing it, assimilating it, nutrition and growth.
q: it digests the food in the stomach and the intestines, and conveys the product of its working-up into the body, and alters it into body and attaches it to our bodies, in nutrition and in growth.
n: Lycus' physiology of nutrition and growth closely matches Galen's own scheme. At 229-230 Lycus holds the strongest heat is the most well-proportioned (τὸ μάλιστα σύμμετρον), not the most intense.

wt: On Plethora
t: Empiricists' 'plethoric syndrome'
s: Empiricists claim long experience shows phlebotomy helps a syndrome: distended vessels, redness and heaviness, reluctance to move, tension of limbs, ulcerous and lassitude sensations, idle life with rich diet and suppressed excretions.

s: Since purgatives harm the belly and its sinewy, sensitive mouth, fragrant seeds of attenuating and incisive power are mixed in to blunt harm without hindering action.
q: the admixture of fragrant substances was devised, so that their power might not touch the body of the belly alone and unmixed.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing

n: K7.867-869 gives the pain ('heaviness with pain' in the belly) and repeated coldness of the extremities.

s: Healthy people purge with dizziness, griping and exhaustion because the drug, lacking its proper humour, melts blood and flesh to draw it.
q: the cathartic drug strives to draw the humour proper to it, and, being at a loss for it, melts down the blood and the flesh
n: Attractive (selective) theory of purgatives, argued at length in De purgantium medicamentorum facultate.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Abbreviated Greek 'ἀπιότ. καὶ ἀχειρόπ.' left in the draft
s: The draft carries untranslated abbreviated Greek in the description of the Parian's irregular illness.
q: often made many changes (ἀπιότ. καὶ ἀχειρόπ.) towards the opposite conditions
n: The Kühn text itself is abbreviated here; the words are probably forms of ἀπιστότερον/ἀχειροποίητον or similar, and the rendering is a guess.

wt: On Coma according to Hippocrates
t: Odd rendering 'incoherently (χωρίς) and in a knavish manner'
s: The draft renders χωρὶς and πανούργως in a description of lethargics in a way that reads oddly.
q: For neither do they say anything incoherently (χωρίς) and in a knavish manner (πανούργως)
n: The Greek appears corrupt (χωρὶς φράζουσι ... πανούργως); 'knavish' for πανούργως is doubtful here.

wt: On the Shoulder Dislocated in Ways Hippocrates Did Not See
t: Corrupt phrase in bandaging lemma: οἵη ἑκάστῳ εἴη χωρίου
s: The draft marks the phrase οἵη ἑκάστῳ εἴη χωρίου as corrupt and guesses the sense 'farthest from the place the head slipped into'.
q: for in this way it would be (as it seems, 'farthest' from—the text οἵη ἑκάστῳ εἴη χωρίου is corrupt) the place into which the head of the shoulder slipped.
n: Compare the Hippocratic text of De articulis 11 (ἑκαστάτω, 'farthest'), which supports the draft's guess.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: 'Rough arteries' is a mistranslation: the windpipe and bronchi
s: Throughout the work the draft renders τραχεῖαι ἀρτηρίαι as 'rough arteries'. In Galen the phrase means the windpipe and its branches in the lung, the air passages.
q: when viscous and thick humours collect in the rough arteries in the lung
n: Known mis-rendering, recorded once for the whole work; read 'bronchi/air-passages' wherever 'rough arteries' appears. The 'smooth arteries' (K7.801) are ordinary arteries.

wt: On Difficulty of Breathing
t: 'Hippocrates used baths over the head' in Meton's case
s: The draft says Hippocrates 'used baths over the head', followed by a quotation about repeated nosebleeds after the crisis. The Greek says this literally, but it fits the argument poorly.
q: whence Hippocrates used baths over the head, saying, 'he bled from the nose often after the crisis.'
n: The Greek may be corrupt, or a fragment of the Epidemics lemma may be misplaced. Check against Epid. I (Meton) and the critical apparatus.

wt: On Leeches, Revulsion, Cupping, Incision and Scarification
t: Acrid drugs applied to the 'kolpoi'
s: The draft leaves κόλποις untranslated ('kolpoi'): acrid drugs applied there draw humours back from head and viscera.
q: Acrid drugs, too, applied to the kolpoi
n: κόλποι is ambiguous (hollows, folds, sinuses, possibly the vagina/womb in gynaecological usage); the referent here is unclear and needs a specialist reading.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Akraton ('unmixed') in the Greek; draft renders 'of no avail'
s: The Greek says melikraton's slight cleansing power is ἄκρατον ('unmixed'), which makes no sense. The draft silently renders 'of no avail', as if reading ἄπρακτον.
q: This slight smegmatic quality of melikraton, then, is of no avail (ἄκρατον) not because it is smegmatic, but because it is slight
n: The text is probably corrupt (ἄπρακτον or ἀχρεῖον?). The draft's rendering is reasonable but unsignalled.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: 'Work of swiftness' in peristalsis passage looks corrupt
s: The draft says it is 'the work of swiftness' to thrust contents away. This does not fit the argument about the direction of peristaltic movement.
q: and it is the work of swiftness (ταχύτητος) to thrust away the contents from those parts in which they are contained
n: Perhaps the text should read something like 'of the contraction' (συστολῆς?). The draft keeps the transmitted word literally.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: 'Meta tēn kephalēn' rendered 'in the region of the head'
s: The draft renders μετὰ τὴν κεφαλήν as 'in the region of the head'. With the accusative μετά normally means 'after', so κατὰ τὴν κεφαλήν is probably the right reading.
q: which either has its local origin in the region of the head (μετὰ τὴν κεφαλὴν), or is carried up from below
n: The draft translates the sense correctly, but the text needs emending.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Even days called 'odd' (perittai) in the critical-days list
s: The draft says the 20th, 34th and 40th days 'too are odd', which is arithmetically false. The 14th also stands in a list of 'odd' days.
q: Intermediate between these are the 20th and 34th and 40th, and these too are odd.
n: περιττός may mean 'remarkable or powerful' here rather than 'odd-numbered', or the numerals are corrupt. The draft's 'odd' should be checked.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' Regimen in Acute Diseases, Books II–IV
t: Garbled clause on grass-eating animals in the goat-meat passage
s: The draft's 'even as (καθάπερ) the grass-eating animals are bad' breaks the argument about why goat meat is best in summer. The sentence looks corrupt or mistranslated.
q: even as (καθάπερ) the grass-eating animals are bad, because they no longer have the grass green
n: The intended contrast is probably that grazers are worse in summer when the grass dries, while goats are better.

wt: Commentary on Hippocrates' (or Polybus') Regimen in Health for Private Persons
t: Suspected copyist error: 'not very cold' wine
s: Galen thinks the text bidding 'not very cold' wine may be a copyist's error, since cold wine tightens the body and the author wants to relax it. The draft's account of the intended correction ('not at all hot' / 'not too cold') is confused.
q: Perhaps, then, it was written otherwise, and the one who copied it erred; for many such things are seen happening even now
n: The Greek reads δέον ἀντὶ τοῦ μήθ᾿ ὅλως θερμὸν αὐτὸν γράψαι, μὴ λίαν ψυχρόν; which of the two phrases is the transmitted reading and which the proposed one is ambiguous, and the draft's order may be inverted. The next sentence, on very hot wine also tightening the stomach, needs checking against this.

wt: On the Power of Purgative Drugs
t: 'When his belly had become fixed' in the poisoner story
s: The draft renders πηξάσης τῆς γαστρός literally as the belly 'becoming fixed', the reason the man set the liver down.
q: when his belly had become fixed (πηξάσης τῆς γαστρός), he set it down upon a plant
n: The sense is unclear: possibly a sudden call of nature, a cramp, or a textual problem. Literal rendering leaves the narrative opaque.

wt: Whom to Purge, with Which Cathartic Drugs, and When
t: 'Narrow' thorax rests on a corrupt στέρνον ἔχοντε
s: The draft renders 'narrow' though the Greek reads στέρνον ἔχοντε ('having a chest'), which makes no sense as it stands.
q: Those who have a narrow (στέρνον ἔχοντε) thorax
n: Probably a corruption of στενὸν ἔχοντες ('having narrow'); the dual ἔχοντε is also odd. The draft's sense is likely right, but it is an emendation.
